abstract: learning representations during Rumelhart (1987). has proposed a method for choosing minimal or "simple" in Back-propagation networks. This approach can be used to (a) dynamically select the number of hidden units. (b) construct a representation that is appropriate for the problem and (c) thus improve the generalization ability of Back-propagation networks. The method Rumelhart suggests involves adding penalty terms to the usual error function. In this paper we introduce Rumelhart·s minimal networks idea and compare two possible biases on the weight search space. These biases are compared in both simple counting problems and a speech recognition problem. In general. the constrained search does seem to minimize the number of hidden units required with an expected increase in local minima.

paragraphs: This paper examines how backpropagation can be encouraged to construct simpler networks while learning a task. It builds on a proposal to add penalty terms to the usual training error. Those penalties bias the search toward simpler representations and can help determine how many hidden units are needed.

The authors compare two such biases on simple counting tasks and a speech recognition problem. The underlying aim is to let training shape both the solution and its internal representation. A network that needs fewer hidden units may express the problem more compactly, which motivates the proposed connection to improved generalization.

The reported result is that constrained search generally appears to reduce the number of hidden units required. It also brings an expected increase in local minima, creating more opportunities for training to settle into locally favorable solutions. The comparison therefore identifies a tradeoff within the learning objective: encouraging simplicity can produce smaller representations while making the search for a satisfactory set of weights more difficult.
summary.tldr: Penalties favoring simpler networks reduce required hidden units in the reported tasks but increase the prevalence of local minima.

title: Comparing Biases for Minimal Network Construction with Back-Propagation

abstract: In a multi-layered neural network, anyone of the hidden layers can be viewed as computing a distributed representation of the input. Several "encoder" experiments have shown that when the representation space is small it can be fully used. But computing with such a representation requires completely dependable nodes. In the case where the hidden nodes are noisy and unreliable, we find that error correcting schemes emerge simply by using noisy units during training; random errors in(cid:173) jected during backpropagation result in spreading representations apart. Average and minimum distances increase with misfire probability, as predicted by coding-theoretic considerations. Furthennore, the effect of this noise is to protect the machine against permanent node failure, thereby potentially extending the useful lifetime of the machine.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a neural network can represent inputs reliably when its hidden units are unreliable. A hidden layer provides a distributed representation, with information spread across its units. Using a small representation space fully can be efficient, but it also makes dependable operation important because errors can confuse nearby representations.

The authors inject random errors into hidden units during backpropagation training. Error-correcting representations emerge from this procedure: the learned representations move farther apart. Both average and minimum distances increase as the probability of a unit misfiring rises, consistent with coding-theoretic expectations. The network therefore adapts its internal organization to the unreliability encountered while learning.

The resulting protection also extends to permanent node failure. This is significant because temporary noise during training produces representations that remain useful under a different form of damage. The abstract presents a potential extension of machine lifetime as an implication of this robustness. The central finding is that error tolerance can emerge through the training conditions themselves.
summary.tldr: Training with unreliable hidden units spreads representations apart, producing error-correcting behavior and resistance to permanent node failure.

title: Nets with Unreliable Hidden Nodes Learn Error-Correcting Codes

abstract: We have analyzed the relationship between correlated spike count and the peak in the cross-correlation of spike trains for pairs of si(cid:173) multaneously recorded neurons from a previous study of area MT in the macaque monkey (Zohary et al., 1994). We conclude that common input, responsible for creating peaks on the order of ten milliseconds wide in the spike train cross-correlograms (CCGs), is also responsible for creating the correlation in spike count ob(cid:173) served at the two second time scale of the trial. We argue that both common excitation and inhibition may play significant roles in establishing this correlation.

paragraphs: Neurons can show related activity at different time scales. Their spikes may occur close together in time, and their total spike counts over an entire trial may also vary together. This paper examines the connection between these two observations using pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons from a previous study of macaque visual area MT.

The analysis relates correlations in trial-level spike counts to peaks in cross-correlograms, which describe the timing relationship between two spike trains. The peaks have widths on the order of ten milliseconds, whereas the spike counts cover two-second trials. The question is whether a shared source can account for correlations observed across these very different windows.

The authors conclude that common input responsible for the short-time peaks also produces the correlations in whole-trial spike counts. They argue that shared excitation and shared inhibition can both contribute. The result connects fine temporal coordination with slower count variability, giving the two measurements a common mechanistic interpretation in these recordings.
summary.tldr: Shared input links millisecond-scale spike coordination to correlations in neuronal spike counts over two-second trials.

title: Correlated Neuronal Response: Time Scales and Mechanisms

abstract: In nature, animals encounter high dimensional sensory stimuli that have complex statistical and dynamical structure. Attempts to study the neu- ral coding of these natural signals face challenges both in the selection of the signal ensemble and in the analysis of the resulting neural responses. For zebra ﬁnches, naturalistic stimuli can be deﬁned as sounds that they encounter in a colony of conspeciﬁc birds. We assembled an ensemble of these sounds by recording groups of 10-40 zebra ﬁnches, and then ana- lyzed the response of single neurons in the songbird central auditory area (ﬁeld L) to continuous playback of long segments from this ensemble. Following methods developed in the ﬂy visual system, we measured the information that spike trains provide about the acoustic stimulus with- out any assumptions about which features of the stimulus are relevant. Preliminary results indicate that large amounts of information are carried by spike timing, with roughly half of the information accessible only at time resolutions better than 10 ms; additional information is still be- ing revealed as time resolution is improved to 2 ms. Information can be decomposed into that carried by the locking of individual spikes to the stimulus (or modulations of spike rate) vs. that carried by timing in spike patterns. Initial results show that in ﬁeld L, temporal patterns give at least  % extra information. Thus, single central auditory neurons can pro- vide an informative representation of naturalistic sounds, in which spike timing may play a signiﬁcant role.

paragraphs: The researchers study how individual auditory neurons encode sounds resembling those zebra finches encounter in a colony. They recorded groups of 10–40 birds and played long, continuous segments of those recordings while measuring single-neuron responses in field L, a central auditory area.

Their information analysis measures what spike trains reveal about the sound without first specifying which acoustic features matter. Preliminary results suggest that roughly half the available information requires timing resolution finer than 10 milliseconds. Additional information continues to emerge when resolution improves to 2 milliseconds. This indicates that coarse descriptions of neural activity can miss substantial information in these responses.

The analysis also distinguishes information associated with individual spikes aligning to the stimulus from information carried by temporal patterns of spikes. Initial results indicate that patterns contribute extra information, although the percentage in the supplied abstract is unreadable. Overall, the preliminary findings support the possibility that precise spike timing plays a significant role in single neurons’ representations of naturalistic sounds.
summary.tldr: Preliminary songbird recordings suggest that precise spike timing carries substantial information about naturalistic colony sounds.

title: Spike timing and the coding of naturalistic sounds in a central auditory area of songbirds

abstract: There has been substantial progress in the past decade in the development of object classifiers for images, for example of faces, humans and vehicles. Here we address the problem of contaminations (e.g. occlusion, shadows) in test images which have not explicitly been encountered in training data. The Variational Ising Classifier (VIC) algorithm models contamination as a mask (a field of binary variables) with a strong spatial coherence prior. Variational inference is used to marginalize over contamination and obtain robust classification. In this way the VIC approach can turn a kernel classifier for clean data into one that can tolerate contamination, without any specific training on contaminated positives.

paragraphs: The paper addresses image classification when test images contain disruptions such as shadows or occlusion that were not explicitly encountered during training. A classifier trained on clean examples must still identify the object despite the affected image regions. The proposed Variational Ising Classifier treats the location of contamination as an unknown part of the inference problem.

It represents contamination with a mask of binary variables and a strong spatial coherence prior. This prior expresses a preference for contamination that forms spatially related regions. The mask therefore models structure in the disruption, rather than treating each affected image location as unrelated to its neighbors.

Variational inference is used to marginalize over contamination, accounting approximately for uncertainty about the mask during classification. The resulting approach can adapt a kernel classifier for clean data to tolerate contamination without specific training on contaminated positive examples. Its key contribution is to put a structured model of test-image disruption into inference, allowing the clean-data classifier to be used under the modeled form of contamination.
summary.tldr: VIC uses a spatially coherent contamination mask and variational inference to make clean-data kernel classifiers tolerate disrupted test images.

title: The Variational Ising Classifier (VIC) Algorithm for Coherently Contaminated Data

abstract: Under natural viewing conditions, small movements of the eye and body prevent the maintenance of a steady direction of gaze. It is known that stimuli tend to fade when they are stabilized on the retina for several sec- onds. However, it is unclear whether the physiological self-motion of the retinal image serves a visual purpose during the brief periods of natural visual ﬁxation. This study examines the impact of ﬁxational instability on the statistics of visual input to the retina and on the structure of neural activity in the early visual system. Fixational instability introduces ﬂuc- tuations in the retinal input signals that, in the presence of natural images, lack spatial correlations. These input ﬂuctuations strongly inﬂuence neu- ral activity in a model of the LGN. They decorrelate cell responses, even if the contrast sensitivity functions of simulated cells are not perfectly tuned to counter-balance the power-law spectrum of natural images. A decorrelation of neural activity has been proposed to be beneﬁcial for discarding statistical redundancies in the input signals. Fixational insta- bility might, therefore, contribute to establishing efﬁcient representations of natural stimuli.

paragraphs: Even during fixation, small eye and body movements keep the retinal image from remaining perfectly still. Although prolonged retinal stabilization is known to make stimuli fade, this paper asks whether ordinary fixation movements serve a visual purpose over much shorter viewing periods. It examines their effects on retinal input statistics and modeled early visual activity.

With natural images, fixation instability introduces input fluctuations that lack spatial correlations. In a model of the lateral geniculate nucleus, these fluctuations strongly affect neural responses and reduce correlations between cells. This happens even when the simulated cells' contrast sensitivity is not perfectly matched to counteract the power-law spectrum of natural images.

Reduced response correlation has been proposed as a way to discard statistical redundancy in visual input. On that basis, the authors suggest that fixation instability might help establish efficient representations of natural scenes. The modeled decorrelation is the reported result; improved coding efficiency is its proposed interpretation. This makes small gaze movements a possible contributor to visual encoding during natural fixation.
summary.tldr: Small fixation movements decorrelate responses in an early-vision model and may help reduce redundancy in natural-image encoding.

title: Visual Encoding with Jittering Eyes

abstract: There have been many graph-based approaches for semi-supervised clas- siﬁcation. One problem is that of hyperparameter learning: performance depends greatly on the hyperparameters of the similarity graph, trans- formation of the graph Laplacian and the noise model. We present a Bayesian framework for learning hyperparameters for graph-based semi- supervised classiﬁcation. Given some labeled data, which can contain inaccurate labels, we pose the semi-supervised classiﬁcation as an in- ference problem over the unknown labels. Expectation Propagation is used for approximate inference and the mean of the posterior is used for classiﬁcation. The hyperparameters are learned using EM for evidence maximization. We also show that the posterior mean can be written in terms of the kernel matrix, providing a Bayesian classiﬁer to classify new points. Tests on synthetic and real datasets show cases where there are signiﬁcant improvements in performance over the existing approaches.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised classification depends strongly on how its similarity graph, graph Laplacian transformation, and noise model are configured. This paper develops a Bayesian framework for learning those hyperparameters. It treats the unknown labels as quantities to infer from available labeled data, including labels that may be inaccurate.

The method uses Expectation Propagation for approximate inference and classifies using the posterior mean. Hyperparameters are learned through expectation maximization aimed at maximizing model evidence. These steps connect label inference with selection of the settings that govern the graph-based model, addressing choices that can strongly influence classification performance.

The authors also show that the posterior mean can be expressed using a kernel matrix. This provides a Bayesian classifier for new points, extending the usefulness of the inferred model beyond the unknown labels initially considered. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show cases of significant improvement over existing approaches. The evidence supports gains in those cases, alongside a framework for learning several influential model settings.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework learns graph-based classification hyperparameters, accommodates inaccurate labels, and provides a kernel-based classifier for new points.

title: Hyperparameter and Kernel Learning for Graph Based Semi-Supervised Classification

abstract: We show how improved sequences for magnetic resonance imaging can be found through automated optimization of Bayesian design scores. Combining recent advances in approximate Bayesian inference and natural image statistics with high-performance numerical computation, we propose the first scalable Bayesian experimental design framework for this problem of high relevance to clinical and brain research. Our solution requires approximate inference for dense, non-Gaussian models on a scale seldom addressed before. We propose a novel scalable variational inference algorithm, and show how powerful methods of numerical mathematics can be modified to compute primitives in our framework. Our approach is evaluated on a realistic setup with raw data from a 3T MR scanner.

Our approach is evaluated on a realistic setup with raw data from a 3T MR scanner.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to choose magnetic resonance imaging sequences through automated statistical design. The authors optimize Bayesian design scores to find improved sequences, bringing the choice of measurements into a computational framework. Their approach combines approximate Bayesian inference, statistical knowledge about natural images, and high-performance numerical computation.

A major obstacle is the scale of the inference problem. The models are dense and non-Gaussian, so the framework must handle extensive interactions without relying on a simple Gaussian description. The authors introduce a scalable variational inference algorithm and adapt numerical methods to calculate the basic quantities needed for design optimization. These computational contributions make the proposed design procedure feasible at the scale they study.

The framework is evaluated in a realistic setting using raw data from a 3T magnetic resonance scanner. That evaluation connects the statistical design approach to actual scanner measurements. The stated contribution is a scalable route to automated Bayesian sequence design, with potential relevance to clinical imaging and brain research through better choices of imaging sequences.
summary.tldr: The paper makes Bayesian optimization of MRI sequences scalable through new approximate inference and numerical computation methods.

title: Bayesian Experimental Design of Magnetic Resonance Imaging Sequences

abstract: We analyze the estimation of information theoretic measures of continuous random variables such as: differential entropy, mutual information or Kullback-Leibler divergence. The objective of this paper is two-fold. First, we prove that the information theoretic measure estimates using the k-nearest-neighbor density estimation with fixed k converge almost surely, even though the k-nearest-neighbor density estimation with fixed k does not converge to its true measure. Second, we show that the information theoretic measure estimates do not converge for k growing linearly with the number of samples. Nevertheless, these nonconvergent estimates can be used for solving the two-sample problem and assessing if two random variables are independent. We show that the two-sample and independence tests based on these nonconvergent estimates compare favorably with the maximum mean discrepancy test and the Hilbert Schmidt independence criterion, respectively.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate quantities such as differential entropy, mutual information, and Kullback-Leibler divergence from continuous data. It focuses on estimates built using nearest-neighbor density estimation. The central issue is how the number of neighbors, k, affects whether the resulting information-theoretic estimates approach the desired quantities as more samples become available.

For fixed k, the authors prove almost-sure convergence of the information-measure estimates even though the underlying density estimates do not themselves converge to the true density. This separates two questions that might otherwise seem inseparable: accurately estimating a whole distribution and accurately estimating a particular quantity derived from it. The latter can succeed under the studied construction despite failure of the former.

When k instead grows linearly with sample size, the information-measure estimates do not converge. Even so, the authors show that these estimates can support two-sample and independence testing. The resulting tests compare favorably with maximum mean discrepancy and the Hilbert Schmidt independence criterion, respectively. Thus, usefulness for a testing task can persist even when convergence as a numerical measure estimate fails.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor information estimates can converge despite inconsistent density estimates, and even nonconvergent variants can support useful statistical tests.

title: Estimation of Information Theoretic Measures for Continuous Random Variables

abstract: We present a new framework for semi-supervised learning with sparse eigenfunction bases of kernel matrices. It turns out that when the \emph{cluster assumption} holds, that is, when the high density regions are sufficiently separated by low density valleys, each high density area corresponds to a unique representative eigenvector. Linear combination of such eigenvectors (or, more precisely, of their Nystrom extensions) provide good candidates for good classification functions. By first choosing an appropriate basis of these eigenvectors from unlabeled data and then using labeled data with Lasso to select a classifier in the span of these eigenvectors, we obtain a classifier, which has a very sparse representation in this basis. Importantly, the sparsity appears naturally from the cluster assumption. Experimental results on a number of real-world data-sets show that our method is competitive with the state of the art semi-supervised learning algorithms and outperforms the natural base-line algorithm (Lasso in the Kernel PCA basis).

paragraphs: The paper uses unlabeled data to construct a compact set of functions for semi-supervised classification. Its foundation is the cluster assumption: high-density regions are sufficiently separated by low-density valleys. Under this condition, each dense region corresponds to a unique representative eigenvector of a kernel matrix.

The method first chooses an appropriate eigenvector basis from unlabeled examples. It then uses labeled examples and Lasso to select a classifier formed from those components. More precisely, the classification functions use Nyström extensions of the eigenvectors. The resulting classifier has a sparse representation, with sparsity arising naturally from the assumed cluster structure.

This separates two roles for the data: unlabeled observations reveal candidate structure, while labels determine how to combine that structure for prediction. Experiments on real-world datasets show performance competitive with leading semi-supervised methods and better than Lasso applied in a kernel PCA basis. The results support the value of choosing a basis that reflects separated clusters when that assumption is appropriate.
summary.tldr: Under a cluster assumption, unlabeled-data eigenfunctions provide a naturally sparse basis for classifiers selected with labeled data and Lasso.

title: Semi-supervised Learning using Sparse Eigenfunction Bases

abstract: Tensor completion from incomplete observations is a problem of significant practical interest. However, it is unlikely that there exists an efficient algorithm with provable guarantee to recover a general tensor from a limited number of observations. In this paper, we study the recovery algorithm for pairwise interaction tensors, which has recently gained considerable attention for modeling multiple attribute data due to its simplicity and effectiveness. Specifically, in the absence of noise, we show that one can exactly recover a pairwise interaction tensor by solving a constrained convex program which minimizes the weighted sum of nuclear norms of matrices from $O(nr\log^2(n))$ observations. For the noisy cases, we also prove error bounds for a constrained convex program for recovering the tensors. Our experiments on the synthetic dataset demonstrate that the recovery performance of our algorithm agrees well with the theory. In addition, we apply our algorithm on a temporal collaborative filtering task and obtain state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Tensor completion seeks to recover a multidimensional array from only some of its entries. The paper focuses on pairwise interaction tensors, a structured family used to model data with multiple attributes. This narrower setting is central: the authors describe efficient, guaranteed recovery of general tensors from limited observations as unlikely.

Their recovery method solves a constrained convex optimization problem that minimizes a weighted sum of matrix nuclear norms. In the noiseless setting, they prove exact recovery from O(nr log²(n)) observations. For noisy observations, they analyze a constrained convex program and establish error bounds, replacing exact reconstruction with a quantified statement about recovery accuracy.

Synthetic experiments show recovery behavior that agrees well with the theoretical analysis. The method also achieves state-of-the-art results on a temporal collaborative filtering task. Together, these findings connect a tractable optimization procedure with both recovery guarantees for the studied tensor family and evidence of usefulness in a recommendation setting involving time.
summary.tldr: A convex recovery method provides exact noiseless recovery and noisy error bounds for pairwise interaction tensors, with supporting experiments.

title: Exact and Stable Recovery of Pairwise Interaction Tensors

abstract: Neural population activity in cortical circuits is not solely driven by external inputs, but is also modulated by endogenous states which vary on multiple time-scales. To understand information processing in cortical circuits, we need to understand the statistical structure of internal states and their interaction with sensory inputs. Here, we present a statistical model for extracting hierarchically organised neural population states from multi-channel recordings of neural spiking activity. Population states are modelled using a hidden Markov decision tree with state-dependent tuning parameters and a generalised linear observation model. We present a variational Bayesian inference algorithm for estimating the posterior distribution over parameters from neural population recordings. On simulated data, we show that we can identify the underlying sequence of population states and reconstruct the ground truth parameters. Using population recordings from visual cortex, we find that a model with two levels of population states outperforms both a one-state and a two-state generalised linear model. Finally, we find that modelling of state-dependence also improves the accuracy with which sensory stimuli can be decoded from the population response.

paragraphs: A population of cortical neurons responds to sensory input while also being influenced by internal states that change over different timescales. This paper develops a statistical model for separating those influences in recordings of neural spikes. Its aim is to recover an organized hierarchy of population states and describe how those states affect responses to sensory input.

The model combines a hidden Markov decision tree with a generalized linear observation model. The tree represents the hierarchy of unobserved states, while state-dependent tuning parameters allow neural responses to vary with the current state. A variational Bayesian algorithm estimates a posterior distribution over the model parameters from recordings, rather than treating their values as known.

On simulated data, the method recovers state sequences and reconstructs the underlying parameters. In visual cortex recordings, a model with two hierarchical levels outperforms both one-state and two-state generalized linear models. Accounting for state dependence also improves sensory decoding, suggesting that internal population states contain information relevant to interpreting neural responses.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model recovers internal neural population states and improves sensory decoding by accounting for state-dependent responses.

title: A Bayesian model for identifying hierarchically organised states in neural population activity

abstract: Despite the success of kernel-based nonparametric methods, kernel selection still requires considerable expertise, and is often described as a “black art.” We present a sophisticated method for automatically searching for an appropriate kernel from an infinite space of potential choices. Previous efforts in this direction have focused on traversing a kernel grammar, only examining the data via computation of marginal likelihood. Our proposed search method is based on Bayesian optimization in model space, where we reason about model evidence as a function to be maximized. We explicitly reason about the data distribution and how it induces similarity between potential model choices in terms of the explanations they can offer for observed data. In this light, we construct a novel kernel between models to explain a given dataset. Our method is capable of finding a model that explains a given dataset well without any human assistance, often with fewer computations of model evidence than previous approaches, a claim we demonstrate empirically.
originalAbstract: Despite the success of kernel-based nonparametric methods, kernel selection still requires considerable expertise, and is often described as a “black art.” We present a sophisticated method for automatically searching for an appropriate kernel from an infinite space of potential choices. Previous efforts in this direction have focused on traversing a kernel grammar, only examining the data via computation of marginal likelihood. Our proposed search method is based on Bayesian optimization in model space, where we reason about model evidence as a function to be maximized. We explicitly reason about the data distribution and how it induces similarity between potential model choices in terms of the explanations they can offer for observed data. In this light, we construct a novel kernel between models to explain a given dataset. Our method is capable of finding a model that explains a given dataset well without any human assistance, often with fewer computations of model evidence than previous approaches, a claim we demonstrate empirically.

paragraphs: Kernel selection determines which kinds of explanations a kernel-based model can express, but choosing a suitable kernel often requires expertise. This paper treats that choice as an optimization problem over an infinite collection of possible kernels. The target is model evidence: a measure of how well a candidate model explains the observed data.

The proposed method applies Bayesian optimization directly in model space. Its central ingredient is a new kernel between models, which describes how similar their explanations of a particular dataset are. This similarity takes the data distribution into account. It gives the search a way to relate candidate models beyond simply traversing a grammar and evaluating each candidate’s evidence.

The authors empirically demonstrate that the method can find a model that explains a dataset well without human assistance, often requiring fewer evidence calculations than earlier approaches. The contribution is therefore both automated selection and a more informed search strategy. The reported computational advantage is an empirical tendency, rather than a guarantee that every dataset requires fewer evaluations.
summary.tldr: Bayesian optimization searches for suitable kernels by learning how candidate models offer similar explanations of the observed data.

title: Bayesian optimization for automated model selection

abstract: We propose a novel approach to reduce the computational cost of evaluation of convolutional neural networks, a factor that has hindered their deployment in low-power devices such as mobile phones. Inspired by the loop perforation technique from source code optimization, we speed up the bottleneck convolutional layers by skipping their evaluation in some of the spatial positions. We propose and analyze several strategies of choosing these positions. We demonstrate that perforation can accelerate modern convolutional networks such as AlexNet and VGG-16 by a factor of 2x - 4x. Additionally, we show that perforation is complementary to the recently proposed acceleration method of Zhang et al.

paragraphs: The paper targets the computational cost of evaluating convolutional neural networks, a barrier to using them on low-power devices such as phones. Its central idea is to reduce work inside the convolutional layers that dominate computation. Rather than evaluating a convolution at every spatial position, the method skips selected positions.

This approach draws inspiration from loop perforation in source-code optimization, where some repeated computations are omitted. Applied to convolutional networks, the important design choice becomes which spatial evaluations to leave out. The authors propose and analyze several selection strategies, making the placement of skipped computations an explicit part of the acceleration method.

Experiments demonstrate acceleration factors of two to four for networks including AlexNet and VGG-16. The paper also finds that perforation complements an existing acceleration approach by Zhang and colleagues. These findings establish spatially selective evaluation as a useful source of computational savings in the tested networks. The reported speedups concern network evaluation and should be understood as demonstrated results, rather than a guaranteed factor for every architecture or deployment.
summary.tldr: Skipping selected spatial convolution evaluations accelerates tested networks such as AlexNet and VGG-16 by factors of two to four.

title: PerforatedCNNs: Acceleration through Elimination of Redundant Convolutions

abstract: The recently proposed Temporal Ensembling has achieved state-of-the-art results in several semi-supervised learning benchmarks. It maintains an exponential moving average of label predictions on each training example, and penalizes predictions that are inconsistent with this target. However, because the targets change only once per epoch, Temporal Ensembling becomes unwieldy when learning large datasets. To overcome this problem, we propose Mean Teacher, a method that averages model weights instead of label predictions. As an additional benefit, Mean Teacher improves test accuracy and enables training with fewer labels than Temporal Ensembling. Without changing the network architecture, Mean Teacher achieves an error rate of 4.35% on SVHN with 250 labels, outperforming Temporal Ensembling trained with 1000 labels. We also show that a good network architecture is crucial to performance. Combining Mean Teacher and Residual Networks, we improve the state of the art on CIFAR-10 with 4000 labels from 10.55% to 6.28%, and on ImageNet 2012 with 10% of the labels from 35.24% to 9.11%.

Temporal Ensembling forms these targets by averaging past predictions for each training example, but updates them only once per epoch. This paper introduces Mean Teacher, which averages model weights instead, addressing the difficulty of using slowly refreshed prediction targets on large datasets.

The authors report improved test accuracy and a reduced need for labels compared with Temporal Ensembling. Without changing the network architecture, Mean Teacher reaches 4.35% error on SVHN using 250 labels, outperforming Temporal Ensembling trained with 1,000 labels. This comparison demonstrates the benefit of the training method under the reported experimental conditions.

The paper also finds that architecture remains crucial. Together, the results show gains from weight-averaged consistency targets and further gains from pairing the method with a strong architecture.
summary.tldr: Mean Teacher averages model weights to form consistency targets, improving semi-supervised accuracy and label efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Mean teachers are better role models: Weight-averaged consistency targets improve semi-supervised deep learning results

abstract: We propose a generic algorithmic building block to accelerate training of machine learning models on heterogeneous compute systems. Our scheme allows to efficiently employ compute accelerators such as GPUs and FPGAs for the training of large-scale machine learning models, when the training data exceeds their memory capacity. Also, it provides adaptivity to any system's memory hierarchy in terms of size and processing speed. Our technique is built upon novel theoretical insights regarding primal-dual coordinate methods, and uses duality gap information to dynamically decide which part of the data should be made available for fast processing. To illustrate the power of our approach we demonstrate its performance for training of generalized linear models on a large-scale dataset exceeding the memory size of a modern GPU, showing an order-of-magnitude speedup over existing approaches.

paragraphs: Fast accelerators are useful for training models, but their memory may be too small to hold the training dataset. This paper proposes an algorithmic building block for heterogeneous systems, where devices have different storage capacities and processing speeds. Its aim is to make effective use of accelerators such as GPUs and FPGAs even when the data exceed their memory.

The method uses theoretical insights from primal-dual coordinate optimization to decide dynamically which data should be available for fast processing. Its selection signal comes from duality-gap information, connecting data placement to the optimization problem. Instead of treating memory management as separate from learning, the scheme uses information from learning to guide access to limited fast memory.

The approach is designed to adapt to the sizes and speeds within a system's memory hierarchy. In a demonstration involving generalized linear models and a dataset larger than the GPU's memory, the authors report an order-of-magnitude speedup over existing approaches. This result illustrates how optimization-aware data selection can improve training without requiring the full dataset to fit on the accelerator.
summary.tldr: Using duality-gap information to select data for fast memory accelerates linear-model training when datasets exceed accelerator capacity.

title: Efficient Use of Limited-Memory Accelerators for Linear Learning on Heterogeneous Systems

abstract: An increasing need of running Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models on mobile devices with limited computing power and memory resource encourages studies on efficient model design. A number of efficient architectures have been proposed in recent years, for example, MobileNet, ShuffleNet, and MobileNetV2. However, all these models are heavily dependent on depthwise separable convolution which lacks efficient implementation in most deep learning frameworks. In this study, we propose an efficient architecture named PeleeNet, which is built with conventional convolution instead. On ImageNet ILSVRC 2012 dataset, our proposed PeleeNet achieves a higher accuracy and 1.8 times faster speed than MobileNet and MobileNetV2 on NVIDIA TX2. Meanwhile, PeleeNet is only 66% of the model size of MobileNet. We then propose a real-time object detection system by combining PeleeNet with Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD) method and optimizing the architecture for fast speed. Our proposed detection system, named Pelee, achieves 76.4% mAP (mean average precision) on PASCAL VOC2007 and 22.4 mAP on MS COCO dataset at the speed of 23.6 FPS on iPhone 8 and 125 FPS on NVIDIA TX2. The result on COCO outperforms YOLOv2 in consideration of a higher precision, 13.6 times lower computational cost and 11.3 times smaller model size. The code and models are open sourced.

On COCO, it exceeds YOLOv2's precision while using 13.6-times lower computational cost and an 11.3-times smaller model. These results connect architecture choices to measured efficiency on the specified devices.
summary.tldr: Pelee combines a conventional-convolution backbone with an optimized SSD detector to deliver accurate, real-time detection on the tested mobile hardware.

title: Pelee: A Real-Time Object Detection System on Mobile Devices

abstract: Intelligent behaviour in the real-world requires the ability to acquire new knowledge from an ongoing sequence of experiences while preserving and reusing past knowledge. We propose a novel algorithm for unsupervised representation learning from piece-wise stationary visual data: Variational Autoencoder with Shared Embeddings (VASE). Based on the Minimum Description Length principle, VASE automatically detects shifts in the data distribution and allocates spare representational capacity to new knowledge, while simultaneously protecting previously learnt representations from catastrophic forgetting. Our approach encourages the learnt representations to be disentangled, which imparts a number of desirable properties: VASE can deal sensibly with ambiguous inputs, it can enhance its own representations through imagination-based exploration, and most importantly, it exhibits semantically meaningful sharing of latents between different datasets. Compared to baselines with entangled representations, our approach is able to reason beyond surface-level statistics and perform semantically meaningful cross-domain inference.

paragraphs: A system learning continuously must incorporate new experiences while preserving useful earlier knowledge. VASE, a variational autoencoder with shared embeddings, addresses this problem through unsupervised learning from visual data. Its setting is piecewise stationary: the data distribution remains stable for stretches of experience and then changes.

Using the Minimum Description Length principle, VASE automatically detects distribution shifts and assigns spare representational capacity to new knowledge. At the same time, it protects representations learned earlier from catastrophic forgetting. The approach encourages disentanglement, so different aspects of the data can receive more separable internal representations rather than becoming tightly mixed together.

The authors report several consequences of this organization. VASE handles ambiguous inputs sensibly, improves its representations through imagination-based exploration, and shares latent variables across datasets in semantically meaningful ways. Compared with baselines whose representations are entangled, it supports cross-domain inference beyond surface statistics. The contribution connects continual learning with reusable internal structure: preserving previous knowledge and discovering meaningful relationships between domains are treated as parts of the same representation-learning problem.
summary.tldr: VASE detects distribution shifts, preserves earlier representations, and shares meaningful latent structure across visual domains.

title: Life-Long Disentangled Representation Learning with Cross-Domain Latent Homologies

abstract: End-to-end deep-learning networks recently demonstrated extremely good performance for stereo matching. However, existing networks are difficult to use for practical applications since (1) they are memory-hungry and unable to process even modest-size images, (2) they have to be fully re-trained to handle a different disparity range. The Practical Deep Stereo (PDS) network that we propose addresses both issues: First, its architecture relies on novel bottleneck modules that drastically reduce the memory footprint in inference, and additional design choices allow to handle greater image size during training. This results in a model that leverages large image context to resolve matching ambiguities. Second, a novel sub-pixel cross-entropy loss combined with a MAP estimator make this network less sensitive to ambiguous matches, and applicable to any disparity range without re-training. We compare PDS to state-of-the-art methods published over the recent months, and demonstrate its superior performance on FlyingThings3D and KITTI sets.

paragraphs: Stereo matching finds corresponding image locations across two views. Deep networks perform well at this task, but large memory requirements can limit image size, and changing the supported disparity range can require complete retraining. Practical Deep Stereo, or PDS, addresses both obstacles to using these networks in applications.

The architecture introduces bottleneck modules that sharply reduce memory use during inference. Additional design choices allow larger images during training, giving the model access to wider image context when resolving ambiguous correspondences. The memory improvements therefore support a modeling benefit as well as making execution more practical.

PDS also combines a subpixel cross-entropy loss with a maximum-a-posteriori estimator. This combination makes matching less sensitive to ambiguity and allows the network to handle any disparity range without retraining, according to the abstract. Comparisons on FlyingThings3D and KITTI show superior performance against the contemporary methods evaluated. The paper’s contribution connects resource-efficient architecture and output estimation to both deployment flexibility and measured stereo-matching quality.
summary.tldr: PDS reduces stereo-network memory use and supports changing disparity ranges without retraining while improving performance on the evaluated datasets.

title: Practical Deep Stereo (PDS): Toward applications-friendly deep stereo matching

abstract: Introducing variability while maintaining coherence is a core task in learning to generate utterances in conversation. Standard neural encoder-decoder models and their extensions using conditional variational autoencoder often result in either trivial or digressive responses. To overcome this, we explore a novel approach that injects variability into neural encoder-decoder via the use of external memory as a mixture model, namely Variational Memory Encoder-Decoder (VMED). By associating each memory read with a mode in the latent mixture distribution at each timestep, our model can capture the variability observed in sequential data such as natural conversations. We empirically compare the proposed model against other recent approaches on various conversational datasets. The results show that VMED consistently achieves significant improvement over others in both metric-based and qualitative evaluations.

paragraphs: Generating conversational responses requires both variety and coherence. A system that produces little variation can give trivial replies, while poorly controlled variation can produce digressions. This paper introduces the Variational Memory Encoder-Decoder, or VMED, to address that tension by connecting variability in generation to an external memory.

The model uses the external memory as a mixture model. At each time step, each memory read is associated with a mode in a latent mixture distribution. This provides a structured way to represent different possibilities during sequence generation. The design is intended to capture the variability found in conversations while keeping that variability connected to the encoder-decoder's memory mechanism.

The authors compare VMED with other recent approaches on several conversational datasets. They report consistent, significant improvements in both metric-based evaluation and qualitative assessment. These complementary findings support the proposed memory-based treatment of variability in the evaluated dialogue tasks. The contribution is an architectural way to make diverse generation part of the model's evolving latent representation throughout a sequence.
summary.tldr: VMED links external memory reads to a latent mixture distribution, improving conversational generation in reported quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

title: Variational Memory Encoder-Decoder

abstract: Bayesian Optimisation (BO) refers to a class of methods for global optimisation of a function f which is only accessible via point evaluations. It is typically used in settings where f is expensive to evaluate. A common use case for BO in machine learning is model selection, where it is not possible to analytically model the generalisation performance of a statistical model, and we resort to noisy and expensive training and validation procedures to choose the best model. Conventional BO methods have focused on Euclidean and categorical domains, which, in the context of model selection, only permits tuning scalar hyper-parameters of machine learning algorithms. However, with the surge of interest in deep learning, there is an increasing demand to tune neural network architectures. In this work, we develop NASBOT, a Gaussian process based BO framework for neural architecture search. To accomplish this, we develop a distance metric in the space of neural network architectures which can be computed efficiently via an optimal transport program. This distance might be of independent interest to the deep learning community as it may find applications outside of BO. We demonstrate that NASBOT outperforms other alternatives for architecture search in several cross validation based model selection tasks on multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks.

paragraphs: Choosing a neural network architecture requires expensive training and validation evaluations. Bayesian optimization is designed for objectives accessible through such costly evaluations, but conventional approaches focus on Euclidean or categorical search spaces. Those formulations naturally accommodate scalar hyperparameters and make searching over network architectures a separate challenge.

NASBOT extends Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization to architecture search. Its central ingredient is a distance between neural network architectures that can be computed efficiently using an optimal transport program. Providing this notion of architectural similarity gives the optimization framework a way to work with networks as structured candidates in its search space.

The authors evaluate NASBOT on several model-selection tasks using cross-validation, covering multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks. They report that it outperforms the alternative architecture-search methods considered. The distance itself is also proposed as potentially useful beyond Bayesian optimization. That broader role is presented as a possible application, while the empirical findings concern the architecture-search tasks evaluated in the paper.
summary.tldr: NASBOT uses an optimal-transport distance between architectures to enable Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization of neural networks.

title: Neural Architecture Search with Bayesian Optimisation and Optimal Transport

abstract: We study a secretary problem which captures the task of ranking in online settings. We term this problem the secretary ranking problem: elements from an ordered set arrive in random order and instead of picking the maximum element, the algorithm is asked to assign a rank, or position, to each of the elements. The rank assigned is irrevocable and is given knowing only the pairwise comparisons with elements previously arrived. The goal is to minimize the distance of the rank produced to the true rank of the elements measured by the Kendall-Tau distance, which corresponds to the number of pairs that are inverted with respect to the true order. Our main result is a matching upper and lower bound for the secretary ranking problem. We present an algorithm that ranks n elements with only O(n^{3/2}) inversions in expectation, and show that any algorithm necessarily suffers \Omega(n^{3/2}) inversions when there are n available positions. In terms of techniques, the analysis of our algorithm draws connections to linear probing in the hashing literature, while our lower bound result relies on a general anti-concentration bound for a generic balls and bins sampling process. We also consider the case where the number of positions m can be larger than the number of secretaries n and provide an improved bound by showing a connection of this problem with random binary trees.

paragraphs: The secretary ranking problem asks an algorithm to place arriving elements into an ordering without revising earlier placements. Elements arrive in random order, and each decision uses only comparisons with elements already seen. Quality is measured by inversions: pairs whose assigned order disagrees with their true order.

For n elements and n available positions, the paper gives an algorithm with expected inversion count of order n raised to 3/2. It also proves a matching lower bound for any algorithm. Together, these results identify the optimal growth rate of ranking error under the stated information and irrevocability constraints.

The analysis connects the algorithm to linear probing in hashing, while the lower bound uses an anti-concentration result for a balls-and-bins sampling process. The authors also consider having more available positions than arriving elements and derive an improved bound through a connection with random binary trees. Thus, the work characterizes the standard setting and shows how additional placement space can improve the guarantee.
summary.tldr: Matching bounds show that irrevocably ranking n randomly arriving elements into n positions requires expected inversion error of order n to the 3/2.

title: Secretary Ranking with Minimal Inversions

abstract: We study the performance of the certainty equivalent controller on Linear Quadratic (LQ) control problems with unknown transition dynamics. We show that for both the fully and partially observed settings, the sub-optimality gap between the cost incurred by playing the certainty equivalent controller on the true system and the cost incurred by using the optimal LQ controller enjoys a fast statistical rate, scaling as the square of the parameter error. To the best of our knowledge, our result is the first sub-optimality guarantee in the partially observed Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) setting. Furthermore, in the fully observed Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR), our result improves upon recent work by Dean et al., who present an algorithm achieving a sub-optimality gap linear in the parameter error. A key part of our analysis relies on perturbation bounds for discrete Riccati equations. We provide two new perturbation bounds, one that expands on an existing result from Konstantinov, and another based on a new elementary proof strategy.

paragraphs: When a system's transition dynamics are unknown, a certainty equivalent controller uses estimated dynamics to design its actions as though those estimates were correct. This paper analyzes the performance cost of that approach in linear quadratic control, comparing the controller's cost on the true system with the cost achieved by the optimal controller.

The main result is that the suboptimality gap scales with the square of the parameter estimation error. This is a fast statistical rate: reducing estimation error yields a quadratic reduction in the corresponding bound. The analysis covers both fully observed systems and partially observed systems, where the controller does not directly observe the complete state.

For fully observed linear quadratic regulation, the result improves on a prior guarantee that scaled linearly with parameter error. The authors also report the first such suboptimality guarantee, to their knowledge, for partially observed linear quadratic Gaussian control. Two new perturbation bounds for discrete Riccati equations support the analysis by controlling how the relevant equations respond to changes in system parameters.
summary.tldr: Certainty equivalent linear quadratic controllers have a suboptimality gap that scales quadratically with parameter estimation error.

title: Certainty Equivalence is Efficient for Linear Quadratic Control

abstract: Artificial agents have been shown to learn to communicate when needed to complete a cooperative task. Some level of language structure (e.g., compositionality) has been found in the learned communication protocols. This observed structure is often the result of specific environmental pressures during training. By introducing new agents periodically to replace old ones, sequentially and within a population, we explore such a new pressure — ease of teaching — and show its impact on the structure of the resulting language.

paragraphs: Artificial agents can develop communication protocols when cooperation requires them to exchange information. Those protocols sometimes display language-like structure, including compositionality: the organization of messages from meaningful parts. This paper asks how the conditions under which agents learn to communicate influence the structure that eventually emerges.

The authors introduce ease of teaching as a training pressure. They periodically replace established agents with new ones, studying replacement both sequentially and within a population. This makes the arrival of inexperienced participants part of the communication setting. The intervention examines language development when communication must accommodate new learners as well as support the cooperative task.

The paper reports that this pressure affects the structure of the resulting language. Its contribution is to connect agent replacement with properties of learned communication protocols, extending the investigation of how training environments shape emergent language. The stated finding is an effect on structure; the abstract does not characterize that effect as a universal increase in compositionality. The study therefore focuses on teachability as a factor in language formation.
summary.tldr: Periodically introducing new agents creates an ease-of-teaching pressure that affects the structure of emergent communication.

title: Ease-of-Teaching and Language Structure from Emergent Communication

abstract: Abstraction reasoning is a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence. Recent studies suggest that many of the deep architectures that have triumphed over other domains failed to work well in abstract reasoning. In this paper, we first illustrate that one of the main challenges in such a reasoning task is the presence of distracting features, which requires the learning algorithm to leverage counter-evidence and to reject any of false hypothesis in order to learn the true patterns. We later show that carefully designed learning trajectory over different categories of training data can effectively boost learning performance by mitigating the impacts of distracting features. Inspired this fact, we propose feature robust abstract reasoning (FRAR) model, which consists of a reinforcement learning based teacher network to determine the sequence of training and a student network for predictions. Experimental results demonstrated strong improvements over baseline algorithms and we are able to beat the state-of-the-art models by 18.7\% in RAVEN dataset and 13.3\% in the PGM dataset.

paragraphs: Abstract reasoning requires identifying a pattern while ignoring features that happen to accompany it. This paper argues that distracting features are a major obstacle for deep learning systems on such tasks. Learning the relevant rule requires using counterexamples to reject plausible but incorrect hypotheses, rather than simply accumulating evidence for an initially attractive pattern.

The authors show that carefully arranging the progression through different training-data categories can reduce the effects of these distractions. They build on this observation with feature robust abstract reasoning, or FRAR. Its teacher network uses reinforcement learning to determine the training sequence, while a student network learns to make predictions.

The experiments report strong improvements over baseline algorithms, including improvements of 18.7% on RAVEN and 13.3% on PGM over the state-of-the-art models considered. These results support training order as a useful part of reasoning-system design. The contribution connects a specific learning obstacle—misleading features—to a mechanism for choosing the examples through which the student learns.
summary.tldr: FRAR uses a reinforcement-learning teacher to arrange training examples so a student can better learn abstract patterns despite distracting features.

title: Abstract Reasoning with Distracting Features

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNN) are an emerging field for learning on non-Euclidean data. Recently, there has been increased interest in designing GNN that scales to large graphs. Most existing methods use "graph sampling" or "layer-wise sampling" techniques to reduce training time; However, these methods still suffer from degrading performance and scalability problems when applying to graphs with billions of edges. In this paper, we present GBP, a scalable GNN that utilizes a localized bidirectional propagation process from both the feature vector and the training/testing nodes. Theoretical analysis shows that GBP is the first method that achieves sub-linear time complexity for both the precomputation and the training phases. An extensive empirical study demonstrates that GBP achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly less training/testing time. Most notably, GBP is able to deliver superior performance on a graph with over 60 million nodes and 1.8 billion edges in less than 2,000 seconds on a single machine.

Its central mechanism is localized bidirectional propagation, proceeding from both the feature vector and the nodes used for training or testing. The theoretical analysis establishes sublinear time complexity for both precomputation and training. The authors identify this combination of guarantees as a first, addressing preparation costs as well as the subsequent learning phase.

In the largest highlighted example, GBP delivers superior performance on a graph containing more than 60 million nodes and 1.8 billion edges in under 2,000 seconds on one machine. This demonstrates the practical scale reached by the method alongside its theoretical efficiency results.
summary.tldr: GBP uses localized bidirectional propagation to make graph neural network precomputation and training scalable to billion-edge graphs.

title: Scalable Graph Neural Networks via Bidirectional Propagation

abstract: We propose and study Collapsing Bandits, a new restless multi-armed bandit (RMAB) setting in which each arm follows a binary-state Markovian process with a special structure: when an arm is played, the state is fully observed, thus“collapsing” any uncertainty, but when an arm is passive, no observation is made, thus allowing uncertainty to evolve. The goal is to keep as many arms in the “good” state as possible by planning a limited budget of actions per round. Such CollapsingBandits are natural models for many healthcare domains in which health workers must simultaneously monitor patients and deliver interventions in a way that maximizes the health of their patient cohort. Our main contributions are as follows: (i) Building on the Whittle index technique for RMABs, we derive conditions under which the Collapsing Bandits problem is indexable. Our derivation hinges on novel conditions that characterize when the optimal policies may take the form of either“forward” or “reverse” threshold policies. (ii) We exploit the optimality of threshold policies to build fast algorithms for computing the Whittle index, including a closed-form. (iii) We evaluate our algorithm on several data distributions including data from a real-world healthcare task in which a worker must monitor and deliver interventions to maximize their patients’ adherence to tuberculosis medication. Our algorithm achieves a 3-order-of-magnitude speedup compared to state-of-the-art RMAB techniques, while achieving similar performance. The code is available at:https://github.com/AdityaMate/collapsing_bandits

Evaluations use several data distributions, including data concerning adherence to tuberculosis medication. The algorithm achieves a three-order-of-magnitude speedup over the compared RMAB techniques while maintaining similar performance. The contribution combines a model of observation-dependent uncertainty with conditional structural results that make intervention planning much faster in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Collapsing Bandits model actions that reveal hidden states and use threshold-policy structure to accelerate budgeted intervention planning.

title: Collapsing Bandits and Their Application to Public Health Intervention

abstract: Modern neural networks are often regarded as complex black-box functions whose behavior is difficult to understand owing to their nonlinear dependence on the data and the nonconvexity in their loss landscapes. In this work, we show that these common perceptions can be completely false in the early phase of learning. In particular, we formally prove that, for a class of well-behaved input distributions, the early-time learning dynamics of a two-layer fully-connected neural network can be mimicked by training a simple linear model on the inputs. We additionally argue that this surprising simplicity can persist in networks with more layers and with convolutional architecture, which we verify empirically. Key to our analysis is to bound the spectral norm of the difference between the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and an affine transform of the data kernel; however, unlike many previous results utilizing the NTK, we do not require the network to have disproportionately large width, and the network is allowed to escape the kernel regime later in training.

paragraphs: Neural networks are nonlinear models trained on nonconvex objectives, but those properties need not make every stage of learning equally complicated. This paper studies the beginning of training. For a class of well-behaved input distributions, it proves that training a simple linear model on the inputs can mimic the early learning dynamics of a two-layer fully connected network.

The analysis compares the Neural Tangent Kernel with an affine transformation of the data kernel and bounds their difference in spectral norm. This supplies a mathematical basis for the early linear approximation. Unlike many analyses using the Neural Tangent Kernel, the result does not require disproportionately wide networks.

The authors also argue that similar early simplicity can occur in deeper networks and convolutional architectures, and provide empirical verification of that extension. The time restriction is central: networks may leave the kernel regime later in training. The findings therefore describe an initially simple learning phase while allowing later behavior to develop beyond the approximation used to explain that phase.
summary.tldr: Under suitable input-distribution conditions, a linear model can mimic a two-layer network's early training dynamics without requiring extreme width.

title: The Surprising Simplicity of the Early-Time Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks

abstract: Numerous deep reinforcement learning agents have been proposed, and each of them has its strengths and flaws. In this work, we present a Cooperative Heterogeneous Deep Reinforcement Learning (CHDRL) framework that can learn a policy by integrating the advantages of heterogeneous agents. Specifically, we propose a cooperative learning framework that classifies heterogeneous agents into two classes: global agents and local agents. Global agents are off-policy agents that can utilize experiences from the other agents. Local agents are either on-policy agents or population-based evolutionary algorithms (EAs) agents that can explore the local area effectively. We employ global agents, which are sample-efficient, to guide the learning of local agents so that local agents can benefit from the sample-efficient agents and simultaneously maintain their advantages, e.g., stability. Global agents also benefit from effective local searches. Experimental studies on a range of continuous control tasks from the Mujoco benchmark show that CHDRL achieves better performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Different reinforcement learning methods have different strengths, so this paper explores whether agents using different methods can improve one another during training. Its Cooperative Heterogeneous Deep Reinforcement Learning framework organizes this collaboration around two roles: global agents that reuse experience and local agents that conduct effective local exploration.

Global agents use off-policy learning, allowing them to learn from experiences generated by other agents. Local agents use either on-policy learning or population-based evolutionary algorithms. The global agents guide local learning with their sample-efficient updates, while the local agents retain advantages such as stability. In return, useful local searches provide experience that benefits the global agents.

This arrangement makes cooperation a two-way exchange between learning approaches. The framework aims to combine economical use of experience with productive local exploration when learning a policy. Experiments on continuous-control tasks from the MuJoCo benchmark report better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered. The evidence supports the proposed combination on those tasks, without implying that every heterogeneous grouping will offer the same benefit.
summary.tldr: CHDRL combines experience-sharing global agents with locally exploring agents to improve performance on tested continuous-control tasks.

title: Cooperative Heterogeneous Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: When modeling dynamical systems from real-world data samples, the distribution of data often changes according to the environment in which they are captured, and the dynamics of the system itself vary from one environment to another. Generalizing across environments thus challenges the conventional frameworks. The classical settings suggest either considering data as i.i.d and learning a single model to cover all situations or learning environment-specific models. Both are sub-optimal: the former disregards the discrepancies between environments leading to biased solutions, while the latter does not exploit their potential commonalities and is prone to scarcity problems. We propose LEADS, a novel framework that leverages the commonalities and discrepancies among known environments to improve model generalization. This is achieved with a tailored training formulation aiming at capturing common dynamics within a shared model while additional terms capture environment-specific dynamics. We ground our approach in theory, exhibiting a decrease in sample complexity w.r.t classical alternatives. We show how theory and practice coincides on the simplified case of linear dynamics. Moreover, we instantiate this framework for neural networks and evaluate it experimentally on representative families of nonlinear dynamics. We show that this new setting can exploit knowledge extracted from environment-dependent data and improves generalization for both known and novel environments.

paragraphs: A dynamical system can behave differently depending on the environment where its data are collected. Learning one model across all environments can overlook those differences, while fitting separate models wastes shared information and can leave each model short of data. LEADS addresses this tension by explicitly representing both common and environment-specific dynamics.

Its training formulation combines a shared model with additional terms that capture how individual environments differ. The shared component gathers information useful across environments, while the additional components accommodate variation. This makes the distinction between common structure and local differences part of the learning problem instead of forcing either complete pooling or complete separation.

The authors provide theoretical results showing reduced sample complexity relative to classical alternatives and examine how theory matches practice for linear dynamics. They also implement the framework with neural networks and evaluate representative nonlinear systems. The reported results show improved generalization in both known and new environments. Together, these findings support using environmental variation as structured information that can help learning, rather than simply treating it as a source of inconsistency.
summary.tldr: LEADS separates shared and environment-specific dynamics to improve sample efficiency and generalization across environments.

title: LEADS: Learning Dynamical Systems that Generalize Across Environments

abstract: We analyze the meta-learning of the initialization and step-size of learning algorithms for piecewise-Lipschitz functions, a non-convex setting with applications to both machine learning and algorithms. Starting from recent regret bounds for the exponential forecaster on losses with dispersed discontinuities, we generalize them to be initialization-dependent and then use this result to propose a practical meta-learning procedure that learns both the initialization and the step-size of the algorithm from multiple online learning tasks. Asymptotically, we guarantee that the average regret across tasks scales with a natural notion of task-similarity that measures the amount of overlap between near-optimal regions of different tasks. Finally, we instantiate the method and its guarantee in two important settings: robust meta-learning and multi-task data-driven algorithm design.

paragraphs: The paper studies how experience across online learning tasks can improve an algorithm's initialization and step-size. Its setting involves non-convex, piecewise-Lipschitz functions, where controlled variation within pieces coexists with discontinuities. The goal is to learn useful algorithm settings across tasks while providing a theoretical account of when shared experience helps.

The authors begin with regret bounds for an exponential forecaster operating on losses with dispersed discontinuities. They extend those bounds to depend on initialization, making the starting point part of the analysis. This supports a practical meta-learning procedure that learns both initialization and step-size from multiple tasks, rather than treating those choices as fixed external settings.

Asymptotically, average regret across tasks scales with a notion of task similarity based on overlap between their near-optimal regions. The guarantee therefore connects transfer to shared regions of good solutions. The authors instantiate the procedure and its guarantee in robust meta-learning and multi-task data-driven algorithm design, demonstrating two concrete settings covered by the analysis.
summary.tldr: A meta-learning procedure learns initialization and step-size for non-convex online tasks, with regret guarantees tied to overlap among near-optimal regions.

title: Learning-to-learn non-convex piecewise-Lipschitz functions

abstract: In low-level vision such as single image super-resolution (SISR), traditional MSE or L_1 loss function treats every pixel equally with the assumption that the importance of all pixels is the same. However, it has been long recognized that texture and edge areas carry more important visual information than smooth areas in photographic images. How to achieve such spatial adaptation in a principled manner has been an open problem in both traditional model-based and modern learning-based approaches toward SISR. In this paper, we propose a new adaptive weighted loss for SISR to train deep networks focusing on challenging situations such as textured and edge pixels with high uncertainty. Specifically, we introduce variance estimation characterizing the uncertainty on a pixel-by-pixel basis into SISR solutions so the targeted pixels in a high-resolution image (mean) and their corresponding uncertainty (variance) can be learned simultaneously. Moreover, uncertainty estimation allows us to leverage conventional wisdom such as sparsity prior for regularizing SISR solutions. Ultimately, pixels with large certainty (e.g., texture and edge pixels) will be prioritized for SISR according to their importance to visual quality. For the first time, we demonstrate that such uncertainty-driven loss can achieve better results than MSE or L_1 loss for a wide range of network architectures. Experimental results on three popular SISR networks show that our proposed uncertainty-driven loss has achieved better PSNR performance than traditional loss functions without any increased computation during testing. The code is available at https://see.xidian.edu.cn/faculty/wsdong/Projects/UDL-SR.htm
