paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution reconstructs a higher-resolution image from one lower-resolution input. Standard mean-squared-error and ℓ1 losses weight pixels equally, even though edges and textures carry important visual information and can be difficult to reconstruct. This paper proposes spatially adaptive weighting based on estimated uncertainty.

The network learns both the target image values and a variance estimate for each pixel. Those variances characterize uncertainty and guide a weighted training loss toward challenging image regions. The uncertainty estimates also provide a way to incorporate a sparsity prior when regularizing the reconstruction. The method thus couples learning what each pixel should be with learning how uncertain its reconstruction is.

Experiments on three commonly used super-resolution networks report better PSNR than training with conventional losses. The improvement requires no additional computation during testing, because the reported benefit comes from the training loss. These results support uncertainty estimation as a practical mechanism for allocating training emphasis across an image, with gains demonstrated across the evaluated architectures rather than confined to one network design.
summary.tldr: A pixel-wise uncertainty-based training loss improves reported super-resolution PSNR across three networks without increasing test-time computation.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Loss for Single Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Recent unsupervised representation learning methods have shown to be effective in a range of vision tasks by learning representations invariant to data augmentations such as random cropping and color jittering. However, such invariance could be harmful to downstream tasks if they rely on the characteristics of the data augmentations, e.g., location- or color-sensitive. This is not an issue just for unsupervised learning; we found that this occurs even in supervised learning because it also learns to predict the same label for all augmented samples of an instance. To avoid such failures and obtain more generalizable representations, we suggest to optimize an auxiliary self-supervised loss, coined AugSelf, that learns the difference of augmentation parameters (e.g., cropping positions, color adjustment intensities) between two randomly augmented samples. Our intuition is that AugSelf encourages to preserve augmentation-aware information in learned representations, which could be beneficial for their transferability. Furthermore, AugSelf can easily be incorporated into recent state-of-the-art representation learning methods with a negligible additional training cost. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our simple idea consistently improves the transferability of representations learned by supervised and unsupervised methods in various transfer learning scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/hankook/AugSelf.

paragraphs: Representation learning often encourages different augmented versions of an image to receive similar representations. That can be helpful, but it may discard information needed for later tasks, particularly when position or color matters. The paper finds this issue in supervised learning as well, since augmented examples are typically assigned the same label.

The proposed AugSelf objective adds a self-supervised task: predict how the augmentation parameters differ between two randomly transformed versions of an image. Examples include differences in crop positions and color-adjustment intensities. Learning these differences encourages representations to retain information about transformations that an invariance-focused objective might otherwise suppress.

AugSelf can be added to existing representation-learning methods with negligible additional training cost. Across the reported transfer-learning experiments, it consistently improves the transferability of representations learned with both supervised and unsupervised methods. These results support preserving augmentation-related information as a useful complement to invariance when a representation must serve multiple downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: AugSelf improves representation transfer by adding a task that preserves information about differences between image augmentations.

title: Improving Transferability of Representations via Augmentation-Aware Self-Supervision

abstract: To build agents that can collaborate effectively with others, recent research has trained artificial agents to communicate with each other in Lewis-style referential games. However, this often leads to successful but uninterpretable communication. We argue that this is due to the game objective: communicating about a single object in a shared visual context is prone to overfitting and does not encourage language useful beyond concrete reference. In contrast, human language conveys a rich variety of abstract ideas. To promote such skills, we propose games that require communicating generalizations over sets of objects representing abstract visual concepts, optionally with separate contexts for each agent. We find that these games greatly improve systematicity and interpretability of the learned languages, according to several metrics in the literature. Finally, we propose a method for identifying logical operations embedded in the emergent languages by learning an approximate compositional reconstruction of the language.

paragraphs: Artificial agents can learn to communicate successfully while developing messages that people find difficult to interpret. The authors argue that a common training objective contributes to this problem: identifying one object in a shared visual scene can encourage overfitting to concrete references. It offers little pressure to develop messages expressing ideas that apply across objects.

The paper proposes communication games centered on generalizations over sets of objects representing abstract visual concepts. Agents must communicate something broader than the identity of a single item. The games can also give agents separate contexts, changing the information available to each participant while preserving the need to convey the relevant generalization.

Across several established metrics, these games substantially improve the systematicity and interpretability of the learned languages. The paper also introduces an analysis method that learns an approximate compositional reconstruction of a language to identify embedded logical operations. Together, the training and analysis contributions connect more abstract communication objectives with more structured emergent languages, while treating the reconstruction as approximate rather than a complete account of their meaning.
summary.tldr: Training agents to communicate generalizations about object sets produces more systematic and interpretable languages in the reported evaluations.

title: Emergent Communication of Generalizations

abstract: Humans and animals have a natural ability to quickly adapt to their surroundings, but machine-learning models, when subjected to changes, often require a complete retraining from scratch. We present Knowledge-adaptation priors (K-priors) to reduce the cost of retraining by enabling quick and accurate adaptation for a wide-variety of tasks and models. This is made possible by a combination of weight and function-space priors to reconstruct the gradients of the past, which recovers and generalizes many existing, but seemingly-unrelated, adaptation strategies. Training with simple first-order gradient methods can often recover the exact retrained model to an arbitrary accuracy by choosing a sufficiently large memory of the past data. Empirical results show that adaptation with K-priors achieves performance similar to full retraining, but only requires training on a handful of past examples.

paragraphs: Adapting a machine-learning model to changes can require expensive retraining on earlier data. Knowledge-adaptation priors, or K-priors, aim to preserve enough of the old learning signal to make adaptation faster while remaining accurate. The framework is intended to apply across a wide variety of tasks and models.

K-priors combine information about model weights with information about the functions those weights produce. Together, these weight-space and function-space priors reconstruct gradients associated with past learning. This perspective also recovers and generalizes several existing adaptation strategies, providing a shared explanation for methods that might otherwise appear unrelated.

The paper states that simple first-order gradient methods can often approximate the exactly retrained model to arbitrary accuracy when a sufficiently large memory of past data is available. That qualification matters: the recovery claim depends on the memory and applicable setting. Empirically, adaptation using only a handful of past examples achieves performance similar to full retraining, suggesting that useful adaptation can sometimes require much less historical data.
summary.tldr: K-priors combine weight and function information to reconstruct past gradients, enabling adaptation that empirically approaches full-retraining performance with few past examples.

title: Knowledge-Adaptation Priors

abstract: In imperfect-information games, subgame solving is significantly more challenging than in perfect-information games, but in the last few years, such techniques have been developed. They were the key ingredient to the milestone of superhuman play in no-limit Texas hold'em poker. Current subgame-solving techniques analyze the entire common-knowledge closure of the player's current information set, that is, the smallest set of nodes within which it is common knowledge that the current node lies. While this is acceptable in games like poker where the common-knowledge closure is relatively small, many practical games have more complex information structure, which renders the common-knowledge closure impractically large to enumerate or even reasonably approximate. We introduce an approach that overcomes this obstacle, by instead working with only low-order knowledge. Our approach allows an agent, upon arriving at an infoset, to basically prune any node that is no longer reachable, thereby massively reducing the game tree size relative to the common-knowledge subgame. We prove that, as is, our approach can increase exploitability compared to the blueprint strategy. However, we develop three avenues by which safety can be guaranteed. First, safety is guaranteed if the results of subgame solves are incorporated back into the blueprint. Second, we provide a method where safety is achieved by limiting the infosets at which subgame solving is performed. Third, we prove that our approach, when applied at every infoset reached during play, achieves a weaker notion of equilibrium, which we coin affine equilibrium, and which may be of independent interest. We show that affine equilibria cannot be exploited by any Nash strategy of the opponent, so an opponent who wishes to exploit must open herself to counter-exploitation. Even without the safety-guaranteeing additions, experiments on medium-sized games show that our approach always reduced exploitability in practical games even when applied at every infoset, and a depth-limited version of it led to---to our knowledge---the first strong AI for the challenge problem dark chess.

title: Subgame solving without common knowledge

abstract: To deal with changing environments, a new performance measure—adaptive regret, defined as the maximum static regret over any interval, was proposed in online learning. Under the setting of online convex optimization, several algorithms have been successfully developed to minimize the adaptive regret. However, existing algorithms lack universality in the sense that they can only handle one type of convex functions and need apriori knowledge of parameters. By contrast, there exist universal algorithms, such as MetaGrad, that attain optimal static regret for multiple types of convex functions simultaneously. Along this line of research, this paper presents the first universal algorithm for minimizing the adaptive regret of convex functions. Specifically, we borrow the idea of maintaining multiple learning rates in MetaGrad to handle the uncertainty of functions, and utilize the technique of sleeping experts to capture changing environments. In this way, our algorithm automatically adapts to the property of functions (convex, exponentially concave, or strongly convex), as well as the nature of environments (stationary or changing). As a by product, it also allows the type of functions to switch between rounds.

paragraphs: Online learning must sometimes cope with an environment that changes during the sequence of decisions. Adaptive regret evaluates performance over intervals, using the largest static regret on any interval. This exposes periods of poor adaptation that a single comparison over the entire sequence might obscure, making it a useful objective for changing environments.

Earlier adaptive-regret algorithms described in the paper handle particular types of convex functions and require prior parameter knowledge. The proposed algorithm combines two ideas: maintaining multiple learning rates, as in MetaGrad, and using sleeping experts to respond to changes over time. Together, these mechanisms address uncertainty about both the functions and the environment.

The resulting method adapts automatically to convex, exponentially concave, or strongly convex functions, as well as to stationary or changing conditions. It also permits the function type to change between rounds. The paper presents this as the first universal algorithm for minimizing adaptive regret of convex functions, bringing function-class adaptation and adaptation over time into a shared approach.
summary.tldr: Combining multiple learning rates with sleeping experts yields an online algorithm that adapts to both changing environments and different convex function types.

title: Dual Adaptivity: A Universal Algorithm for Minimizing the Adaptive Regret of Convex Functions

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are promising deep learning approaches in learning representations for graph-structured data. Despite the proliferation of such methods, it is well known that they are vulnerable to carefully crafted adversarial attacks on the graph structure. In this paper, we first conduct an adversarial vulnerability analysis based on matrix perturbation theory. We prove that the low- frequency components of the symmetric normalized Laplacian, which is usually used as the convolutional filter in GCNs, could be more robust against structural perturbations when their eigenvalues fall into a certain robust interval. Our results indicate that not all low-frequency components are robust to adversarial attacks and provide a deeper understanding of the relationship between graph spectrum and robustness of GCNs. Motivated by the theory, we present GCN-LFR, a general robust co-training paradigm for GCN-based models, that encourages transferring the robustness of low-frequency components with an auxiliary neural network. To this end, GCN-LFR could enhance the robustness of various kinds of GCN-based models against poisoning structural attacks in a plug-and-play manner. Extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets and five GCN-based models also confirm that GCN-LFR is resistant to the adversarial attacks without compromising on performance in the benign situation.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks can be vulnerable when an adversary changes the graph structure. This paper examines that vulnerability through matrix perturbation theory, focusing on the symmetric normalized Laplacian commonly used in graph convolution. The central question is which parts of the graph’s spectrum remain comparatively stable under structural changes.

The analysis shows that low-frequency components could be more robust when their eigenvalues lie within a particular robust interval. Low frequency by itself therefore does not establish robustness. This conditional result motivates GCN-LFR, a co-training framework that uses an auxiliary neural network to encourage transfer of robustness from low-frequency components to a GCN-based model.

The framework is designed to attach to different GCN models and improve resistance to structural poisoning attacks. Experiments cover five benchmark datasets and five GCN-based models. They report resistance to adversarial attacks without sacrificing performance when the graph is benign. The contribution combines a more selective theoretical account of spectral robustness with an adaptable training mechanism supported by those empirical evaluations.
summary.tldr: A conditional analysis of spectral robustness motivates GCN-LFR, which improves resistance to structural attacks across the reported GCN experiments.

title: Not All Low-Pass Filters are Robust in Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: We introduce SciGen, a new challenge dataset consisting of tables from scientific articles and their corresponding descriptions, for the task of reasoning-aware data-to-text generation. Describing scientific tables goes beyond the surface realization of the table content and requires reasoning over table values. The unique properties of SciGen are that (1) tables mostly contain numerical values, and (2) the corresponding descriptions require arithmetic reasoning. SciGen is the first dataset that assesses the arithmetic reasoning capabilities of generation models on complex input structures, such as tables from scientific articles, and thus it opens new avenues for future research in reasoning-aware text generation and evaluation. The core part of SciGen, including the test data, is annotated by one of the authors of the corresponding articles. Such expert annotations do not scale to large training data sizes. To tackle this, we propose a pipeline for automatically extracting high-quality table-description pairs from the LaTeX sources of scientific articles. We study the effectiveness of state-of-the-art data-to-text generation models on SciGen and evaluate the results using common metrics and human evaluation. Our results and analyses show that adding high-quality unsupervised training data improves the correctness and reduces the hallucination in generated descriptions, however, the ability of state-of-the-art models is still severely limited on this task.

paragraphs: Describing a scientific table can require calculations and interpretation of numerical relationships. SciGen introduces a dataset of scientific tables and associated descriptions to evaluate text generation that involves this arithmetic reasoning. Its mostly numerical tables create a structured input setting in which producing fluent text also demands reasoning about values.

The core dataset, including the test portion, uses annotations supplied by an author of each corresponding scientific article. Because this expert involvement is difficult to scale, the researchers also develop a pipeline that automatically extracts high-quality table-description pairs from article LaTeX sources. The approach combines an expert-annotated core with a way to obtain additional training material.

The authors evaluate leading data-to-text systems using common metrics and human judgments. Adding high-quality unsupervised training data improves correctness and reduces hallucination in generated descriptions. However, the evaluated models remain severely limited on the task. These findings show both the value of additional suitable training data and the continuing difficulty of generating accurate descriptions that depend on arithmetic reasoning.
summary.tldr: SciGen tests arithmetic reasoning in scientific table descriptions, where additional training data helps but tested models remain severely limited.

title: SciGen: a Dataset for Reasoning-Aware Text Generation from Scientific Tables

abstract: Understanding and creating mathematics using natural mathematical language - the mixture of symbolic and natural language used by humans - is a challenging and important problem for driving progress in machine learning. As a step in this direction, we develop NaturalProofs, a multi-domain corpus of mathematical statements and their proofs, written in natural mathematical language. NaturalProofs unifies broad coverage, deep coverage, and low-resource mathematical sources, allowing for evaluating both in-distribution and zero-shot generalization. Using NaturalProofs, we benchmark strong neural methods on mathematical reference retrieval and generation tasks which test a system's ability to determine key results that appear in a proof. Large-scale sequence models show promise compared to classical information retrieval methods, yet their performance and out-of-domain generalization leave substantial room for improvement. NaturalProofs opens many avenues for research on challenging mathematical tasks.

paragraphs: Human mathematical writing combines ordinary language with symbols. NaturalProofs provides a corpus of mathematical statements and proofs written in that form, supporting research on systems that understand mathematics as people express it. The collection spans multiple domains and combines sources with broad coverage, detailed coverage, and relatively limited available material.

The benchmark focuses on identifying key mathematical results used in proofs. It includes reference retrieval and generation tasks, testing whether a model can determine which results belong in a proof's supporting material. Its range of sources also enables evaluation within familiar distributions and zero-shot evaluation when generalizing to new settings.

The authors compare strong neural approaches with classical information retrieval methods. Large sequence models show promise, but their overall performance and generalization beyond the training domain still leave substantial room for improvement. These findings establish reference identification as a meaningful challenge for mathematical language models. The dataset supplies a basis for that evaluation and for further research involving naturally written mathematical statements and proofs.
summary.tldr: NaturalProofs benchmarks identifying supporting mathematical results in human-written proofs and reveals substantial generalization challenges.

title: NaturalProofs: Mathematical Theorem Proving in Natural Language

abstract: Addressing the interpretability problem of NMF on Boolean data, Boolean Matrix Factorization (BMF) uses Boolean algebra to decompose the input into low-rank Boolean factor matrices. These matrices are highly interpretable and very useful in practice, but they come at the high computational cost of solving an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem. To reduce the computational burden, we propose to relax BMF continuously using a novel elastic-binary regularizer, from which we derive a proximal gradient algorithm. Through an extensive set of experiments, we demonstrate that our method works well in practice: On synthetic data, we show that it converges quickly, recovers the ground truth precisely, and estimates the simulated rank exactly. On real-world data, we improve upon the state of the art in recall, loss, and runtime, and a case study from the medical domain confirms that our results are easily interpretable and semantically meaningful.

paragraphs: Boolean matrix factorization represents a Boolean input matrix using lower-rank Boolean factors combined through Boolean algebra. This can produce interpretable structure where ordinary nonnegative matrix factorization has interpretability difficulties on Boolean data. The obstacle is computational: finding the factors involves an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem.

The authors reduce the practical burden by replacing the discrete formulation with a continuous relaxation. A new elastic-binary regularizer encourages the relaxed solution toward the intended binary structure. From this formulation, they derive a proximal gradient algorithm. The approach therefore connects a continuous optimization procedure with the goal of obtaining interpretable Boolean factors.

Experiments on synthetic data show rapid convergence, precise recovery of the underlying factors, and exact estimation of the simulated rank. On real-world data, the method improves on the evaluated state of the art in recall, loss, and runtime. A medical case study also finds the resulting factors interpretable and semantically meaningful. These are practical experimental successes for the proposed relaxation, supporting its usefulness for reducing the computational cost of Boolean factorization.
summary.tldr: A continuous relaxation with an elastic-binary regularizer makes Boolean matrix factorization faster in experiments while retaining interpretable factors.

title: Efficiently Factorizing Boolean Matrices using Proximal Gradient Descent

abstract: Approximating Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) as a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) has allowed researchers to enjoy the benefits of studying a continuous optimization trajectory while carefully preserving the stochasticity of SGD. Analogous study of adaptive gradient methods, such as RMSprop and Adam, has been challenging because there were no rigorously proven SDE approximations for these methods. This paper derives the SDE approximations for RMSprop and Adam, giving theoretical guarantees of their correctness as well as experimental validation of their applicability to common large-scaling vision and language settings. A key practical result is the derivation of a square root scaling rule to adjust the optimization hyperparameters of RMSprop and Adam when changing batch size, and its empirical validation in deep learning settings.

paragraphs: A stochastic differential equation can describe optimization as a continuous trajectory while retaining the randomness of stochastic training. Such approximations had already been useful for studying stochastic gradient descent. This paper develops rigorously justified counterparts for the adaptive optimizers RMSprop and Adam, filling a gap identified by the authors.

The contribution includes theoretical guarantees for the correctness of these approximations and experimental evidence that they apply to common large-scale vision and language settings. Preserving stochasticity matters to the purpose of the model: the continuous description is intended to represent the noisy optimization process, rather than only a deterministic path through the parameters.

A practical outcome is a square-root scaling rule for adjusting optimization hyperparameters when batch size changes. The authors derive this rule for RMSprop and Adam and validate it empirically in deep learning settings. The work therefore connects a mathematical description of adaptive optimization to a concrete training decision: how to adjust optimizer settings when changing the amount of data processed in each batch.
summary.tldr: Rigorous stochastic differential equation approximations for Adam and RMSprop yield empirically validated square-root batch-size scaling rules.

title: On the SDEs and Scaling Rules for Adaptive Gradient Algorithms

abstract: Transformer is a transformative framework for deep learning which models sequential data and has achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of tasks, but with high computational and energy cost. To improve its efficiency, a popular choice is to compress the models via binarization which constrains the floating-point values into binary ones to save resource consumption owing to cheap bitwise operations significantly. However, existing binarization methods only aim at minimizing the information loss for the input distribution statistically, while ignoring the pairwise similarity modeling at the core of the attention mechanism. To this end, we propose a new binarization paradigm customized to high-dimensional softmax attention via kernelized hashing, called EcoFormer, to map the original queries and keys into low-dimensional binary codes in Hamming space. The kernelized hash functions are learned to match the ground-truth similarity relations extracted from the attention map in a self-supervised way. Based on the equivalence between the inner product of binary codes and the Hamming distance as well as the associative property of matrix multiplication, we can approximate the attention in linear complexity by expressing it as a dot-product of binary codes. Moreover, the compact binary representations of queries and keys in EcoFormer enable us to replace most of the expensive multiply-accumulate operations in attention with simple accumulations to save considerable on-chip energy footprint on edge devices. Extensive experiments on both vision and language tasks show that EcoFormer consistently achieves comparable performance with standard attentions while consuming much fewer resources. For example, based on PVTv2-B0 and ImageNet-1K, EcoFormer achieves a 73% reduction in on-chip energy footprint with only a slight performance drop of 0.33% compared to the standard attention. Code is available at https://github.com/ziplab/EcoFormer.

paragraphs: Transformer attention depends on similarities between queries and keys, but computing it can consume substantial energy and computation. Ordinary binarization methods compress numerical values without specifically preserving those pairwise relationships. EcoFormer designs the compression around attention's similarity structure so that reducing numerical precision also respects the operation being approximated.

The method learns kernelized hash functions that turn queries and keys into compact binary codes. Training uses similarity relationships extracted from the attention map as self-supervision. Relationships between binary inner products and Hamming distance, together with reassociation of matrix multiplication, allow attention to be approximated with linear complexity. Binary representations also replace many multiply-accumulate operations with simpler accumulations.

Experiments across vision and language tasks find performance comparable to standard attention with substantially fewer resources. For PVTv2-B0 on ImageNet-1K, the authors report a 73% reduction in on-chip energy footprint with a 0.33% performance drop. The result illustrates the intended tradeoff: preserve useful attention relationships while reducing the arithmetic and energy needed to process them.
summary.tldr: EcoFormer learns binary query and key representations that preserve attention similarities while reducing computational and energy costs.

title: EcoFormer: Energy-Saving Attention with Linear Complexity

abstract: We propose a very general framework for deriving rigorous bounds on the approximation error for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and operator learning architectures such as DeepONets and FNOs as well as for physics-informed operator learning. These bounds guarantee that PINNs and (physics-informed) DeepONets or FNOs will efficiently approximate the underlying solution or solution-operator of generic partial differential equations (PDEs). Our framework utilizes existing neural network approximation results to obtain bounds on more-involved learning architectures for PDEs. We illustrate the general framework by deriving the first rigorous bounds on the approximation error of physics-informed operator learning and by showing that PINNs (and physics-informed DeepONets and FNOs) mitigate the curse of dimensionality in approximating nonlinear parabolic PDEs.

paragraphs: Neural approaches to partial differential equations can approximate an individual solution or learn a solution operator that maps problem inputs to solutions. Physics-informed approaches additionally incorporate the governing equations. This paper develops a general mathematical framework for bounding approximation error across these related architectures, including PINNs, DeepONets, FNOs, and physics-informed operator models.

The framework builds on existing neural network approximation results and carries them into the more involved architectures used for differential equations. This matters because a result about a basic network does not by itself establish how accurately an entire solution-learning architecture can represent its target. The authors provide a common route from those existing results to rigorous bounds for these larger constructions.

They use the framework to derive what they describe as the first rigorous approximation-error bounds for physics-informed operator learning. They also show that the covered architectures mitigate the curse of dimensionality when approximating nonlinear parabolic equations. The guarantees concern efficient approximation of solutions or solution operators. Their significance is to establish representational accuracy mathematically, rather than to assert that every training procedure will find the corresponding approximation.
summary.tldr: A general framework derives rigorous approximation bounds for physics-informed and operator-learning networks, including results that mitigate dimensionality costs for nonlinear parabolic PDEs.

title: Generic bounds on the approximation error for physics-informed (and) operator learning

abstract: Molecule representation learning (MRL) has been extensively studied and current methods have shown promising power for various tasks, e.g., molecular property prediction and target identification. However, a common hypothesis of existing methods is that either the model development or experimental evaluation is mostly based on i.i.d. data across training and testing. Such a hypothesis can be violated in real-world applications where testing molecules could come from new environments, bringing about serious performance degradation or unexpected prediction. We propose a new representation learning framework entitled MoleOOD to enhance the robustness of MRL models against such distribution shifts, motivated by an observation that the (bio)chemical properties of molecules are usually invariantly associated with certain privileged molecular substructures across different environments (e.g., scaffolds, sizes, etc.). Specifically, We introduce an environment inference model to identify the latent factors that impact data generation from different distributions in a fully data-driven manner. We also propose a new learning objective to guide the molecule encoder to leverage environment-invariant substructures that more stably relate with the labels across environments. Extensive experiments on ten real-world datasets demonstrate that our model has a stronger generalization ability than existing methods under various out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, despite the absence of manual specifications of environments. Particularly, our method achieves up to 5.9\% and 3.9\% improvement over the strongest baselines on OGB and DrugOOD benchmarks in terms of ROC-AUC, respectively. Our source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/yangnianzu0515/MoleOOD}.

paragraphs: Molecular prediction models are often developed and evaluated with training and test data drawn from the same distribution. In applications, molecules may instead come from unfamiliar environments, including different scaffold or size distributions. MoleOOD addresses the resulting loss of reliability by seeking molecular features whose relationship with the prediction target remains more stable.

The framework is motivated by the observation that molecular properties are often associated with particular substructures across environments. An environment-inference model learns latent factors affecting how data arise from different distributions. A separate learning objective guides the molecule encoder toward substructures that relate consistently to labels across those inferred environments. Environment specifications do not have to be supplied manually.

Experiments on ten real-world datasets show stronger generalization than existing methods across several out-of-distribution settings. The authors report improvements of up to 5.9% on OGB and 3.9% on DrugOOD over the strongest baselines, measured by ROC-AUC. These are reported maximum gains, not uniform improvements across every dataset. The results support learning stable substructure–label relationships while inferring environmental variation from data.
summary.tldr: MoleOOD learns latent environments and stable molecular substructures to improve prediction under distribution shifts.

title: Learning Substructure Invariance for Out-of-Distribution Molecular Representations

abstract: In this paper, we study the combinatorial semi-bandits (CMAB) and focus on reducing the dependency of the batch-size $K$ in the regret bound, where $K$ is the total number of arms that can be pulled or triggered in each round. First, for the setting of CMAB with probabilistically triggered arms (CMAB-T), we discover a novel (directional) triggering probability and variance modulated (TPVM) condition that can replace the previously-used smoothness condition for various applications, such as cascading bandits, online network exploration and online influence maximization. Under this new condition, we propose a BCUCB-T algorithm with variance-aware confidence intervals and conduct regret analysis which reduces the $O(K)$ factor to $O(\log K)$ or $O(\log^2 K)$ in the regret bound, significantly improving the regret bounds for the above applications. Second, for the setting of non-triggering CMAB with independent arms, we propose a SESCB algorithm which leverages on the non-triggering version of the TPVM condition and completely removes the dependency on $K$ in the leading regret. As a valuable by-product, the regret analysis used in this paper can improve several existing results by a factor of $O(\log K)$. Finally, experimental evaluations show our superior performance compared with benchmark algorithms in different applications.

paragraphs: In combinatorial semi-bandits, a decision can involve several arms, including arms activated probabilistically by that decision. The paper studies how learning performance depends on K, the maximum number pulled or triggered in a round. Its target is regret: the accumulated performance shortfall associated with learning which choices work best.

Under this condition, their BCUCB-T algorithm uses confidence intervals that reflect variance. The analysis reduces a linear dependence on K to a logarithmic or squared-logarithmic dependence. The analysis also sharpens several existing results by a logarithmic factor. Experiments report improvements over benchmark algorithms, complementing the theoretical distinction between reduced batch-size dependence in the triggered setting and its removal from the leading term in the independent setting.
summary.tldr: New conditions and algorithms reduce batch-size dependence in semi-bandit regret bounds, eliminating it from the leading term for independent, non-triggered arms.

title: Batch-Size Independent Regret Bounds for Combinatorial Semi-Bandits with Probabilistically Triggered Arms or Independent Arms

abstract: Designing neural networks with bounded Lipschitz constant is a promising way to obtain certifiably robust classifiers against adversarial examples. However, the relevant progress for the important $\ell_\infty$ perturbation setting is rather limited, and a principled understanding of how to design expressive $\ell_\infty$ Lipschitz networks is still lacking. In this paper, we bridge the gap by studying certified $\ell_\infty$ robustness from a novel perspective of representing Boolean functions. We derive two fundamental impossibility results that hold for any standard Lipschitz network: one for robust classification on finite datasets, and the other for Lipschitz function approximation. These results identify that networks built upon norm-bounded affine layers and Lipschitz activations intrinsically lose expressive power even in the two-dimensional case, and shed light on how recently proposed Lipschitz networks (e.g., GroupSort and $\ell_\infty$-distance nets) bypass these impossibilities by leveraging order statistic functions. Finally, based on these insights, we develop a unified Lipschitz network that generalizes prior works, and design a practical version that can be efficiently trained (making certified robust training free). Extensive experiments show that our approach is scalable, efficient, and consistently yields better certified robustness across multiple datasets and perturbation radii than prior Lipschitz networks.

paragraphs: Bounding a network’s Lipschitz constant limits how strongly its output can respond to input changes, supporting certified adversarial robustness. This paper studies the expressiveness of such networks for perturbations bounded coordinate by coordinate, the infinity-norm setting. It approaches the problem through the ability to represent Boolean functions.

The authors prove two impossibility results for standard architectures built from norm-bounded affine layers and Lipschitz activations. The results connect architectural expressiveness to robustness guarantees, showing why the particular operations used to enforce Lipschitz constraints matter.
summary.tldr: Boolean-function analysis reveals expressiveness limits in standard Lipschitz networks and motivates an architecture with better empirical certified robustness.

title: Rethinking Lipschitz Neural Networks and Certified Robustness: A Boolean Function Perspective

abstract: Variational quantum algorithms have been acknowledged as the leading strategy to realize near-term quantum advantages in meaningful tasks, including machine learning and optimization. When applied to tasks involving classical data, such algorithms generally begin with data encoding circuits and train quantum neural networks (QNNs) to minimize target functions. Although QNNs have been widely studied to improve these algorithms' performance on practical tasks, there is a gap in systematically understanding the influence of data encoding on the eventual performance. In this paper, we make progress in filling this gap by considering the common data encoding strategies based on parameterized quantum circuits. We prove that, under reasonable assumptions, the distance between the average encoded state and the maximally mixed state could be explicitly upper-bounded with respect to the width and depth of the encoding circuit. This result in particular implies that the average encoded state will concentrate on the maximally mixed state at an exponential speed on depth. Such concentration seriously limits the capabilities of quantum classifiers, and strictly restricts the distinguishability of encoded states from a quantum information perspective. To support our findings, we numerically verify these results on both synthetic and public data sets. Our results highlight the significance of quantum data encoding and may shed light on the future design of quantum encoding strategies.

paragraphs: Quantum learning methods operating on classical data first encode those data into quantum states. This paper studies how that encoding step can constrain later performance. It focuses on common encodings built from parameterized quantum circuits, addressing an aspect of the learning pipeline that is less systematically understood than the quantum neural network trained afterward.

Under the paper’s assumptions, the authors bound the distance between the average encoded state and the maximally mixed state in terms of circuit width and depth. summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, deeper quantum data encodings concentrate the average state toward a maximally mixed state, constraining classification and distinguishability.

title: Concentration of Data Encoding in Parameterized Quantum Circuits

abstract: We present a novel method for the safety verification of nonlinear dynamical models that uses neural networks to represent abstractions of their dynamics. Neural networks have extensively been used before as approximators; in this work, we make a step further and use them for the first time as abstractions. For a given dynamical model, our method synthesises a neural network that overapproximates its dynamics by ensuring an arbitrarily tight, formally certified bound on the approximation error. For this purpose, we employ a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis procedure. We show that this produces a neural ODE with non-deterministic disturbances that constitutes a formal abstraction of the concrete model under analysis. This guarantees a fundamental property: if the abstract model is safe, i.e., free from any initialised trajectory that reaches an undesirable state, then the concrete model is also safe. By using neural ODEs with ReLU activation functions as abstractions, we cast the safety verification problem for nonlinear dynamical models into that of hybrid automata with affine dynamics, which we verify using SpaceEx. We demonstrate that our approach performs comparably to the mature tool Flow* on existing benchmark nonlinear models. We additionally demonstrate and that it is effective on models that do not exhibit local Lipschitz continuity, which are out of reach to the existing technologies.

paragraphs: A neural network can approximate a dynamical system without being reliable enough to prove that the system is safe. This paper turns neural approximations into formal abstractions by certifying their approximation error. The resulting abstraction covers the original system’s dynamics, allowing safety reasoning to account for the approximation’s uncertainty.

The method uses counterexample-guided inductive synthesis to construct a network with an arbitrarily tight, formally certified error bound. It represents the result as a neural ordinary differential equation with nondeterministic disturbances. The key guarantee is directional: if no initialized trajectory of the abstract model reaches an undesirable state, the original model is safe as well.

On existing nonlinear benchmarks, the approach performs comparably to Flow*. They also demonstrate effectiveness on models lacking local Lipschitz continuity, which the abstract identifies as beyond existing technologies. The contribution makes certified neural representations usable as a bridge to formal safety verification.
summary.tldr: Certified neural abstractions allow safety proofs for an abstract dynamical model to transfer to the original system.

title: Neural Abstractions

abstract: Generalization and invariance are two essential properties of machine learning models. Generalization captures a model's ability to classify unseen data while invariance measures consistency of model predictions on transformations of the data. Existing research suggests a positive relationship: a model generalizing well should be invariant to certain visual factors. Building on this qualitative implication we make two contributions. First, we introduce effective invariance (EI), a simple and reasonable measure of model invariance which does not rely on image labels. Given predictions on a test image and its transformed version, EI measures how well the predictions agree and with what level of confidence. Second, using invariance scores computed by EI, we perform large-scale quantitative correlation studies between generalization and invariance, focusing on rotation and grayscale transformations. From a model-centric view, we observe generalization and invariance of different models exhibit a strong linear relationship, on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets. From a dataset-centric view, we find a certain model's accuracy and invariance linearly correlated on different test sets. Apart from these major findings, other minor but interesting insights are also discussed.

paragraphs: Generalization concerns how well a model handles unseen data, while invariance concerns whether its predictions stay consistent when inputs are transformed. This paper quantitatively investigates the relationship between these properties. It focuses on image rotation and grayscale conversion, rather than treating invariance as an unspecified property.

The authors introduce effective invariance, a measure that does not require image labels. It compares a model's predictions for an image and its transformed version, accounting for both agreement and confidence. This provides a way to measure prediction consistency directly from model outputs and then study how that consistency relates to accuracy.

Large-scale experiments reveal a strong linear relationship across different models between generalization and measured invariance, on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets. Looking across test sets for a fixed model also reveals a linear correlation between accuracy and invariance. These findings give quantitative support to the proposed relationship in the studied settings; they establish correlation rather than showing that increasing invariance necessarily causes better generalization.
summary.tldr: A label-free measure of prediction invariance shows strong linear correlations with generalization across models and test datasets.

title: On the Strong Correlation Between Model Invariance and Generalization

abstract: Topic models infer latent topic distributions based on observed word co-occurrences in a text corpus. While typically a corpus contains documents of variable lengths, most previous topic models treat documents of different lengths uniformly, assuming that each document is sufficiently informative. However, shorter documents may have only a few word co-occurrences, resulting in inferior topic quality. Some other previous works assume that all documents are short, and leverage external auxiliary data, e.g., pretrained word embeddings and document connectivity. Orthogonal to existing works, we remedy this problem within the corpus itself by proposing a Meta-Complement Topic Model, which improves topic quality of short texts by transferring the semantic knowledge learned on long documents to complement semantically limited short texts. As a self-contained module, our framework is agnostic to auxiliary data and can be further improved by flexibly integrating them into our framework. Specifically, when incorporating document connectivity, we further extend our framework to complement documents with limited edges. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of our framework.

paragraphs: Topic models learn themes from patterns of words appearing together. Short documents provide fewer such patterns, so treating all document lengths alike can produce weaker topics for short texts. This paper uses the variation in document length within a corpus as a source of help for those less informative documents.

The Meta-Complement Topic Model transfers semantic knowledge learned from long documents to short ones. Its aim is to supplement the limited evidence in short texts using information already present in the same corpus. This makes the framework self-contained rather than dependent on external resources such as pretrained word embeddings or document connections.

The framework can still incorporate auxiliary information when it is available. When document connectivity is included, the authors extend the same idea to documents with few edges, complementing another form of limited evidence. Experiments demonstrate an advantage for the framework. The contribution is a way to share information between richly and sparsely represented documents, while retaining flexibility to benefit from additional sources of semantic structure.
summary.tldr: The Meta-Complement Topic Model improves short-text topics by transferring semantic knowledge from longer documents in the same corpus.

title: Meta-Complementing the Semantics of Short Texts in Neural Topic Models

abstract: We consider a distributed online convex optimization problem when streaming data are distributed among computing agents over a connected communication network. Since the data are high-dimensional or the network is large-scale, communication load can be a bottleneck for the efficiency of distributed algorithms. To tackle this bottleneck, we apply the state-of-art data compression scheme to the fundamental GD-based distributed online algorithms. Three algorithms with difference-compressed communication are proposed for full information feedback (DC-DOGD), one-point bandit feedback (DC-DOBD), and two-point bandit feedback (DC-DO2BD), respectively. We obtain regret bounds explicitly in terms of time horizon, compression ratio, decision dimension, agent number, and network parameters. Our algorithms are proved to be no-regret and match the same regret bounds, w.r.t. time horizon, with their uncompressed versions for both convex and strongly convex losses. Numerical experiments are given to validate the theoretical findings and illustrate that the proposed algorithms can effectively reduce the total transmitted bits for distributed online training compared with the uncompressed baseline.

paragraphs: This paper studies online optimization when streaming data arrive at multiple computing agents connected by a communication network. Agents need to exchange information, but high-dimensional data or large networks can make those exchanges expensive. The proposed approach compresses communicated differences within gradient-descent-based distributed algorithms to reduce that burden.

The authors develop three versions for different feedback settings: full information, one-point bandit feedback, and two-point bandit feedback. Their regret bounds explicitly include the time horizon, compression ratio, decision dimension, number of agents, and network properties. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison decision, so its growth describes how well learning keeps pace over time.

For convex and strongly convex losses, the algorithms are proved to have no regret and match the time-horizon dependence of their uncompressed counterparts. That matching concerns how the bounds scale with time; the analysis still tracks other relevant factors. summary.tldr: Compressed communication reduces transmitted data while preserving the time-horizon regret rates of distributed online optimization algorithms.

title: Distributed Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication

abstract: "Bayesian Optimization is a very effective tool for optimizing expensive black-box functions. Inspired by applications developing and characterizing reaction chemistry using droplet microfluidic reactors, we consider a novel setting where the expense of evaluating the function can increase significantly when making large input changes between iterations. We further assume we are working asynchronously, meaning we have to decide on new queries before we finish evaluating previous experiments. This paper investigates the problem and introduces 'Sequential Bayesian Optimization via Adaptive Connecting Samples' (SnAKe), which provides a solution by considering large batches of queries and preemptively building optimization paths that minimize input costs. We investigate some convergence properties and empirically show that the algorithm is able to achieve regret similar to classical Bayesian Optimization algorithms in both the synchronous and asynchronous settings, while reducing the input costs significantly. We show the method is robust to the choice of its single hyper-parameter and provide a parameter-free alternative."

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to functions that are expensive to evaluate. This paper considers an additional cost: making a large change between successive inputs can itself be expensive. Motivated by reaction chemistry with droplet microfluidic reactors, it also considers asynchronous experiments, where new queries must be selected before earlier evaluations finish.

The proposed method, SnAKe, plans over large batches of candidate queries and builds paths intended to minimize the costs of changing inputs. This makes the order of experiments an explicit part of optimization. Planning connected sequences of queries addresses the expense associated with moving between experimental settings.

The authors investigate convergence properties and compare the method empirically with classical Bayesian optimization algorithms. SnAKe achieves similar regret in both synchronous and asynchronous settings while substantially reducing input costs in the reported experiments. The method is also reported to be robust to the choice of its single hyperparameter, and a parameter-free alternative is provided. These findings support path planning when experimental transitions contribute meaningfully to total cost.
summary.tldr: SnAKe plans low-cost paths through Bayesian optimization queries, reporting similar regret with substantially lower input-transition costs.

title: SnAKe: Bayesian Optimization with Pathwise Exploration

abstract: In the last years, neural networks (NN) have evolved from laboratory environments to the state-of-the-art for many real-world problems. It was shown that NN models (i.e., their weights and biases) evolve on unique trajectories in weight space during training. Following, a population of such neural network models (referred to as model zoo) would form structures in weight space. We think that the geometry, curvature and smoothness of these structures contain information about the state of training and can reveal latent properties of individual models. With such model zoos, one could investigate novel approaches for (i) model analysis, (ii) discover unknown learning dynamics, (iii) learn rich representations of such populations, or (iv) exploit the model zoos for generative modelling of NN weights and biases. Unfortunately, the lack of standardized model zoos and available benchmarks significantly increases the friction for further research about populations of NNs. With this work, we publish a novel dataset of model zoos containing systematically generated and diverse populations of NN models for further research. In total the proposed model zoo dataset is based on eight image datasets, consists of 27 model zoos trained with varying hyperparameter combinations and includes 50’360 unique NN models as well as their sparsified twins, resulting in over 3’844’360 collected model states. Additionally, to the model zoo data we provide an in-depth analysis of the zoos and provide benchmarks for multiple downstream tasks. The dataset can be found at www.modelzoos.cc.

The release also provides detailed analyses and benchmarks for multiple downstream tasks. These resources support research on model analysis, learning dynamics, representations of model populations, and potentially generating network weights and biases. The suggested information in weight-space geometry is a research motivation, while the concrete contribution is a standardized collection and evaluation foundation for investigating it.
summary.tldr: A dataset of diverse neural-network populations and training states supports systematic research on models as data.

title: Model Zoos: A Dataset of Diverse Populations of Neural Network Models

abstract: Recent advances in attention-free sequence models rely on convolutions as alternatives to the attention operator at the core of Transformers. In particular, long convolution sequence models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in many domains, but incur a significant cost during auto-regressive inference workloads -- naively requiring a full pass (or caching of activations) over the input sequence for each generated token -- similarly to attention-based models. In this paper, we seek to enable $\mathcal O(1)$ compute and memory cost per token in any pre-trained long convolution architecture to reduce memory footprint and increase throughput during generation. Concretely, our methods consist in extracting low-dimensional linear state-space models from each convolution layer, building upon rational interpolation and model-order reduction techniques. We further introduce architectural improvements to convolution-based layers such as Hyena: by weight-tying the filters across channels into heads, we achieve higher pre-training quality and reduce the number of filters to be distilled. The resulting model achieves 10x higher throughput than Transformers and 1.5x higher than Hyena at 1.3B parameters, without any loss in quality after distillation.

paragraphs: Long-convolution sequence models offer an alternative to attention, but generating tokens one at a time can still be expensive. A naive implementation repeatedly processes the input sequence or stores its activations. This paper seeks to turn pretrained long convolutions into compact recurrences with constant computation and memory per generated token.

The method extracts a low-dimensional linear state-space model from each convolution layer, using rational interpolation and model-order reduction. This gives the layer a compact recurrent form for generation. The authors also modify convolution-based architectures such as Hyena by sharing filters across channels within heads, improving pretraining quality and reducing how many filters require distillation.

At 1.3 billion parameters, the resulting model achieves ten times the throughput of Transformers and 1.5 times that of Hyena, with no observed quality loss after distillation. These results connect an architectural change with a conversion procedure for faster generation. The throughput comparisons and quality preservation describe the reported model, while the broader method aims to make pretrained long-convolution architectures more efficient during autoregressive inference.
summary.tldr: Compact recurrent approximations of long convolutions enable faster generation, with reported throughput gains and no quality loss after distillation.

title: Laughing Hyena Distillery: Extracting Compact Recurrences From Convolutions

abstract: In this work, we present SEEM, a promotable and interactive model for segmenting everything everywhere all at once in an image. In SEEM, we propose a novel and versatile decoding mechanism that enables diverse prompting for all types of segmentation tasks, aiming at a universal interface that behaves like large language models (LLMs). More specifically, SEEM is designed with four desiderata:i) Versatility. We introduce a new visual prompt to unify different spatial queries including points, boxes, scribbles, and masks, which can further generalize to a different referring image; ii) Compositionality. We learn a joint visual-semantic space between text and visual prompts, which facilitates the dynamic composition of two prompt types required for various segmentation tasks, as shown in Fig. 1;iii) Interactivity. We further incorporate learnable memory prompts into the decoder to retain segmentation history through mask-guided cross-attention from the decoder to image features; iv) Semantic awareness. We use a text encoder to encode text queries and mask labels into the same semantic space for open-vocabulary segmentation. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study to validate the effectiveness of SEEM across diverse segmentation tasks. The results demonstrate that SEEM exhibits robust generalizing to unseen user intents as it learns to compose prompts of different types in a unified representation space. Our approach achieves competitive performance on interactive segmentation, generic segmentation, referring segmentation, and video object segmentation on 9 datasets with minimum 1/100 supervision in a single set of weights.

summary.tldr: SEEM combines visual prompts, text, and interaction memory in one model for diverse segmentation tasks.

title: Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once

abstract: In safety-critical robotic tasks, potential failures must be reduced, and multiple constraints must be met, such as avoiding collisions, limiting energy consumption, and maintaining balance.Thus, applying safe reinforcement learning (RL) in such robotic tasks requires to handle multiple constraints and use risk-averse constraints rather than risk-neutral constraints.To this end, we propose a trust region-based safe RL algorithm for multiple constraints called a safe distributional actor-critic (SDAC).Our main contributions are as follows: 1) introducing a gradient integration method to manage infeasibility issues in multi-constrained problems, ensuring theoretical convergence, and 2) developing a TD($\lambda$) target distribution to estimate risk-averse constraints with low biases. We evaluate SDAC through extensive experiments involving multi- and single-constrained robotic tasks.While maintaining high scores, SDAC shows 1.93 times fewer steps to satisfy all constraints in multi-constrained tasks and 1.78 times fewer constraint violations in single-constrained tasks compared to safe RL baselines.Code is available at: https://github.com/rllab-snu/Safe-Distributional-Actor-Critic.

paragraphs: Robotic learning can involve several simultaneous requirements, such as avoiding collisions, conserving energy, and maintaining balance. Handling only average costs may be insufficient when failures matter. This paper introduces the safe distributional actor-critic, or SDAC, a trust-region-based reinforcement-learning algorithm designed to handle multiple constraints with a risk-averse treatment of their outcomes.

SDAC contributes two mechanisms. A gradient integration method addresses infeasibility issues that arise in problems with several constraints and comes with a theoretical convergence result. A TD(lambda) target distribution supports estimation of risk-averse constraints with low bias. Together, these mechanisms address both how to update the policy and how to estimate the risks those updates should respect.

The evaluation covers robotic tasks with multiple constraints and with a single constraint. Relative to safe reinforcement-learning baselines, the paper reports 1.93 times fewer steps to satisfy all constraints in the former and 1.78 times fewer violations in the latter, while maintaining high scores. These findings show improved constraint handling in the tested tasks alongside strong task performance.
summary.tldr: SDAC combines multi-constraint policy updates with distributional risk estimation to improve constraint satisfaction in robotic reinforcement-learning experiments.

title: Trust Region-Based Safe Distributional Reinforcement Learning for Multiple Constraints

abstract: Visual Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents trained on limited views face significant challenges in generalizing their learned abilities to unseen views. This inherent difficulty is known as the problem of $\textit{view generalization}$. In this work, we systematically categorize this fundamental problem into four distinct and highly challenging scenarios that closely resemble real-world situations. Subsequently, we propose a straightforward yet effective approach to enable successful adaptation of visual $\textbf{Mo}$del-based policies for $\textbf{Vie}$w generalization ($\textbf{MoVie}$) during test time, without any need for explicit reward signals and any modification during training time. Our method demonstrates substantial advancements across all four scenarios encompassing a total of $\textbf{18}$ tasks sourced from DMControl, xArm, and Adroit, with a relative improvement of $\mathbf{33}$%, $\mathbf{86}$%, and $\mathbf{152}$% respectively. The superior results highlight the immense potential of our approach for real-world robotics applications. Code and videos are available at https://yangsizhe.github.io/MoVie/.

paragraphs: A visually controlled agent may learn a task from a limited set of camera views and struggle when the viewpoint changes. The paper studies this problem of view generalization, organizing it into four challenging scenarios intended to resemble situations that arise in practice. This gives the evaluation a broader scope than a single type of view change.

MoVie adapts visual model-based policies at test time. The proposed approach requires neither explicit reward signals during adaptation nor modifications to the original training process. These properties address a practical deployment problem: an already trained agent encounters unfamiliar views and needs to adjust without receiving task rewards that directly score its behavior.

Experiments cover 18 tasks from DMControl, xArm, and Adroit across the four scenarios. The authors report relative improvements of 33%, 86%, and 152% for these three task sources, respectively. The results support the effectiveness of test-time adaptation in the evaluated settings and suggest potential for robotics applications where the deployment viewpoint differs from those available during training.
summary.tldr: MoVie adapts visual model-based policies to unfamiliar views at test time without explicit rewards or training changes.

title: MoVie: Visual Model-Based Policy Adaptation for View Generalization

abstract: The advancement of Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) critically depends on the availability of high-quality, pre-collected offline datasets that represent real-world complexities and practical applications. However, existing datasets often fall short in their simplicity and lack of realism. To address this gap, we propose Hokoff, a comprehensive set of pre-collected datasets that covers both offline RL and offline MARL, accompanied by a robust framework, to facilitate further research. This data is derived from Honor of Kings, a recognized Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) game known for its intricate nature, closely resembling real-life situations. Utilizing this framework, we benchmark a variety of offline RL and offline MARL algorithms. We also introduce a novel baseline algorithm tailored for the inherent hierarchical action space of the game. We reveal the incompetency of current offline RL approaches in handling task complexity, generalization and multi-task learning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning depends on previously collected experience rather than learning solely through fresh interaction. The quality and complexity of that experience therefore shape what researchers can evaluate. Hokoff introduces datasets from Honor of Kings to provide a demanding game-based setting for studying both individual-agent and multi-agent offline learning.

The contribution includes a framework for working with the collected data and benchmarking a range of algorithms. The authors also introduce a baseline designed for the game's hierarchical action space. This makes the structure of action selection part of the benchmark, alongside the broader challenge of learning useful behavior from recorded play.

The evaluations reveal shortcomings in current offline approaches when confronting task complexity, generalization, and multi-task learning. These findings make Hokoff useful as a diagnostic resource: researchers can investigate whether an algorithm handles several demands that simpler datasets may not expose together. The paper's central contribution is both the shared dataset collection and the accompanying evaluation framework for studying these difficulties in a complex multiplayer game.
summary.tldr: Hokoff provides Honor of Kings datasets and benchmarks that expose weaknesses in offline reinforcement learning on complex game tasks.

title: Hokoff: Real Game Dataset from Honor of Kings and its Offline Reinforcement Learning Benchmarks

abstract: Single image 3D reconstruction is an important but challenging task that requires extensive knowledge of our natural world. Many existing methods solve this problem by optimizing a neural radiance field under the guidance of 2D diffusion models but suffer from lengthy optimization time, 3D inconsistency results, and poor geometry. In this work, we propose a novel method that takes a single image of any object as input and generates a full 360-degree 3D textured mesh in a single feed-forward pass. Given a single image, we first use a view-conditioned 2D diffusion model, Zero123, to generate multi-view images for the input view, and then aim to lift them up to 3D space. Since traditional reconstruction methods struggle with inconsistent multi-view predictions, we build our 3D reconstruction module upon an SDF-based generalizable neural surface reconstruction method and propose several critical training strategies to enable the reconstruction of 360-degree meshes. Without costly optimizations, our method reconstructs 3D shapes in significantly less time than existing methods. Moreover, our method favors better geometry, generates more 3D consistent results, and adheres more closely to the input image. We evaluate our approach on both synthetic data and in-the-wild images and demonstrate its superiority in terms of both mesh quality and runtime. In addition, our approach can seamlessly support the text-to-3D task by integrating with off-the-shelf text-to-image diffusion models.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a complete 3D object from one image requires predicting surfaces that the image does not show. Existing approaches often optimize a neural radiance field under guidance from a 2D diffusion model, taking substantial time and sometimes producing inconsistent geometry. One-2-3-45 instead generates a textured, full-view mesh without optimizing separately for each object.

The method first uses Zero123, a view-conditioned diffusion model, to generate images from additional viewpoints. Those predictions can disagree with one another, which makes conventional reconstruction difficult. The authors therefore build on a generalizable neural surface reconstruction method based on signed distance functions and introduce training strategies for recovering complete 360-degree meshes.

The resulting reconstruction uses a feed-forward approach, with the title reporting a 45-second runtime. Evaluations on synthetic and in-the-wild images show better mesh quality and runtime than the compared methods, alongside improved geometry, 3D consistency, and adherence to the input image. The system can also support text-to-3D generation by taking an image produced by an existing text-to-image diffusion model as its input.
summary.tldr: One-2-3-45 turns a single image into a textured 3D mesh using generated views and feed-forward reconstruction without per-object optimization.

title: One-2-3-45: Any Single Image to 3D Mesh in 45 Seconds without Per-Shape Optimization

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a surge of certified robust training pipelines against text adversarial perturbation constructed by synonym substitutions. Given a base model, existing pipelines provide prediction certificates either in the discrete word space or the continuous latent space. However, they are isolated from each other with a structural gap. We observe that existing training frameworks need unification to provide stronger certified robustness. Additionally, they mainly focus on building the certification process but neglect to improve the robustness of the base model. To mitigate the aforementioned limitations, we propose a unified framework named UniT that enables us to train flexibly in either fashion by working in the word embedding space. It can provide a stronger robustness guarantee obtained directly from the word embedding space without extra modules. In addition, we introduce the decoupled regularization (DR) loss to improve the robustness of the base model, which includes two separate robustness regularization terms for the feature extraction and classifier modules. Experimental results on widely used text classification datasets further demonstrate the effectiveness of the designed unified framework and the proposed DR loss for improving the certified robust accuracy.

paragraphs: Text classifiers can be challenged by replacing words with synonyms. Certified robust training aims to provide guarantees about predictions under such perturbations, but existing approaches operate either in discrete word space or continuous latent space. UniT addresses the structural separation between those approaches by working in the word embedding space.

This shared representation lets the framework support training in either fashion and obtain a stronger robustness guarantee directly from embeddings without adding extra modules. The paper also targets the robustness of the underlying classifier, rather than focusing solely on its certification procedure. It introduces a decoupled regularization loss with separate terms for feature extraction and classification.

The separation lets robustness training explicitly address both the representation-producing component and the component that turns representations into predictions. Experiments on commonly used text classification datasets show improvements in certified robust accuracy from the unified framework and the proposed loss. The contribution therefore combines a common setting for previously separated certification approaches with changes to base-model training, within the paper's synonym-substitution threat model.
summary.tldr: UniT unifies text robustness training in embedding space and separately regularizes feature extraction and classification to improve certified robust accuracy.

title: UniT: A Unified Look at Certified Robust Training against Text Adversarial Perturbation

abstract: To deploy and operate deep neural models in production, the quality of their predictions, which might be contaminated benignly or manipulated maliciously by input distributional deviations, must be monitored and assessed. Specifically, we study the case of monitoring the healthy operation of a deep neural network (DNN) receiving a stream of data, with the aim of detecting input distributional deviations over which the quality of the network's predictions is potentially damaged. Using selective prediction principles, we propose a distribution deviation detection method for DNNs. The proposed method is derived from a tight coverage generalization bound computed over a sample of instances drawn from the true underlying distribution. Based on this bound, our detector continuously monitors the operation of the network over a test window and fires off an alarm whenever a deviation is detected. Our novel detection method performs on-par or better than the state-of-the-art, while consuming substantially lower computation time (five orders of magnitude reduction) and space complexity. Unlike previous methods, which require at least linear dependence on the size of the source distribution for each detection, rendering them inapplicable to ``Google-Scale'' datasets, our approach eliminates this dependence, making it suitable for real-world applications. Code is available at [https://github.com/BarSGuy/Window-Based-Distribution-Shift-Detection](https://github.com/BarSGuy/Window-Based-Distribution-Shift-Detection).
