paragraphs: A deployed neural network may encounter a changing stream of inputs, and some distribution changes can damage prediction quality. This paper develops a monitoring method that examines windows of incoming data and raises an alarm when it detects a deviation. It addresses both benign changes and maliciously manipulated inputs.

The detector uses selective prediction principles and is derived from a tight coverage generalization bound. That bound is computed using a sample drawn from the underlying source distribution, then used to monitor the network over test windows. This gives the alarm mechanism a statistical foundation tied to the source sample and the network’s behavior.

The reported detection performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods while reducing computation time by five orders of magnitude and lowering space complexity. A central scaling benefit is that each detection avoids the dependence on source-dataset size required by previous methods. This makes monitoring more practical for very large source datasets. The alarms identify distributional deviations associated with potential quality damage; a detected change is not itself a direct measurement of prediction error.
summary.tldr: A statistically grounded window-based detector monitors distribution shifts with competitive detection performance and substantially lower computational costs.

title: Window-Based Distribution Shift Detection for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Color is a crucial visual cue readily exploited by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for object recognition. However, CNNs struggle if there is data imbalance between color variations introduced by accidental recording conditions. Color invariance addresses this issue but does so at the cost of removing all color information, which sacrifices discriminative power. In this paper, we propose Color Equivariant Convolutions (CEConvs), a novel deep learning building block that enables shape feature sharing across the color spectrum while retaining important color information. We extend the notion of equivariance from geometric to photometric transformations by incorporating parameter sharing over hue-shifts in a neural network. We demonstrate the benefits of CEConvs in terms of downstream performance to various tasks and improved robustness to color changes, including train-test distribution shifts. Our approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing architectures, such as ResNets, and offers a promising solution for addressing color-based domain shifts in CNNs.

paragraphs: Color helps convolutional neural networks recognize objects, but recording conditions can make some color variations much more common in training than others. This imbalance can undermine performance when colors change. Simply making a model ignore color addresses that sensitivity at the cost of discarding potentially useful visual evidence.

The paper introduces Color Equivariant Convolutions, or CEConvs, which share shape features across different hues while retaining color information. The mechanism shares network parameters over hue shifts. This extends equivariance from changes in geometry to changes in appearance: the model handles specified color transformations in a structured way instead of removing color from its representation.

The authors report improvements in downstream tasks and greater robustness to color changes, including shifts between training and test distributions. CEConvs can be incorporated into existing architectures such as ResNets. The results support treating color variation as structure that a network can explicitly accommodate, allowing it to reuse shape knowledge while keeping the discriminative information that color provides.
summary.tldr: Color Equivariant Convolutions share features across hue shifts while preserving useful color information, improving robustness in the reported evaluations.

title: Color Equivariant Convolutional Networks

abstract: This paper studies the use of a machine learning-based estimator as a control variate for mitigating the variance of Monte Carlo sampling. Specifically, we seek to uncover the key factors that influence the efficiency of control variates in reducing variance. We examine a prototype estimation problem that involves simulating the moments of a Sobolev function based on observations obtained from (random) quadrature nodes. Firstly, we establish an information-theoretic lower bound for the problem. We then study a specific quadrature rule that employs a nonparametric regression-adjusted control variate to reduce the variance of the Monte Carlo simulation. We demonstrate that this kind of quadrature rule can improve the Monte Carlo rate and achieve the minimax optimal rate under a sufficient smoothness assumption. Due to the Sobolev Embedding Theorem, the sufficient smoothness assumption eliminates the existence of rare and extreme events. Finally, we show that, in the presence of rare and extreme events, a truncated version of the Monte Carlo algorithm can achieve the minimax optimal rate while the control variate cannot improve the convergence rate.

paragraphs: A learned regression model can serve as a control variate to reduce the variance of a Monte Carlo estimate. This paper asks when that strategy improves convergence. It studies estimation of moments of a Sobolev function from observations at random quadrature nodes, providing a mathematical setting for examining smoothness and rare extreme values.

The authors first establish an information-theoretic lower bound that defines the best achievable rate for the problem. They then analyze a quadrature rule using a nonparametric regression-adjusted control variate. Under a sufficient smoothness assumption, this rule improves on the Monte Carlo rate and reaches the minimax optimal rate.

The Sobolev Embedding Theorem explains an important implication of that assumption: it rules out rare and extreme events. When such events are present in the analyzed setting, the control variate cannot improve the convergence rate, while a truncated Monte Carlo algorithm can attain the minimax rate. The findings therefore connect the value of regression adjustment to the function class and its allowance for extreme behavior.
summary.tldr: Regression-based control variates achieve optimal Monte Carlo improvements under sufficient smoothness, while rare extremes favor truncation in the analyzed setting.

title: When can Regression-Adjusted Control Variate Help? Rare Events, Sobolev Embedding and Minimax Optimality

abstract: Real-world datasets are typically imbalanced in the sense that only a few classes have numerous samples, while many classes are associated with only a few samples. As a result, a naive ERM learning process will be biased towards the majority classes, making it difficult to generalize to the minority classes. To address this issue, one simple but effective approach is to modify the loss function to emphasize the learning on minority classes, such as re-weighting the losses or adjusting the logits via class-dependent terms. However, existing generalization analysis of such losses is still coarse-grained and fragmented, failing to explain some empirical results. To bridge this gap between theory and practice, we propose a novel technique named data-dependent contraction to capture how these modified losses handle different classes. On top of this technique, a fine-grained generalization bound is established for imbalanced learning, which helps reveal the mystery of re-weighting and logit-adjustment in a unified manner. Furthermore, a principled learning algorithm is developed based on the theoretical insights. Finally, the empirical results on benchmark datasets not only validate the theoretical results but also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

However, existing generalization analysis of such losses is still coarse-grained and fragmented, failing to explain some empirical results. On top of this technique, a fine-grained generalization bound is established for imbalanced learning, which helps reveal the mystery of re-weighting and logit-adjustment in a unified manner. paragraphs: When some classes have many more examples than others, minimizing average training error can favor the common classes. Two ways to compensate are to give different classes different loss weights or to adjust their prediction scores, called logits. Both change what training emphasizes, but existing theory has not fully explained their observed behavior.

This paper develops a shared analysis of these approaches using a technique called data-dependent contraction. The technique accounts for how modified losses affect individual classes, rather than treating their effects only in aggregate. It supports a more detailed generalization bound: a theoretical description of how learning from the available examples relates to performance beyond those examples.

The authors also turn their theoretical insights into a learning algorithm. Benchmark experiments support the analysis and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution connects two common practical interventions through one class-sensitive framework, helping explain their behavior and providing a principled basis for designing a loss for imbalanced data.
summary.tldr: A class-sensitive generalization analysis unifies loss re-weighting and logit adjustment and motivates an effective algorithm for imbalanced learning.

title: A Unified Generalization Analysis of Re-Weighting and Logit-Adjustment for Imbalanced Learning

abstract: Over recent years, an increasing amount of compute and data has been poured into training large language models (LLMs), usually by doing one-pass learning on as many tokens as possible randomly selected from large-scale web corpora. While training on ever-larger portions of the internet leads to consistent performance improvements, the size of these improvements diminishes with scale, and there has been little work exploring the effect of data selection on pre-training and downstream performance beyond simple de-duplication methods such as MinHash. Here, we show that careful data selection (on top of de-duplicated data) via pre-trained model embeddings can speed up training (20% efficiency gains) and improves average downstream accuracy on 16 NLP tasks (up to 2%) at the 6.7B model scale. Furthermore, we show that repeating data intelligently consistently outperforms baseline training (while repeating random data performs worse than baseline training). Our results indicate that clever data selection can significantly improve LLM pre-training, calls into question the common practice of training for a single epoch on as much data as possible, and demonstrates a path to keep improving our models past the limits of randomly sampling web data.

title: D4: Improving LLM Pretraining via Document De-Duplication and Diversification

abstract: This study focuses on the evaluation of the Open Question Answering (Open-QA) task, which can directly estimate the factuality of large language models (LLMs). Current automatic evaluation methods have shown limitations, indicating that human evaluation still remains the most reliable approach. We introduce a new task, QA Evaluation (QA-Eval) and the corresponding dataset EVOUNA, designed to assess the accuracy of AI-generated answers in relation to standard answers within Open-QA. Our evaluation of these methods utilizes human-annotated results to measure their performance. Specifically, the work investigates methods that show high correlation with human evaluations, deeming them more reliable. We also discuss the pitfalls of current methods and methods to improve LLM-based evaluators. We believe this new QA-Eval task and corresponding dataset EVOUNA will facilitate the development of more effective automatic evaluation tools and prove valuable for future research in this area. All resources are available at https://github.com/wangcunxiang/QA-Eval and it is under the Apache-2.0 License.

The authors expect these resources to support better automatic assessment tools; the stated goal is progress toward more effective evaluation, with human judgments anchoring how that progress is measured.
summary.tldr: QA-Eval and EVOUNA assess how reliably automatic methods judge open-ended answers by comparing their evaluations with human annotations.

title: Evaluating Open-QA Evaluation

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful method for controlling dynamic systems, but its learning mechanism can lead to unpredictable actions that undermine the safety of critical systems. Here, we propose RL with Adaptive Regularization (RL-AR), an algorithm that enables safe RL exploration by combining the RL policy with a policy regularizer that hard-codes the safety constraints. RL-AR performs policy combination via a "focus module," which determines the appropriate combination depending on the state—relying more on the safe policy regularizer for less-exploited states while allowing unbiased convergence for well-exploited states. In a series of critical control applications, we demonstrate that RL-AR not only ensures safety during training but also achieves a return competitive with the standards of model-free RL that disregards safety.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning controllers improve through interaction, but exploratory actions can be unpredictable. That creates a problem in critical control settings where safety must hold during learning itself. RL with Adaptive Regularization, or RL-AR, combines a learned policy with a policy regularizer in which safety constraints are explicitly encoded.

A focus module determines how much the combined controller should rely on each policy at the current state. In states that have received less exploration, it places more weight on the safe regularizer. In well-exploited states, it allows the learned policy to converge without bias from that regularization. The balance therefore changes with the state rather than imposing the same restriction everywhere.

The authors demonstrate the approach across a series of critical control applications. They report safety throughout training together with returns competitive with model-free reinforcement learning that disregards safety. These findings support adaptive policy combination as a way to retain protective behavior during exploration while allowing useful learned behavior to emerge where the controller has accumulated more experience.
summary.tldr: RL-AR adaptively combines a learned controller with an explicitly constrained safe policy, reporting safe training and competitive returns.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Regularization for Safe Control of Critical Systems

abstract: Collaborative perception is dedicated to tackling the constraints of single-agent perception, such as occlusions, based on the multiple agents' multi-view sensor inputs. However, most existing works assume an ideal condition that all agents' multi-view cameras are continuously available. In reality, cameras may be highly noisy, obscured or even failed during the collaboration. In this work, we introduce a new robust camera-insensitivity problem: how to overcome the issues caused by the failed camera perspectives, while stabilizing high collaborative performance with low calibration cost? To address above problems, we propose RCDN, a Robust Camera-insensitivity collaborative perception with a novel Dynamic feature-based 3D Neural modeling mechanism. The key intuition of RCDN is to construct collaborative neural rendering field representations to recover failed perceptual messages sent by multiple agents. To better model collaborative neural rendering field, RCDN first establishes a geometry BEV feature based time-invariant static field with other agents via fast hash grid modeling. Based on the static background field, the proposed time-varying dynamic field can model corresponding motion vector for foregrounds with appropriate positions. To validate RCDN, we create OPV2V-N, a new large-scale dataset with manual labelling under different camera failed scenarios. Extensive experiments conducted on OPV2V-N show that RCDN can be ported to other baselines and improve their robustness in extreme camera-insensitivity setting. Our code and datasets will be available soon.

paragraphs: Collaborative perception combines views from multiple agents to overcome problems such as occlusion. Many existing approaches assume that every camera remains available, although real cameras can become noisy, obscured, or fail. RCDN targets maintaining collaborative perception when camera perspectives fail, with low calibration cost included in the problem formulation.

The method constructs shared neural rendering field representations to recover failed perceptual messages. It first builds a static field from geometric bird's-eye-view features shared with other agents, using fast hash-grid modeling. A time-varying dynamic field then models foreground motion and positions against that static background, separating persistent scene structure from moving content.

To evaluate this setting, the authors introduce OPV2V-N, a large-scale dataset with manual labels covering different camera-failure scenarios. Experiments show that RCDN can be added to other baselines and improve their robustness under extreme camera-insensitivity conditions. The contribution combines a recovery mechanism with a dedicated evaluation resource, making camera availability an explicit variable in collaborative-perception design rather than assuming ideal multi-view input throughout.
summary.tldr: RCDN reconstructs missing collaborative-perception messages using static and dynamic neural fields, improving baseline robustness in camera-failure experiments.

title: RCDN: Towards Robust Camera-Insensitivity Collaborative Perception via Dynamic Feature-based 3D Neural Modeling

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress in processing extensive contexts, with the Key-Value (KV) cache playing a vital role in enhancing their performance. However, the growth of the KV cache in response to increasing input length poses challenges to memory and time efficiency. To address this problem, this paper introduces SnapKV, an innovative and fine-tuning-free approach that efficiently minimizes KV cache size while still delivering comparable performance in real-world applications.We discover that each attention head in the model consistently focuses on specific prompt attention features during generation. Meanwhile, this robust pattern can be obtained from an `observation' window located at the end of the prompts. Drawing on this insight, SnapKV automatically compresses KV caches by selecting clustered important KV positions for each attention head. Our approach significantly reduces the growing computational overhead and memory footprint when processing long input sequences. Specifically, SnapKV achieves a consistent decoding speed with a 3.6x increase in generation speed and an 8.2x enhancement in memory efficiency compared to baseline when processing inputs of 16K tokens. At the same time, it maintains comparable performance to baseline models across 16 long sequence datasets. Moreover, SnapKV can process up to 380K context tokens on a single A100-80GB GPU using HuggingFace implementation with minor changes, exhibiting only a negligible accuracy drop in the Needle-in-a-Haystack test. Further comprehensive studies suggest SnapKV's potential for practical applications.

These results support substantial practical efficiency gains under the reported evaluation conditions.
summary.tldr: SnapKV uses attention patterns near the end of a prompt to compress KV caches without fine-tuning, substantially improving reported long-context efficiency.

title: SnapKV: LLM Knows What You are Looking for Before Generation

abstract: Weather forecasting is a fundamental problem for anticipating and mitigating the impacts of climate change. Recently, data-driven approaches for weather forecasting based on deep learning have shown great promise, achieving accuracies that are competitive with operational systems. However, those methods often employ complex, customized architectures without sufficient ablation analysis, making it difficult to understand what truly contributes to their success. Here we introduce Stormer, a simple transformer model that achieves state-of-the art performance on weather forecasting with minimal changes to the standard transformer backbone. We identify the key components of Stormer through careful empirical analyses, including weather-specific embedding, randomized dynamics forecast, and pressure-weighted loss. At the core of Stormer is a randomized forecasting objective that trains the model to forecast the weather dynamics over varying time intervals. During inference, this allows us to produce multiple forecasts for a target lead time and combine them to obtain better forecast accuracy. On WeatherBench 2, Stormer performs competitively at short to medium-range forecasts and outperforms current methods beyond 7 days, while requiring orders-of-magnitude less training data and compute. Additionally, we demonstrate Stormer’s favorable scaling properties, showing consistent improvements in forecast accuracy with increases in model size and training tokens. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/tung-nd/stormer.

paragraphs: Stormer is a weather forecasting model built with minimal changes to a standard Transformer. The paper responds to a difficulty in interpreting earlier systems: complex customized architectures can make it unclear which components drive success. The authors use empirical analyses to identify useful elements, including weather-specific embeddings, a randomized forecasting objective, and pressure-weighted loss.

At inference, this supports producing multiple forecasts for the same target lead time and combining them to improve accuracy. The authors also observe consistent accuracy improvements as model size and training tokens increase. These findings support both the selected forecasting components and the scaling potential of the relatively simple architecture.
summary.tldr: Stormer combines a minimally modified Transformer with variable-interval forecasting to achieve strong weather predictions and favorable scaling.

title: Scaling transformer neural networks for skillful and reliable medium-range weather forecasting

abstract: Synthetic face recognition (SFR) aims to generate synthetic face datasets that mimic the distribution of real face data, which allows for training face recognition models in a privacy-preserving manner. Despite the remarkable potential of diffusion models in image generation, current diffusion-based SFR models struggle with generalization to real-world faces. To address this limitation, we outline three key objectives for SFR: (1) promoting diversity across identities (inter-class diversity), (2) ensuring diversity within each identity by injecting various facial attributes (intra-class diversity), and (3) maintaining identity consistency within each identity group (intra-class identity preservation). Inspired by these goals, we introduce a diffusion-fueled SFR model termed $\text{ID}^3$. $\text{ID}^3$ employs an ID-preserving loss to generate diverse yet identity-consistent facial appearances. Theoretically, we show that minimizing this loss is equivalent to maximizing the lower bound of an adjusted conditional log-likelihood over ID-preserving data. This equivalence motivates an ID-preserving sampling algorithm, which operates over an adjusted gradient vector field, enabling the generation of fake face recognition datasets that approximate the distribution of real-world faces. Extensive experiments across five challenging benchmarks validate the advantages of $\text{ID}^3$.

paragraphs: Synthetic face recognition uses generated face datasets to train recognition models while supporting privacy-preserving training. The challenge is to produce useful variation without losing identity consistency. ID³ organizes this problem around three goals: distinct identities, varied appearances within each identity, and preservation of identity across those variations.

The method adds an identity-preserving loss to a diffusion-based generator. The authors show that minimizing this loss is equivalent to maximizing a lower bound on an adjusted conditional log-likelihood over identity-preserving data. This theoretical connection motivates a sampling algorithm that follows an adjusted gradient field to generate varied faces while retaining their intended identity.

The aim is to produce synthetic datasets that approximate the distribution of real faces, addressing the generalization difficulties of earlier diffusion-based approaches. Experiments across five challenging benchmarks support the advantages of ID³. The contribution is the coordinated treatment of diversity and consistency: generated appearances should vary enough to be useful for recognition training while remaining organized into coherent identity groups.
summary.tldr: ID³ combines an identity-preserving diffusion loss and sampling procedure to generate diverse synthetic faces with consistent identities.

title: $\text{ID}^3$: Identity-Preserving-yet-Diversified Diffusion Models for Synthetic Face Recognition

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced and demonstrated impressive capabilities. In-Context Learning (ICL) and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) are currently two mainstream methods for augmenting LLMs to downstream tasks. ICL typically constructs a few-shot learning scenario, either manually or by setting up a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, helping models quickly grasp domain knowledge or question-answering patterns without changing model parameters. However, this approach involves trade-offs, such as slower inference speed and increased space occupancy. PEFT assists the model in adapting to tasks through minimal parameter modifications, but the training process still demands high hardware requirements, even with a small number of parameters involved. To address these challenges, we propose Reference Trustable Decoding (RTD), a paradigm that allows models to quickly adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, maintaining low inference costs. RTD constructs a reference datastore from the provided training examples and optimizes the LLM's final vocabulary distribution by flexibly selecting suitable references based on the input, resulting in more trustable responses and enabling the model to adapt to downstream tasks at a low cost. Experimental evaluations on various LLMs using different benchmarks demonstrate that RTD establishes a new paradigm for augmenting models to downstream tasks. Furthermore, our method exhibits strong orthogonality with traditional methods, allowing for concurrent usage. Our code can be found at https://github.com/ShiLuohe/ReferenceTrustableDecoding.

paragraphs: Reference Trustable Decoding addresses how to adapt a language model to a downstream task without fine-tuning it. Providing examples through context can increase inference time and memory use, while parameter-efficient fine-tuning still requires training resources. RTD instead uses task examples to influence the model’s output distribution during decoding.

The method constructs a reference datastore from the supplied training examples. Given an input, it selects suitable references and uses them to adjust the final probability distribution over vocabulary items. Task information therefore affects which tokens the model produces without requiring changes to its parameters. The approach aims to combine rapid adaptation with low inference costs.

The authors evaluate RTD across multiple language models and benchmarks, reporting support for its use in downstream adaptation. They also find that it works alongside traditional augmentation methods, allowing concurrent use rather than requiring a complete replacement of them. Its central contribution is a reference-based decoding mechanism that provides another route for incorporating task examples into generation, with the reported trustworthiness and efficiency benefits grounded in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: RTD adapts language models without fine-tuning by selecting task references that adjust token probabilities during decoding.

title: Reference Trustable Decoding: A Training-Free Augmentation Paradigm for Large Language Models

abstract: The pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models have been increasingly employed to tackle the real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) problem due to their powerful generative image priors. Most of the existing methods start from random noise to reconstruct the high-quality (HQ) image under the guidance of the given low-quality (LQ) image. While promising results have been achieved, such Real-ISR methods require multiple diffusion steps to reproduce the HQ image, increasing the computational cost. Meanwhile, the random noise introduces uncertainty in the output, which is unfriendly to image restoration tasks. To address these issues, we propose a one-step effective diffusion network, namely OSEDiff, for the Real-ISR problem. We argue that the LQ image contains rich information to restore its HQ counterpart, and hence the given LQ image can be directly taken as the starting point for diffusion, eliminating the uncertainty introduced by random noise sampling. We finetune the pre-trained diffusion network with trainable layers to adapt it to complex image degradations. To ensure that the one-step diffusion model could yield HQ Real-ISR output, we apply variational score distillation in the latent space to conduct KL-divergence regularization. As a result, our OSEDiff model can efficiently and effectively generate HQ images in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSEDiff achieves comparable or even better Real-ISR results, in terms of both objective metrics and subjective evaluations, than previous diffusion model-based Real-ISR methods that require dozens or hundreds of steps. The source codes are released at https://github.com/cswry/OSEDiff.

The paper targets both the computational cost of that repeated process and the output uncertainty introduced by sampling the initial noise.

The authors adapt the pretrained network through trainable layers to handle complex degradation. summary.tldr: OSEDiff starts from the low-quality image and uses one diffusion step to achieve results comparable to or better than evaluated multistep methods.

title: One-Step Effective Diffusion Network for Real-World Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Inverse Optimization (IO) is a framework for learning the unknown objective function of an expert decision-maker from a past dataset.In this paper, we extend the hypothesis class of IO objective functions to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), thereby enhancing feature representation to an infinite-dimensional space.We demonstrate that a variant of the representer theorem holds for a specific training loss, allowing the reformulation of the problem as a finite-dimensional convex optimization program.To address scalability issues commonly associated with kernel methods, we propose the Sequential Selection Optimization (SSO) algorithm to efficiently train the proposed Kernel Inverse Optimization (KIO) model.Finally, we validate the generalization capabilities of the proposed KIO model and the effectiveness of the SSO algorithm through learning-from-demonstration tasks on the MuJoCo benchmark.

paragraphs: Inverse optimization learns an expert's unknown objective from records of their decisions. The paper expands the class of objectives this framework can represent by placing them in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This provides an infinite-dimensional feature representation, allowing the learned objective to be expressed in a richer hypothesis class.

An infinite-dimensional formulation could appear difficult to train directly. For a specific training loss, the authors prove a variant of the representer theorem that turns the learning problem into a finite-dimensional convex optimization program. This result links the expressive kernel formulation to a concrete optimization problem without requiring an explicit infinite list of features.

The paper then addresses the computational scaling associated with kernel methods through Sequential Selection Optimization, an algorithm for training the proposed Kernel Inverse Optimization model efficiently. Learning-from-demonstration tasks on the MuJoCo benchmark validate the model's generalization capabilities and the algorithm's effectiveness. The contribution combines a richer representation of expert objectives, a tractable reformulation for the chosen loss, and a training method aimed at scalability.
summary.tldr: Kernel Inverse Optimization learns richer expert objectives through a finite convex reformulation and a training algorithm designed to improve scalability.

title: Scalable Kernel Inverse Optimization

abstract: Detecting text generated by large language models (LLMs) is of great recent interest. With zero-shot methods like DetectGPT, detection capabilities have reached impressive levels. However, the reliability of existing detectors in real-world applications remains underexplored. In this study, we present a new benchmark, DetectRL, highlighting that even state-of-the-art (SOTA) detection techniques still underperformed in this task. We collected human-written datasets from domains where LLMs are particularly prone to misuse. Using popular LLMs, we generated data that better aligns with real-world applications. Unlike previous studies, we employed heuristic rules to create adversarial LLM-generated text, simulating advanced prompt usages, human revisions like word substitutions, and writing errors. Our development of DetectRL reveals the strengths and limitations of current SOTA detectors. More importantly, we analyzed the potential impact of writing styles, model types, attack methods, the text lengths, and real-world human writing factors on different types of detectors. We believe DetectRL could serve as an effective benchmark for assessing detectors in real-world scenarios, evolving with advanced attack methods, thus providing more stressful evaluation to drive the development of more efficient detectors\footnote{Data and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/NLP2CT/DetectRL.

paragraphs: DetectRL examines whether methods for identifying LLM-generated text remain reliable under conditions resembling real use. Strong detection results in existing evaluations leave this question unresolved. The authors build a benchmark from human-written material in domains where LLM misuse is a concern, alongside text generated by popular language models.

The benchmark includes generated text altered through heuristic rules. These changes simulate advanced prompting, human revisions such as word substitutions, and writing errors. Including these variants makes the evaluation sensitive to how text can change between its initial generation and the form a detector eventually receives.

The study analyzes how writing style, generating model, attack method, text length, and aspects of human writing affect different detectors. It reports that even state-of-the-art detection techniques underperform on the benchmark. The contribution is a more stressful evaluation framework that reveals strengths and weaknesses across conditions, rather than a single detection result being treated as evidence of broad real-world reliability.
summary.tldr: DetectRL exposes weaknesses in AI-text detectors using generated text that simulates realistic prompting, revisions, and writing errors.

title: DetectRL: Benchmarking LLM-Generated Text Detection in Real-World Scenarios

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achievedimpressive advancements across numerous disciplines, yet the critical issue of knowledge conflicts, a major source of hallucinations, has rarely been studied. While a few research explored the conflicts between the inherent knowledge of LLMs and the retrieved contextual knowledge, a comprehensive assessment of knowledge conflict in LLMs is still missing. Motivated by this research gap, we firstly propose ConflictBank, the largest benchmark with 7.45M claim-evidence pairs and 553k QA pairs, addressing conflicts from misinformation, temporal discrepancies, and semantic divergences.Using ConflictBank, we conduct the thorough and controlled experiments for a comprehensive understanding of LLM behavior in knowledge conflicts, focusing on three key aspects: (i) conflicts encountered in retrieved knowledge, (ii) conflicts within the models' encoded knowledge, and (iii) the interplay between these conflict forms.Our investigation delves into four model families and twelve LLM instances and provides insights into conflict types, model sizes, and the impact at different stages.We believe that knowledge conflicts represent a critical bottleneck to achieving trustworthy artificial intelligence and hope our work will offer valuable guidance for future model training and development.Resources are available at https://github.com/zhaochen0110/conflictbank.

paragraphs: Language models can encounter incompatible information in retrieved material and in knowledge encoded during training. Such conflicts contribute to hallucinations, yet studying only disagreement between a model and an external passage leaves other conflict patterns unexplored. ConflictBank provides a benchmark for examining these patterns more comprehensively.

The benchmark contains 7.45 million claim-evidence pairs and 553,000 question-answer pairs. It covers conflicts arising from misinformation, differences over time, and semantic divergences. The authors organize their investigation around conflicts in retrieved knowledge, conflicts within encoded knowledge, and interactions between those two sources.

Controlled experiments examine twelve language-model instances from four model families, considering conflict types, model sizes, and effects at different stages. This design supplies a shared basis for investigating how models respond when their available information disagrees. The paper frames knowledge conflict as a major obstacle to trustworthy AI and offers the benchmark and analysis as resources for future training and development.
summary.tldr: ConflictBank benchmarks how language models handle misinformation, temporal discrepancies, and semantic conflicts across retrieved and encoded knowledge.

title: $\texttt{ConflictBank}$: A Benchmark for Evaluating the Influence of Knowledge Conflicts in LLMs

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) of large language models has proven to be a surprisingly effective method of learning a new task from only a few demonstrative examples. In this paper, we shed light on the efficacy of ICL from the viewpoint of statistical learning theory. We develop approximation and generalization error analyses for a transformer model composed of a deep neural network and one linear attention layer, pretrained on nonparametric regression tasks sampled from general function spaces including the Besov space and piecewise $\gamma$-smooth class. In particular, we show that sufficiently trained transformers can achieve -- and even improve upon -- the minimax optimal estimation risk in context by encoding the most relevant basis representations during pretraining. Our analysis extends to high-dimensional or sequential data and distinguishes the \emph{pretraining} and \emph{in-context} generalization gaps, establishing upper and lower bounds w.r.t. both the number of tasks and in-context examples. These findings shed light on the effectiveness of few-shot prompting and the roles of task diversity and representation learning for ICL.

paragraphs: This paper studies in-context learning through statistical learning theory: how a pretrained transformer can use examples in its input to learn a new regression task. The analyzed architecture combines a deep neural network with one linear attention layer. Its pretraining tasks come from broad nonparametric function classes, including Besov spaces and piecewise smooth functions.

The analysis shows that sufficiently trained transformers can attain, and under the studied setup even improve upon, the minimax estimation-risk benchmark by learning relevant basis representations during pretraining. Minimax risk describes performance against the hardest cases in a specified function class. Learned representations are therefore central to the result, connecting previous task experience with efficient learning from context.

The authors separately analyze generalization during pretraining and during in-context learning. They establish upper and lower bounds involving both the number of pretraining tasks and the number of examples in context, with extensions to high-dimensional or sequential data. These conditional theoretical findings help explain the roles of task diversity and representation learning in few-shot prompting for the model and task families studied.
summary.tldr: For a specified transformer and regression-task setup, learned representations enable sufficiently trained models to reach strong theoretical in-context estimation guarantees.

title: Transformers are Minimax Optimal Nonparametric In-Context Learners

abstract: Images contain objects with deformable boundaries, such as the contours of a human face, yet attention operators act on square windows. This mixes features from perceptually unrelated regions, which can degrade the quality of a denoiser. One can exclude pixels using an estimate of perceptual groupings, such as superpixels, but the naive use of superpixels can be theoretically and empirically worse than standard attention. Using superpixel probabilities rather than superpixel assignments, this paper proposes soft superpixel neighborhood attention (SNA), which interpolates between the existing neighborhood attention and the naive superpixel neighborhood attention. This paper presents theoretical results showing SNA is the optimal denoiser under a latent superpixel model. SNA outperforms alternative local attention modules on image denoising, and we compare the superpixels learned from denoising with those learned with supervision.

paragraphs: Image denoising benefits from combining information from related pixels, but standard attention windows are square while object boundaries are irregular. A window can therefore mix features from perceptually different regions. Superpixels offer a way to group related pixels, yet the paper shows that simply restricting attention to hard superpixel assignments can perform worse than ordinary attention.

Soft Superpixel Neighborhood Attention, or SNA, replaces those fixed assignments with probabilities of superpixel membership. This allows grouping uncertainty to influence attention instead of forcing a strict decision about which pixels belong together. The method interpolates between ordinary neighborhood attention and the naive superpixel-based version, connecting local spatial processing with probabilistic perceptual grouping.

The authors prove that SNA is an optimal denoiser under a latent superpixel model. This is a model-dependent theoretical result, rather than a claim of optimality for every image distribution. Experiments show better image denoising than alternative local attention modules. The paper also compares superpixels learned through denoising with supervised superpixels, examining the groupings that emerge from the reconstruction task.
summary.tldr: SNA uses probabilistic superpixel membership to improve local attention for denoising and is optimal under a latent superpixel model.

title: Soft Superpixel Neighborhood Attention

abstract: One of the roadblocks for training generalist robotic models today is heterogeneity. Previous robot learning methods often collect data to train with one specific embodiment for one task, which is expensive and prone to overfitting. This work studies the problem of learning policy representations through heterogeneous pre-training on robot data across different embodiments and tasks at scale. We propose Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers (HPT), which pre-train a large, shareable trunk of a policy neural network to learn a task and embodiment agnostic shared representation. This general architecture aligns the specific proprioception and vision inputs from distinct embodiments to a short sequence of tokens and then processes such tokens to map to control robots for different tasks. Leveraging the recent large-scale multi-embodiment real-world robotic datasets as well as simulation, deployed robots, and human video datasets, we investigate pre-training policies across heterogeneity. We conduct experiments to investigate the scaling behaviors of training objectives, to the extent of 52 datasets. HPTs outperform several baselines and enhance the fine-tuned policy performance by over 20% on unseen tasks in multiple simulator benchmarks and real-world settings. See the project website (liruiw.github.io/hpt) for code and videos.

paragraphs: Robot learning data vary across bodies, sensors, and tasks, making it difficult to train a shared model. Collecting a separate dataset for each robot-task combination is expensive and can encourage overfitting. This paper investigates whether heterogeneous pretraining can instead learn policy representations that transfer across different robot embodiments and tasks.

Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers, or HPTs, align each embodiment's proprioceptive and visual inputs into a short token sequence. Proprioception describes information about the robot's own physical state. A large shared transformer trunk then processes these tokens, providing a common representation for policies controlling different robots. The architecture separates varied inputs from the shared processing that pretraining aims to improve.

The study explores scaling across as many as 52 datasets, drawing on real robots, simulation, deployed systems, and human video. HPTs outperform several baselines and improve fine-tuned policy performance by over 20% on unseen tasks across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world settings. These findings support heterogeneous pretraining as a way to make diverse experience useful for later robot-policy learning.
summary.tldr: HPT shares a pretrained transformer across diverse robot inputs, improving fine-tuned performance on unseen tasks by over 20% in the reported evaluations.

title: Scaling Proprioceptive-Visual Learning with Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers

abstract: The collected data in recommender systems generally suffers selection bias. Considerable works are proposed to address selection bias induced by observed user and item features, but they fail when hidden features (e.g., user age or salary) that affect both user selection mechanism and feedback exist, which is called hidden confounding. To tackle this issue, methods based on sensitivity analysis and leveraging a few randomized controlled trial (RCT) data for model calibration are proposed. However, the former relies on strong assumptions of hidden confounding strength, whereas the latter relies on the expensive RCT data, thereby limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose to employ heterogeneous observational data to address hidden confounding, wherein some data is subject to hidden confounding while the remaining is not. We argue that such setup is more aligned with practical scenarios, especially when some users do not have complete personal information (thus assumed with hidden confounding), while others do have (thus assumed without hidden confounding). To achieve unbiased learning, we propose a novel meta-learning based debiasing method called MetaDebias. This method explicitly models oracle error imputation and hidden confounding bias, and utilizes bi-level optimization for model training. Extensive experiments on three public datasets validate our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the presence of hidden confounding, regardless of RCT data availability.

paragraphs: Recommendation data can be biased because the factors influencing what users select also influence their feedback. Correcting for recorded features is insufficient when relevant factors remain hidden. Existing approaches described in the paper either assume substantial knowledge about the strength of this hidden confounding or use costly randomized trial data to calibrate a model.

MetaDebias instead uses a mixture of observational datasets, assuming that some are affected by hidden confounding and others are not. The motivating case involves users with incomplete personal information alongside users with complete information. This distinction is an assumption of the setup: the latter group is treated as providing data without hidden confounding.

The method uses meta-learning and a two-level optimization procedure to jointly model oracle error imputation and bias from hidden confounding. Experiments on three public datasets report state-of-the-art performance under hidden confounding, both with and without randomized trial data. The findings support heterogeneous observational data as a useful resource for debiasing when the proposed mixture assumption applies.
summary.tldr: MetaDebias uses observational datasets with differing confounding conditions to improve recommendation learning, with or without randomized trial data.

title: Addressing Hidden Confounding with Heterogeneous Observational Datasets for Recommendation

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has emerged as a prominent architecture for scaling model size while maintaining computational efficiency. In MoE, each token in the input sequence activates a different subset of experts determined by a routing mechanism. However, the unchosen experts in MoE models do not contribute to the output, potentially leading to underutilization of the model's capacity.In this work, we first conduct exploratory studies to demonstrate that increasing the number of activated experts does not necessarily improve and can even degrade the output quality. Then, we show that output distributions from an MoE model using different routing strategies substantially differ, indicating that different experts do not always act synergistically. Motivated by these findings, we propose **S**elf-**C**ontrast **M**ixture-**o**f-**E**xperts (SCMoE), a training-free strategy that utilizes unchosen experts in a self-contrast manner during inference. In SCMoE, the next-token probabilities are determined by contrasting the outputs from strong and weak activation using the same MoE model.Our method is conceptually simple and computationally lightweight, as it incurs minimal latency compared to greedy decoding. Experiments on several benchmarks (GSM8K, StrategyQA, MBPP and HumanEval) demonstrate that SCMoE can consistently enhance Mixtral 8x7B’s reasoning capability across various domains. For example, it improves the accuracy on GSM8K from 61.79 to 66.94. Moreover, combining SCMoE with self-consistency yields additional gains, increasing major@20 accuracy from 75.59 to 78.31.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models route each token to a subset of their experts, leaving others unused for that token. Activating additional experts might appear to offer an easy improvement, but the paper's exploratory studies show that it does not necessarily help and can reduce output quality. Different routing strategies also produce substantially different output distributions.

SCMoE uses these differences through self-contrast during inference. It determines next-token probabilities by contrasting outputs from strong and weak activation within the same model, giving unchosen experts a role in generation. The method requires no training, and the authors report minimal added latency compared with greedy decoding.

Experiments with Mixtral 8x7B show consistent reasoning improvements across GSM8K, StrategyQA, MBPP, and HumanEval. GSM8K accuracy rises from 61.79 to 66.94, while combining the method with self-consistency raises major@20 accuracy from 75.59 to 78.31. The results support using differences between expert activation patterns as useful inference-time information, with additional gains possible when combined with self-consistency.
summary.tldr: SCMoE improves tested MoE reasoning by contrasting strong and weak expert activations during inference without additional training.

title: Unchosen Experts Can Contribute Too: Unleashing MoE Models’ Power by Self-Contrast

abstract: Aligning generative models with human preference via RLHF typically suffers from overoptimization, where an imperfectly learned reward model can misguide the generative model to output even undesired responses. We investigate this problem in a principled manner by identifying the source of the issue as the distributional shift and uncertainty of human preference in dataset. To mitigate overoptimization, we first propose a theoretical algorithm which optimizes the policy against an adversarially chosen reward model, one that simultaneously minimizes its MLE loss and a reward penalty term. The penalty pessimistically biases the uncertain rewards so as to prevent the policy from choosing actions with spursiouly high proxy rewards, resulting in provable sample efficiency of the algorithm under a partial coverage style condition. Moving from theory to practice, the proposed algorithm further enjoys an equivalent but surprisingly easy to implement form. With a clever usage of the equivalence between reward models and the corresponding optimal policy, the algorithm features a simple objective that combines (i) a preference optimization loss that directly aligns the policy with human preference, and (ii) a supervised learning loss which explicitly imitates the policy with a baseline distribution. In the context of aligning large language models (LLM), this objective fuses the direct preference optimization (DPO) loss with the supervised fune-tuning (SFT) loss to help mitigate the overoptimization towards undesired responses, for which we name the algorithm Regularized Preference Optimization (RPO).Experiments of aligning LLMs demonstrate the improved performance of our method when compared with DPO baselines. Our work sheds light on the interplay between preference optimization and SFT in tuning LLMs with both theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback can overoptimize an imperfect reward model, producing unwanted responses that receive high proxy rewards. This paper connects the problem to distribution shift and uncertainty in preference data. It develops a method that treats uncertain reward estimates pessimistically, reducing the incentive to exploit rewards that are spuriously high.

The theoretical algorithm optimizes the policy against an adversarially chosen reward model. That reward model balances fitting the data through maximum likelihood with a reward penalty. The authors prove sample efficiency under a partial-coverage-style condition, so the guarantee depends on the stated kind of data coverage rather than applying without qualification.

The paper then derives an equivalent, simpler objective using the relationship between reward models and their optimal policies. For language models, this combines direct preference optimization with supervised fine-tuning that imitates a baseline distribution. Called Regularized Preference Optimization, the method improves performance over DPO baselines in the reported experiments. The equivalence explains how an SFT term can serve as an implicit adversarial regularizer during preference alignment.
summary.tldr: Regularized Preference Optimization combines DPO and SFT losses to implement a pessimistic reward objective that mitigates overoptimization.

title: Provably Mitigating Overoptimization in RLHF: Your SFT Loss is Implicitly an Adversarial Regularizer

abstract: Diffusion models hold great potential for accelerating antibody design, but their performance is so far limited by the number of antibody-antigen complexes used for model training. Meanwhile, AlphaFold3-like protein folding models, pre-trained on a large corpus of crystal structures, have acquired a broad understanding of biomolecular interaction. Based on this insight, we develop a new antigen-conditioned antibody design model by adapting the diffusion module of AlphaFold3-like models for sequence-structure co-diffusion. Specifically, we extend their structure diffusion module with a sequence diffusion head and fine-tune the entire protein folding model for antibody sequence-structure co-design. Our benchmark results show that sequence-structure co-diffusion models not only surpass state-of-the-art antibody design methods in performance but also maintain structure prediction accuracy comparable to the original folding model. Notably, in the antibody co-design task, our method achieves a CDR-H3 recovery rate of 65% for typical antibodies, outperforming the baselines by 87%, and attains a remarkable 63% recovery rate for nanobodies.

paragraphs: Antibody design models face a shortage of antibody-antigen complexes for training. This paper draws on protein folding models resembling AlphaFold3, which have already learned from a large collection of crystal structures. The authors use that broader understanding of biomolecular interactions as a starting point for designing antibodies conditioned on an antigen.

They adapt the folding model's diffusion module to generate antibody sequence and structure together. A sequence diffusion head is added to the existing structure diffusion module, and the entire folding model is fine-tuned for the joint design task. This transfers knowledge from structure prediction into a model that coordinates the two design outputs.

Benchmarks show better antibody-design performance than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods while retaining structure-prediction accuracy comparable to the original folding model. The reported CDR-H3 recovery rate is 65% for typical antibodies, outperforming baselines by 87%, and 63% for nanobodies. These findings support repurposing broadly pretrained folding models for joint antibody design and demonstrate improvements on the reported recovery and prediction measures.
summary.tldr: Adapting AlphaFold3-like folding models for joint sequence and structure diffusion improves benchmark antibody design while preserving comparable structure-prediction accuracy.

title: Repurposing AlphaFold3-like Protein Folding Models for Antibody Sequence and Structure Co-design

abstract: 3D reconstruction of indoor and urban environments is a prominent research topic with various downstream applications. However, existing geometric priors for addressing low-texture regions in indoor and urban settings often lack global consistency. Moreover, Gaussian Splatting and implicit SDF fields often suffer from discontinuities or exhibit computational inefficiencies, resulting in a loss of detail. To address these issues, we propose an Atlanta-world guided implicit-structured Gaussian Splatting that achieves smooth indoor and urban scene reconstruction while preserving high-frequency details and rendering efficiency. By leveraging the Atlanta-world model, we ensure the accurate surface reconstruction for low-texture regions, while the proposed novel implicit-structured GS representations provide smoothness without sacrificing efficiency and high-frequency details. Specifically, we propose a semantic GS representation to predict the probability of all semantic regions and deploy a structure plane regularization with learnable plane indicators for global accurate surface reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both indoor and urban scenes, delivering superior surface reconstruction quality.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both indoor and urban scenes, delivering superior surface reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: AtlasGS addresses surface reconstruction in indoor and urban scenes, particularly regions with little visual texture. Such areas provide weak cues for recovering geometry, making structural assumptions useful. The paper argues that existing geometric guidance often lacks consistency across the whole scene, while Gaussian Splatting and implicit surface representations can introduce discontinuities or computational costs.

The method combines an Atlanta-world structural model with an implicit-structured Gaussian representation. The structural model guides reconstruction in low-texture regions, and the representation is designed to produce smooth surfaces while retaining fine detail and rendering efficiency. These components address both the large-scale organization of a scene and the quality of its local surfaces.

More specifically, AtlasGS predicts probabilities for semantic regions and applies structural plane regularization with learnable plane indicators. This makes scene structure part of the reconstruction objective rather than relying only on local visual evidence. Experiments on indoor and urban scenes report better surface reconstruction than state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the combination of global structural guidance and a detailed, efficient representation.
summary.tldr: AtlasGS combines global structural guidance with implicit-structured Gaussians to improve smooth, detailed reconstruction of indoor and urban surfaces.

title: AtlasGS: Atlanta-world Guided Surface Reconstruction with Implicit Structured Gaussians

abstract: Solving inverse problems—recovering signals from incomplete or noisy measurements—is fundamental in science and engineering. Score-based generative models (SGMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for this task. Two main paradigms have formed: unsupervised approaches that adapt pretrained generative models to inverse problems, and supervised bridge methods that train stochastic processes conditioned on paired clean and corrupted data. While the former typically assume knowledge of the measurement model, the latter have largely overlooked this structural information. We introduce System-embedded Diffusion Bridge Models (SDBs), a new class of supervised bridge methods that explicitly embed the known linear measurement system into the coefficients of a matrix-valued SDE. This principled integration yields consistent improvements across diverse linear inverse problems and demonstrates robust generalization under system misspecification between training and deployment, offering a promising solution to real-world applications.

The stated scope is linear measurement systems, and the mismatch results describe the robustness demonstrated in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Embedding known linear measurement structure into supervised diffusion bridges improves signal recovery and reported robustness to deployment-time system mismatch.

title: System-Embedded Diffusion Bridge Models

abstract: Real-world applications are stretching context windows to hundreds of thousand of tokens while Large Language Models (LLMs) swell from billions to trillions of parameters. This dual expansion send compute and memory costs skyrocketing, making $\textit{token compression}$ indispensable. We introduce Vision Centric Token Compression ($\textbf{Vist}$), a $\textit{slow–fast}$ compression framework that mirrors human reading: the $\textit{fast}$ path renders distant tokens into images, letting a $\textbf{frozen, lightweight vision encoder}$ skim the low-salience context; the $\textit{slow}$ path feeds the proximal window into the LLM for fine-grained reasoning. A Probability-Informed Visual Enhancement (PVE) objective masks high-frequency tokens during training, steering the Resampler to concentrate on semantically rich regions—just as skilled reader gloss over function words. On eleven in-context learning benchmarks, $\textbf{Vist}$ achieves the same accuracy with 2.3$\times$ fewer tokens, cutting FLOPs by 16\% and memory by 50\%. This method delivers remarkable results, outperforming the strongest text encoder-based compression method CEPE by $\textbf{7.6}$\% on average over benchmarks like TriviaQA, NQ, PopQA, NLUI, and CLIN, setting a new standard for token efficiency in LLMs. The source code will be released.

The framework uses this division to retain context while reducing the number of tokens processed.

The intended effect is to make the compressed visual representation selective about what it preserves. The paper frames this as analogous to skimming less salient material while reading nearby content more carefully.

It also reports a 7.6% average improvement over the text-encoder compression method CEPE on the cited benchmark collection. These results support rendering text visually as a useful compression strategy for the evaluated long-context tasks.
summary.tldr: Vist compresses distant text through a lightweight vision encoder, matching accuracy with 2.3 times fewer tokens across eleven benchmarks.

title: Vision-centric Token Compression in Large Language Model

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a trending paradigm for training large language models (LLMs), particularly for reasoning tasks. Effective RL for LLMs requires massive parallelization and poses an urgent need for efficient training systems. Most existing large-scale RL systems for LLMs are synchronous by alternating generation and training in a batch setting, where the rollouts in each training batch are generated by the same (or latest) model. This stabilizes RL training but suffers from severe system-level inefficiency. Generation must wait until the longest output in the batch is completed before model update, resulting in GPU underutilization. We present AReaL, a fully asynchronous RL system that completely decouples generation from training. Rollout workers in AReaL continuously generate new outputs without waiting, while training workers update the model whenever a batch of data is collected. AReaL also incorporates a collection of system-level optimizations, leading to substantially higher GPU utilization. To stabilize RL training, AReaL balances the workload of rollout and training workers to control data staleness, and adopts a staleness-enhanced PPO variant to better handle outdated training samples. Extensive experiments on math and code reasoning benchmarks show that AReaL achieves up to 2.77x training speedup compared to synchronous systems with the same number of GPUs and matched or even improved final performance. The code of AReaL is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/AReaL/.

paragraphs: Training language models with reinforcement learning involves generating candidate responses and then updating the model from those responses. In synchronous systems, a batch cannot move forward until its longest response finishes. That coordination helps keep training data current, but leaves computing resources waiting when response lengths differ.

AReaL separates generation from training. Generation workers keep producing responses, while training workers update the model whenever enough data is available. This overlap improves GPU utilization, but creates a statistical challenge: some responses were generated by older versions of the model. AReaL balances the two workloads to control that staleness and uses a modified PPO training procedure designed to handle outdated samples.

On mathematics and code reasoning benchmarks, the system achieves up to 2.77 times faster training than synchronous systems using the same number of GPUs. Final performance matches or improves on those comparisons. The result shows that, in these experiments, carefully managing stale data allows higher hardware utilization without losing the benefits of reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: AReaL overlaps response generation and training to achieve up to 2.77 times faster reinforcement learning with matched or improved final performance.

title: AREAL: A Large-Scale Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Reasoning

abstract: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) poses a formidable challenge for autonomous agents, requiring seamless integration of natural language instructions and visual observations to navigate complex 3D indoor spaces. Existing approaches often falter in long-horizon tasks due to limited scene understanding, inefficient planning, and lack of robust decision-making frameworks. We introduce the \textbf{Hierarchical Semantic-Augmented Navigation (HSAN)} framework, a groundbreaking approach that redefines VLN-CE through three synergistic innovations. First, HSAN constructs a dynamic hierarchical semantic scene graph, leveraging vision-language models to capture multi-level environmental representations—from objects to regions to zones—enabling nuanced spatial reasoning. Second, it employs an optimal transport-based topological planner, grounded in Kantorovich's duality, to select long-term goals by balancing semantic relevance and spatial accessibility with theoretical guarantees of optimality. Third, a graph-aware reinforcement learning policy ensures precise low-level control, navigating subgoals while robustly avoiding obstacles. By integrating spectral graph theory, optimal transport, and advanced multi-modal learning, HSAN addresses the shortcomings of static maps and heuristic planners prevalent in prior work. Extensive experiments on multiple challenging VLN-CE datasets demonstrate that HSAN achieves state-of-the-art performance, with significant improvements in navigation success and generalization to unseen environments.

paragraphs: Following language instructions through a continuous indoor environment requires connecting what an agent sees with where it should go. HSAN addresses these demands through a hierarchy that links environmental meaning, long-term goal selection, and low-level navigation.

The planner is grounded in Kantorovich duality, and the authors provide theoretical optimality guarantees for this planning component.

Experiments across multiple vision-language navigation datasets report state-of-the-art performance, including improved navigation success and generalization to unseen environments. The framework's contribution is the coordination of semantic representations and structured planning with control; the planner's optimality guarantees should be understood separately from the empirical performance of the complete navigation system.
summary.tldr: HSAN combines hierarchical scene graphs, optimal transport planning, and reinforcement learning control to improve instruction-following navigation.

title: Hierarchical Semantic-Augmented Navigation: Optimal Transport and Graph-Driven Reasoning for Vision-Language Navigation

abstract: Fluorescence microscopy, while being a key driver for progress in the life sciences, is also subject to technical limitations. To overcome them, computational multiplexing techniques have recently been proposed, which allow multiple cellular structures to be captured in a single image and later be unmixed. Existing image decomposition methods are trained on a set of superimposed input images and the respective unmixed target images. It is critical to note that the relative strength (mixing ratio) of the superimposed images for a given input is a priori unknown. However, existing methods are trained on a fixed intensity ratio of superimposed inputs, making them not cognizant of the range of relative intensities that can occur in fluorescence microscopy. In this work, we propose a novel method called scSplit that is cognizant of the severity of the above-mentioned mixing ratio. Our idea is based on InDI, a popular iterative method for image restoration, and an ideal starting point to embrace the unknown mixing ratio in any given input. We introduce (i) a suitably trained regressor network that predicts the degradation level (mixing asymmetry) of a given input image and (ii) a degradation-specific normalization module, enabling degradation-aware inference across all mixing ratios. We show that this method solves two relevant tasks in fluorescence microscopy, namely image splitting and bleedthrough removal, and empirically demonstrate the applicability of scSplit on 5 public datasets. The source code with pre-trained models is hosted at https://github.com/juglab/scSplit/.

title: scSplit: Bringing Severity Cognizance to Image Decomposition in Fluorescence Microscopy

abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) in scientific machine learning is increasingly critical as neural networks are widely adopted to tackle complex problems across diverse scientific disciplines. For physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), a prominent model in scientific machine learning, uncertainty is typically quantified using Bayesian or dropout methods. However, both approaches suffer from a fundamental limitation: the prior distribution or dropout rate required to construct honest confidence sets cannot be determined without additional information. In this paper, we propose a novel method within the framework of extended fiducial inference (EFI) to provide rigorous uncertainty quantification for PINNs. The proposed method leverages a narrow-neck hyper-network to learn the parameters of the PINN and quantify their uncertainty based on imputed random errors in the observations. This approach overcomes the limitations of Bayesian and dropout methods, enabling the construction of honest confidence sets based solely on observed data. This advancement represents a significant breakthrough for PINNs, greatly enhancing their reliability, interpretability, and applicability to real-world scientific and engineering challenges. Moreover, it establishes a new theoretical framework for EFI, extending its application to large-scale models, eliminating the need for sparse hyper-networks, and significantly improving the automaticity and robustness of statistical inference.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Extended Fiducial Inference

abstract: Enhancing large language models by simply scaling up datasets has begun to yield diminishing returns, shifting the spotlight to data quality. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) has emerged as a powerful technique for generating high-quality chain-of-thought data, yet conventional approaches typically retain only the top-scoring trajectory from the search tree, discarding sibling nodes that often contain valuable partial insights, recurrent error patterns, and alternative reasoning strategies. This unconditional rejection of non-optimal reasoning branches may waste vast amounts of informative data in the whole search tree. We propose SIGMA (Sibling Guided Monte Carlo Augmentation), a novel framework that reintegrates these discarded sibling nodes to refine LLM reasoning. SIGMA forges semantic links among sibling nodes along each search path and applies a two-stage refinement: a critique model identifies overlooked strengths and weaknesses across the sibling set, and a revision model conducts text-based backpropagation to refine the top-scoring trajectory in light of this comparative feedback. By recovering and amplifying the underutilized but valuable signals from non-optimal reasoning branches, SIGMA substantially improves reasoning trajectories. On the challenging MATH benchmark, our SIGMA-tuned 7B model achieves 54.92\% accuracy using only 30K samples, outperforming state-of-the-art models trained on 590K samples. This result highlights that our sibling-guided optimization not only significantly reduces data usage but also significantly boosts LLM reasoning.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Search can produce reasoning examples for training language models, but conventional pipelines often retain only the highest-scoring path. SIGMA examines the information lost when neighboring branches are discarded. Those branches can contain useful partial reasoning, alternative strategies, or repeated mistakes even when they do not provide the best complete answer.

summary.tldr: SIGMA improves reasoning training data by using discarded sibling search branches to critique and revise the highest-scoring trajectory.

title: SIGMA: Refining Large Language Model Reasoning via Sibling-Guided Monte Carlo Augmentation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged with many intellectual capacities. While numerous benchmarks assess their intelligence, limited attention has been given to their ability to explore—an essential capacity for discovering new information and adapting to novel environments in both natural and artificial systems. The extent to which LLMs can effectively explore, particularly in open-ended tasks, remains unclear. This study investigates whether LLMs can surpass humans in exploration during an open-ended task, using Little Alchemy 2 as a paradigm, where agents combine elements to discover new ones. Results show most LLMs underperform compared to humans, except for the o1 model, with those traditional LLMs relying primarily on uncertainty-driven strategies, unlike humans who balance uncertainty and empowerment. Results indicate that traditional reasoning-focused LLMs, such as GPT-4o, exhibit a significantly faster and less detailed reasoning process, limiting their exploratory performance. In contrast, the DeepSeek reasoning model demonstrates prolonged, iterative thought processes marked by repetitive analysis of combinations and past trials, reflecting a more thorough and human-like exploration strategy. Representational analysis of the models with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) revealed that uncertainty and choices are represented at earlier transformer blocks, while empowerment values are processed later, causing LLMs to think too fast and make premature decisions, hindering effective exploration. These findings shed light on the limitations of LLM exploration and suggest directions for improving their adaptability.

paragraphs: This paper examines exploration through Little Alchemy 2, an open-ended game in which combining elements reveals new ones. The question is whether language models can explore more effectively than people. Most models in the study fall below human performance, with o1 identified as the exception.
