summary.tldr: In Little Alchemy 2, most tested language models explore less effectively than humans, with analyses linking premature choices to early uncertainty processing.

title: Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively

abstract: Recently, semantically constrained adversarial examples (SemanticAE), which are directly generated from natural language instructions, have become a promising avenue for future research due to their flexible attacking forms, but have not been thoroughly explored yet. To generate SemanticAEs, current methods fall short of satisfactory attacking ability as the key underlying factors of semantic uncertainty in human instructions, such as $\textit{referring diversity}$, $\textit{descriptive incompleteness}$, and $\textit{boundary ambiguity}$, have not been fully investigated. To tackle the issues, this paper develops a multi-dimensional $\textbf{ins}$truction $\textbf{u}$ncertainty $\textbf{r}$eduction ($\textbf{InSUR}$) framework to generate more satisfactory SemanticAE, $\textit{i.e.}$, transferable, adaptive, and effective. Specifically, in the dimension of the sampling method, we propose the residual-driven attacking direction stabilization to alleviate the unstable adversarial optimization caused by the diversity of language references. By coarsely predicting the language-guided sampling process, the optimization process will be stabilized by the designed ResAdv-DDIM sampler, therefore releasing the transferable and robust adversarial capability of multi-step diffusion models. In task modeling, we propose the context-encoded attacking scenario constraint to supplement the missing knowledge from incomplete human instructions. Guidance masking and renderer integration are proposed to regulate the constraints of 2D/3D SemanticAE, activating stronger scenario-adapted attacks. Moreover, in the dimension of generator evaluation, we propose the semantic-abstracted attacking evaluation enhancement by clarifying the evaluation boundary based on the label taxonomy, facilitating the development of more effective SemanticAE generators. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the transfer attack performance of InSUR. Besides, it is worth highlighting that we realize the reference-free generation of semantically constrained 3D adversarial examples by utilizing language-guided 3D generation models for the first time.

The authors argue that instruction uncertainty weakens existing approaches: different expressions can refer to similar things, descriptions can omit relevant context, and the boundaries used to judge an attack can be ambiguous. InSUR addresses these three issues through sampling, task modeling, and evaluation.

For sampling, a residual-driven method stabilizes the adversarial optimization direction. Its ResAdv-DDIM sampler coarsely predicts the language-guided sampling process to reduce instability associated with varied references. For task modeling, contextual constraints supply information missing from instructions. Guidance masking and renderer integration help enforce scenario constraints for two-dimensional and three-dimensional examples.

For evaluation, InSUR uses label taxonomies to clarify semantic boundaries, making the criteria for successful generation more explicit. The authors report superior transfer-attack performance in extensive experiments. They also report the first reference-free generation of semantically constrained three-dimensional adversarial examples using language-guided 3D generation models. The contribution connects attack effectiveness to how language instructions are interpreted and evaluated, showing that ambiguity can affect the entire generation pipeline.
summary.tldr: InSUR improves language-guided adversarial generation by reducing uncertainty in sampling, scenario constraints, and semantic evaluation.

title: Exploring Semantic-constrained Adversarial Example with Instruction Uncertainty Reduction

abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have spurred transformative applications in various domains, ranging from open-source to proprietary LLMs. However, jailbreak attacks, which aim to break safety alignment and user compliance by tricking the target LLMs into answering harmful and risky responses, are becoming an urgent concern. The practice of red-teaming for LLMs is to proactively explore potential risks and error-prone instances before the release of frontier AI technology. This paper proposes an agentic workflow to automate and scale the red-teaming process of LLMs through the Composition-of-Principles (CoP) framework, where human users provide a set of red-teaming principles as instructions to an AI agent to automatically orchestrate effective red-teaming strategies and generate jailbreak prompts. Distinct from existing red-teaming methods, our CoP framework provides a unified and extensible framework to encompass and orchestrate human-provided red-teaming principles to enable the automated discovery of new red-teaming strategies. When tested against leading LLMs, CoP reveals unprecedented safety risks by finding novel jailbreak prompts and improving the best-known single-turn attack success rate by up to 13.8 times.

paragraphs: Red-teaming probes language models for failures before deployment, including prompts that cause them to produce harmful responses despite their safety training. This paper proposes an automated workflow for expanding that testing. Its starting point is a collection of red-teaming principles supplied by people, which an AI agent uses to organize its search.

The Composition-of-Principles framework combines and orchestrates those instructions to develop testing strategies and generate jailbreak prompts. The authors present it as a unified, extensible way to incorporate human-provided principles. Its purpose is to automate the discovery of new strategies, allowing the search to extend beyond individually specified tests.

When evaluated against leading language models, CoP discovers novel jailbreak prompts and improves the best-known single-turn attack success rate by up to 13.8 times. This is a reported maximum improvement in the tested setting, not a uniform gain across all models. The result indicates that composing testing principles can expose safety weaknesses that existing red-teaming approaches had not found as effectively.
summary.tldr: CoP automates the composition of human-supplied red-teaming principles, discovering jailbreaks with up to a 13.8-fold improvement in single-turn attack success.

title: CoP: Agentic Red-teaming for Large Language Models using Composition of Principles

abstract: As the era of autonomous agents making decisions on behalf of users unfolds, ensuring contextual integrity (CI) -- what is the appropriate information to share while carrying out a certain task -- becomes a central question to the field. We posit that CI demands a form of reasoning where the agent needs to reason about the context in which it is operating. To test this, we first prompt LLMs to reason explicitly about CI when deciding what information to disclose. We then extend this approach by developing a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that further instills in models the reasoning necessary to achieve CI. Using a synthetic, automatically created, dataset of only $\sim700$ examples but with diverse contexts and information disclosure norms, we show that our method substantially reduces inappropriate information disclosure while maintaining task performance across multiple model sizes and families. Importantly, improvements transfer from this synthetic dataset to established CI benchmarks such as PrivacyLens that has human annotations and evaluates privacy leakage of AI assistants in actions and tool calls.

paragraphs: An assistant acting for a user must decide which information is appropriate to share for the task at hand. The paper studies this as contextual integrity: disclosure depends on the situation and its information-sharing norms. The authors propose that making these decisions requires reasoning about the surrounding context.

They first prompt language models to reason explicitly about contextual integrity before deciding what to disclose. They then develop a reinforcement learning framework to teach that reasoning. Training uses an automatically generated synthetic dataset of roughly 700 examples, covering varied contexts and disclosure norms. The approach connects privacy decisions to the task the assistant is trying to complete.

Across multiple model sizes and families, the method substantially reduces inappropriate disclosure while maintaining task performance. Improvements also transfer to established evaluations, including PrivacyLens, which uses human annotations and examines leakage through assistant actions and tool calls. This transfer is a central result: learning from a small synthetic collection improves behavior on a separate benchmark involving operational information sharing.
summary.tldr: Training models to reason about context reduces inappropriate information disclosure while preserving task performance, with gains transferring to PrivacyLens.

title: Contextual Integrity in LLMs via Reasoning and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: State-of-the-art medical multi-modal LLMs (med-MLLMs), such as LLaVA-Med and BioMedGPT, primarily depend on scaling model size and data volume, with training driven largely by autoregressive objectives. However, we reveal that this approach can lead to weak vision-language alignment, making these models overly dependent on costly instruction-following data. To address this, we introduce ExGra-Med, a novel multi-graph alignment framework that jointly aligns images, instruction responses, and extended captions in the latent space, advancing semantic grounding and cross-modal coherence. To scale to large LLMs (e.g., LLaMa-7B), we develop an efficient end-to-end training scheme using black-box gradient estimation, enabling fast and scalable optimization. Empirically, ExGra-Med matches LLaVA-Med’s performance using just 10\% of pre-training data, achieving a 20.13\% gain on VQA-RAD and approaching full-data performance. It also outperforms strong baselines like BioMedGPT and RadFM on visual chatbot and zero-shot classification tasks, demonstrating its promise for efficient, high-quality vision-language integration in medical AI.

paragraphs: Medical models that combine images and language need their visual and textual representations to agree. The authors find that increasing model size and training data while relying mainly on next-token prediction can leave this alignment weak. That weakness can make models heavily dependent on expensive instruction-following examples.

ExGra-Med addresses the issue through a framework that jointly aligns medical images, instruction responses, and extended captions in a shared latent space. Its multiple graphs organize these relationships to improve semantic grounding and coherence across modalities. To make this training practical for large language models, the authors introduce an end-to-end optimization scheme based on black-box gradient estimation.

Together, these results support better cross-modal alignment as a promising route to more data-efficient medical vision-language modeling.
summary.tldr: ExGra-Med aligns medical images and text through multiple graphs, achieving strong results with substantially less pre-training data.

title: ExGra-Med: Extended Context Graph Alignment for Medical Vision-Language Models

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) methods have gained significant attention for enhancing the performance of vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP during inference, without requiring additional labeled data. However, current TTA researches generally suffer from major limitations such as duplication of baseline results, limited evaluation metrics, inconsistent experimental settings, and insufficient analysis. These problems hinder fair comparisons between TTA methods and make it difficult to assess their practical strengths and weaknesses. To address these challenges, we introduce TTA-VLM, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating TTA methods on VLMs. Our benchmark implements 8 episodic TTA and 7 online TTA methods within a unified and reproducible framework, and evaluates them across 15 widely used datasets. Unlike prior studies focused solely on CLIP, we extend the evaluation to SigLIP—a model trained with a Sigmoid loss—and include training-time tuning methods such as CoOp, MaPLe, and TeCoA to assess generality. Beyond classification accuracy, TTA-VLM incorporates various evaluation metrics, including robustness, calibration, out-of-distribution detection, and stability, enabling a more holistic assessment of TTA methods. Through extensive experiments, we find that 1) existing TTA methods produce limited gains compared to the previous pioneering work; 2) current TTA methods exhibit poor collaboration with training-time fine-tuning methods; 3) accuracy gains frequently come at the cost of reduced model trustworthiness. We release TTA-VLM to provide fair comparison and comprehensive evaluation of TTA methods for VLMs, and we hope it encourages the community to develop more reliable and generalizable TTA strategies. The code is available in https://github.com/TomSheng21/tta-vlm.

paragraphs: TTA-VLM examines whether test-time adaptation delivers meaningful improvements for vision-language models. These methods adapt during inference without additional labeled data, but inconsistent settings and narrow evaluation can obscure their practical value. The paper introduces a unified, reproducible benchmark to make comparisons more informative.

The benchmark implements eight episodic and seven online adaptation methods across fifteen datasets. It evaluates both CLIP and SigLIP and includes training-time tuning methods to test how adaptation interacts with prior tuning. summary.tldr: TTA-VLM finds limited recent adaptation gains and frequent trustworthiness trade-offs through a unified evaluation beyond accuracy.

title: The Illusion of Progress? A Critical Look at Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models

abstract: The conventional approach in differential privacy (DP) literature formulates the privacy-utility tradeoff with a "privacy-first" perspective: for a predetermined level of privacy, a certain utility is achievable. However, practitioners often operate under a "utility-first" paradigm, prioritizing a desired level of utility and then determining the corresponding privacy cost. Wu et al. [2019] initiated a formal study of this ``utility-first'' perspective by introducing ex-post DP. They demonstrated that by adding correlated Laplace noise and progressively reducing it on demand, a sequence of increasingly accurate estimates of a private parameter can be generated, with the privacy cost attributed only to the least noisy iterate released. This led to a Laplace mechanism variant that achieves a specified utility with minimal privacy loss. However, their work, and similar findings by Whitehouse et al. [2023], are primarily limited to simple mechanisms based on Laplace or Gaussian noise. In this paper, we significantly generalize these results. In particular, we extend the findings of Wu et al. [2019] and Liu and Talwar [2019] to support any sequence of private estimators, incurring at most a doubling of the original privacy budget. Furthermore, we demonstrate that hyperparameter tuning for these estimators, including the selection of an optimal privacy budget, can be performed without additional privacy cost. Finally, we extend our results to ex-post R\'{e}nyi DP, further broadening the applicability of utility-first privacy mechanisms.

paragraphs: Differential privacy research often starts with a fixed privacy budget and asks what utility it permits. Practitioners may instead have a target utility and want to determine the privacy cost of reaching it. This paper develops theoretical tools for that utility-first perspective using ex-post privacy guarantees.

Earlier results showed how progressively reducing correlated noise could produce increasingly accurate estimates, with privacy cost attributed to the least noisy released estimate. Those results largely concerned simple Laplace or Gaussian mechanisms. This work generalizes the approach to any sequence of private estimators, with at most a doubling of the original privacy budget.

The authors further show that hyperparameter tuning for these estimators, including choosing an optimal privacy budget, can be performed without additional privacy cost within their framework. They also extend the results to ex-post Rényi differential privacy. The contribution broadens the types of estimators that utility-first privacy analysis can support and incorporates tuning into the accounting, rather than limiting the analysis to simple noise mechanisms.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes utility-first privacy guarantees to arbitrary sequences of private estimators and supports tuning without additional privacy cost.

title: Private Hyperparameter Tuning with Ex-Post Guarantee

abstract: Neural Processes (NPs) combine the adaptability of neural networks with the efficiency of meta-learning, offering a powerful framework for modeling stochastic processes. However, existing methods focus on empirical performance while lacking a rigorous theoretical understanding of generalization. To address this, we propose an information-theoretic framework to analyze the generalization bounds of NPs, introducing dynamical stability regularization to minimize sharpness and improve optimization dynamics. Additionally, we show how noise-injected parameter updates complement this regularization. The proposed approach, applicable to a wide range of NP models, is validated through experiments on classic benchmarks, including 1D regression, image completion, Bayesian optimization, and contextual bandits. The results demonstrate tighter generalization bounds and superior predictive performance, establishing a principled foundation for advancing generalizable NP models.

paragraphs: Neural Processes combine neural-network adaptability with meta-learning to model stochastic processes efficiently. Existing approaches have emphasized predictive results, leaving a less developed theoretical account of generalization. This paper introduces an information-theoretic framework for analyzing generalization bounds, connecting how these models learn with how reliably they can predict beyond their training observations.

The analysis motivates dynamical stability regularization, which aims to reduce sharpness and improve the behavior of optimization. The authors also show how injecting noise into parameter updates complements this regularization. These mechanisms provide ways to modify training based on the theoretical account, and the proposed approach applies across a wide range of Neural Process models.

Evaluation includes one-dimensional regression, image completion, Bayesian optimization, and contextual bandits. The reported results combine tighter generalization bounds with better predictive performance. The contribution therefore links a mathematical explanation of generalization to practical training changes, with evidence across several uses of Neural Processes rather than only a single prediction task.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis motivates stability regularization and noisy updates that improve Neural Process generalization and prediction.

title: Learning to Generalize: An Information Perspective on Neural Processes

abstract: Dynamic Novel View Synthesis aims to generate photorealistic views of moving subjects from arbitrary viewpoints. This task is particularly challenging when relying on monocular video, where disentangling structure from motion is ill-posed and supervision is scarce. We introduce Video Diffusion-Aware Reconstruction (ViDAR), a novel 4D reconstruction framework that leverages personalised diffusion models to synthesise a pseudo multi-view supervision signal for training a Gaussian splatting representation. By conditioning on scene-specific features, ViDAR recovers fine-grained appearance details while mitigating artefacts introduced by monocular ambiguity. To address the spatio-temporal inconsistency of diffusion-based supervision, we propose a diffusion-aware loss function and a camera pose optimisation strategy that aligns synthetic views with the underlying scene geometry. Experiments on DyCheck, a challenging benchmark with extreme viewpoint variation, show that ViDAR outperforms all state-of-the-art baselines in visual quality and geometric consistency. We further highlight ViDAR’s strong improvement over baselines on dynamic regions and provide a new benchmark to compare performance in reconstructing motion-rich parts of the scene.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving scene from a single-camera video is ambiguous because changes in appearance can reflect both structure and motion. ViDAR addresses the scarcity of viewpoint supervision by using personalized video diffusion models to synthesize additional views. These generated views supervise a Gaussian splatting representation of the scene over time.

The findings support using generated multiview supervision together with mechanisms that account for its inconsistencies, connecting diffusion-based synthesis to reconstruction of both scene appearance and motion.

title: ViDAR: Video Diffusion-Aware 4D Reconstruction From Monocular Inputs

abstract: Recent deep learning approaches for river discharge forecasting have improved the accuracy and efficiency in flood forecasting, enabling more reliable early warning systems for risk management. Nevertheless, existing deep learning approaches in hydrology remain largely confined to local-scale applications and do not leverage the inherent spatial connections of bodies of water. Thus, there is a strong need for new deep learning methodologies that are capable of modeling spatio-temporal relations to improve river discharge and flood forecasting for scientific and operational applications. To address this, we present RiverMamba, a novel deep learning model that is pretrained with long-term reanalysis data and that can forecast global river discharge and floods on a $0.05^\circ$ grid up to 7 days lead time, which is of high relevance in early warning. To achieve this, RiverMamba leverages efficient Mamba blocks that enable the model to capture spatio-temporal relations in very large river networks and enhance its forecast capability for longer lead times. The forecast blocks integrate ECMWF HRES meteorological forecasts, while accounting for their inaccuracies through spatio-temporal modeling. Our analysis demonstrates that RiverMamba provides reliable predictions of river discharge across various flood return periods, including extreme floods, and lead times, surpassing both AI- and physics-based models. The source code and datasets are publicly available at the project page https://hakamshams.github.io/RiverMamba.

title: RiverMamba: A State Space Model for Global River Discharge and Flood Forecasting

abstract: We present a novel enhanced cyclic coordinate descent (ECCD) framework for solving generalized linear models with elastic net constraints that reduces training time in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods. We redesign the CD method by performing a Taylor expansion around the current iterate to avoid nonlinear operations arising in the gradient computation. By introducing this approximation we are able to unroll the vector recurrences occurring in the CD method and reformulate the resulting computations into more efficient batched computations. We show empirically that the recurrence can be unrolled by a tunable integer parameter, $s$, such that $s > 1$ yields performance improvements without affecting convergence, whereas $s = 1$ yields the original CD method. A key advantage of ECCD is that it avoids the convergence delay and numerical instability exhibited by block coordinate descent. Finally, we implement our proposed method in C++ using Eigen to accelerate linear algebra computations. Comparison of our method against existing state-of-the-art solvers show consistent performance improvements of $3\times$ in average for regularization path variant on diverse benchmark datasets. Our implementation is available at [https://github.com/Yixiao-Wang-Stats/ECCD](https://github.com/Yixiao-Wang-Stats/ECCD).

paragraphs: This paper accelerates cyclic coordinate descent for generalized linear models with elastic net constraints. The computational obstacle is that successive updates contain vector recurrences and nonlinear gradient operations. These dependencies make it difficult to organize the work into larger, efficient batches. The proposed enhanced cyclic coordinate descent framework, ECCD, changes how those updates are computed.

That approximation allows the authors to unroll the vector recurrences and batch the resulting calculations. The contribution is therefore a computational reformulation that preserves effective iterative optimization in the reported tests.
summary.tldr: ECCD uses a local approximation to batch coordinate-descent computations, delivering roughly 3× average speed improvements in reported regularization-path experiments.

title: Enhanced Cyclic Coordinate Descent Methods for Elastic Net Penalized Linear Models

abstract: We study the task of agnostically learning general (as opposed to homogeneous) ReLUs under the Gaussian distribution with respect to the squared loss. In the passive learning setting, recent work gave a computationally efficient algorithm that uses $poly(d,1/\epsilon)$ labeled examples and outputs a hypothesis with error $O(opt)+\epsilon$, where $opt$ is the squared loss of the best fit ReLU. Here we focus on the interactive setting, where the learner has some form of query access to the labels of unlabeled examples. Our main result is the first computationally efficient learner that uses $d polylog(1/\epsilon)+\tilde{O}(\min\{1/p, 1/\epsilon\})$ black-box label queries, where $p$ is the bias of the target function, and achieves error $O(opt)+\epsilon$. We complement our algorithmic result by showing that its query complexity bound is qualitatively near-optimal, even ignoring computational constraints. Finally, we establish that query access is essentially necessary to improve on the label complexity of passive learning. Specifically, for pool-based active learning, any active learner requires $\tilde{\Omega}(d/\epsilon)$ labels, unless it draws a super-polynomial number of unlabeled examples.

In the passive learning setting, recent work gave a computationally efficient algorithm that uses $poly(d,1/\epsilon)$ labeled examples and outputs a hypothesis with error $O(opt)+\epsilon$, where $opt$ is the squared loss of the best fit ReLU. Our main result is the first computationally efficient learner that uses $d polylog(1/\epsilon)+\tilde{O}(\min\{1/p, 1/\epsilon\})$ black-box label queries, where $p$ is the bias of the target function, and achieves error $O(opt)+\epsilon$. We complement our algorithmic result by showing that its query complexity bound is qualitatively near-optimal, even ignoring computational constraints. Finally, we establish that query access is essentially necessary to improve on the label complexity of passive learning. Specifically, for pool-based active learning, any active learner requires $\tilde{\Omega}(d/\epsilon)$ labels, unless it draws a super-polynomial number of unlabeled examples.

Performance is measured by squared error relative to the best-fitting ReLU, whose error is called opt. The goal is an efficient learner with error O(opt) plus an adjustable tolerance epsilon.

The authors show that black-box access to label queries can substantially reduce the number of labels required. Their computationally efficient algorithm uses a query count consisting of d times a polylogarithmic function of 1/epsilon, plus a term that is roughly the smaller of 1/p and 1/epsilon. Here d is the dimension, and p is the target function’s bias parameter.

They also prove that the query bound is qualitatively close to optimal, even without computational restrictions. A separate lower bound distinguishes this access from selecting labels out of an unlabeled pool: pool-based active learners require roughly d/epsilon labels unless they draw super-polynomially many unlabeled examples. The findings make the form of interaction a decisive part of label efficiency.
summary.tldr: Black-box label queries enable efficient robust learning of general ReLUs with near-optimal query complexity, exceeding what ordinary pool-based active learning can achieve.

title: Robust Regression of General ReLUs with Queries

abstract: Chance constrained programming (CCP) is a powerful framework for addressing optimization problems under uncertainty. In this paper, we introduce a novel Gradient-Guided Diffusion-based Optimization framework, termed GGDOpt, which tackles CCP through three key innovations. First, GGDOpt accommodates a broad class of CCP problems without requiring the knowledge of the exact distribution of uncertainty—relying solely on a set of samples. Second, to address the nonconvexity of the chance constraints, it reformulates the CCP as a sampling problem over the product of two distributions: an unknown data distribution supported on a nonconvex set and a Boltzmann distribution defined by the objective function, which fully leverages both first- and second-order gradient information. Third, GGDOpt has theoretical convergence guarantees and provides practical error bounds under mild assumptions. By progressively injecting noise during the forward diffusion process to convexify the nonconvex feasible region, GGDOpt enables guided reverse sampling to generate asymptotically optimal solutions. Experimental results on synthetic datasets and a waveform design task in wireless communications demonstrate that GGDOpt outperforms existing methods in both solution quality and stability with nearly 80\% overhead reduction.

paragraphs: Chance constrained programming seeks good decisions while requiring constraints to hold with a specified probability under uncertainty. These results support diffusion as a practical optimization mechanism as well as a sampling framework.

title: A Gradient Guided Diffusion Framework for Chance Constrained Programming

abstract: Large language model-assisted Evolutionary Search (LES) has emerged as a promising approach for Automated Algorithm Discovery (AAD). While many evolutionary search strategies have been developed for classic optimization problems, LES operates in abstract language spaces, presenting unique challenges for applying these strategies effectively. To address this, we propose a general LES framework that incorporates feature-assisted niche construction within abstract search spaces, enabling the seamless integration of niche-based search strategies from evolutionary computation. Building on this framework, we introduce PartEvo, an LES method that combines niche collaborative search and advanced prompting strategies to improve algorithm discovery efficiency. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world optimization problems show that PartEvo outperforms human-designed baselines and surpasses prior LES methods, such as Eoh and Funsearch. In particular, on resource scheduling tasks, PartEvo generates meta-heuristics with low design costs, achieving up to 90.1\% performance improvement over widely-used baseline algorithms, highlighting its potential for real-world applications.

paragraphs: Language models can assist evolutionary search by producing candidate algorithms, but the search takes place in an abstract language space. This makes established evolutionary strategies harder to apply directly. The paper develops a general framework that uses features to construct niches within that space, organizing candidates into regions that support niche-based search.

PartEvo builds on this framework by combining collaboration between niches with specialized prompting strategies. Partitioning the search provides structure for exploring algorithm candidates, while collaborative search connects those regions. The aim is to improve the efficiency of automated algorithm discovery by making techniques from evolutionary computation usable in language-model-assisted search.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world optimization problems report better performance than human-designed baselines and earlier language-model evolutionary methods, including Eoh and Funsearch. On resource scheduling, generated meta-heuristics achieve up to 90.1% performance improvement over widely used baselines, with low design costs. These results demonstrate the approach’s potential in the tested optimization settings, particularly for discovering scheduling heuristics.
summary.tldr: PartEvo organizes language-model-assisted evolutionary search into collaborating niches to improve automated algorithm discovery.

title: Partition to Evolve: Niching-enhanced Evolution with LLMs for Automated Algorithm Discovery

abstract: We study the problem of offline imitation learning in Markov decision processes (MDPs), where the goal is to learn a well-performing policy given a dataset of state-action pairs generated by an expert policy. Complementing a recent line of work on this topic that assumes the expert belongs to a tractable class of known policies, we approach this problem from a new angle and leverage a different type of structural assumption about the environment. Specifically, for the class of linear $Q^\pi$-realizable MDPs, we introduce a new algorithm called saddle-point offline imitation learning (\SPOIL), which is guaranteed to match the performance of any expert up to an additive error $\varepsilon$ with access to $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples. Moreover, we extend this result to possibly nonlinear $Q^\pi$-realizable MDPs at the cost of a worse sample complexity of order $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$. Finally, our analysis suggests a new loss function for training critic networks from expert data in deep imitation learning. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that the neural net implementation of \SPOIL is superior to behavior cloning and competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Offline imitation learning aims to learn a good decision-making policy from recorded expert state-action pairs. Some existing theory assumes the expert belongs to a known, tractable policy class. This paper takes a different route by imposing structure on the environment’s policy-value functions, using the assumption of Q-pi realizability to support learning guarantees.

The proposed algorithm, saddle-point offline imitation learning, is called SPOIL. For linear Q-pi-realizable Markov decision processes, it is guaranteed to match any expert’s performance up to an additive error epsilon using a sample count of order epsilon to the power minus two. The result extends to possibly nonlinear realizable environments, with a worse sample requirement of order epsilon to the power minus four.

The analysis also motivates a loss function for training critic networks from expert data. On standard benchmarks, a neural implementation outperforms behavior cloning and is competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms. The paper thus connects a conditional theoretical guarantee with a practical training objective, while making clear that the stronger sample-efficiency result belongs to the linear setting.
summary.tldr: SPOIL provides offline imitation-learning guarantees under Q-pi realizability and motivates a critic loss with competitive empirical performance.

title: Inverse Q-Learning Done Right: Offline Imitation Learning in $Q^\pi$-Realizable MDPs

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown that generative pretraining can distill vast world knowledge into compact token representations. While LLMs encapsulate extensive world knowledge, they remain limited in modeling the behavioral knowledge contained within user interaction histories. User behavior forms a distinct modality, where each action—defined by multi-dimensional attributes such as time, context, and transaction type—constitutes a behavioral token. Modeling these high-cardinality, sparse, and irregular sequences is challenging, and discriminative models often falter under limited supervision. To bridge this gap, we extend generative pretraining to user behavior, learning transferable representations from unlabeled behavioral data analogous to how LLMs learn from text. We present PANTHER, a hybrid generative–discriminative framework that unifies user behavior pretraining and downstream adaptation, enabling large-scale sequential user representation learning and real-time inference. PANTHER introduces: (1) Structured Tokenization to compress multi-dimensional transaction attributes into an interpretable vocabulary; (2) Sequence Pattern Recognition Module (SPRM) for modeling periodic transaction motifs; (3) a Unified User-Profile Embedding that fuses static demographics with dynamic transaction histories, enabling both personalized predictions and population-level knowledge transfer; and (4) Real-time scalability enabled by offline caching of pre-trained embeddings for millisecond-level inference.Fully deployed and operational online at WeChat Pay, PANTHER delivers a 25.6\% boost in next-transaction prediction HitRate@1 and a 38.6\% relative improvement in fraud detection recall over baselines. Cross-domain evaluations on public benchmarks (CCT, MBD, MovieLens-1M, Yelp) show strong generalization, achieving up to 21\% HitRate@1 gains over transformer baselines, establishing PANTHER as a scalable, high-performance framework for industrial user sequential behavior modeling.

summary.tldr: PANTHER pretrains on user-action sequences to improve behavioral predictions while supporting millisecond-level inference.

title: PANTHER: Generative Pretraining Beyond Language for Sequential User Behavior Modeling

abstract: Integrating ground-level geospatial data with rich geographic context, like OpenStreetMap (OSM), into remote sensing (RS) foundation models (FMs) is essential for advancing geospatial intelligence and supporting a broad spectrum of tasks. However, modality gap between RS and OSM data, including differences in data structure, content, and spatial granularity, makes effective synergy highly challenging, and most existing RS FMs focus on imagery alone. To this end, this study presents GeoLink, a multimodal framework that leverages OSM data to enhance RS FM during both the pretraining and downstream task stages. Specifically, GeoLink enhances RS self-supervised pretraining using multi-granularity learning signals derived from OSM data, guided by cross-modal spatial correlations for information interaction and collaboration. It also introduces image mask-reconstruction to enable sparse input for efficient pretraining. For downstream tasks, GeoLink generates both unimodal and multimodal fine-grained encodings to support a wide range of applications, from common RS interpretation tasks like land cover classification to more comprehensive geographic tasks like urban function zone mapping. Extensive experiments show that incorporating OSM data during pretraining enhances the performance of the RS image encoder, while fusing RS and OSM data in downstream tasks improves the FM’s adaptability to complex geographic scenarios. These results underscore the potential of multimodal synergy in advancing high-level geospatial artificial intelligence. Moreover, we find that spatial correlation plays a crucial role in enabling effective multimodal geospatial data integration. Code, checkpoints, and using examples are released at [GitHub](https://github.com/bailubin/GeoLink_NeurIPS2025).

GeoLink brings these sources together during both foundation-model pretraining and downstream use, aiming to enrich image representations with geographic context.

Together, these results show benefits at two distinct stages: learning better visual representations and using complementary geographic information when solving a task.
summary.tldr: GeoLink uses spatial relationships between remote-sensing imagery and OpenStreetMap to improve pretraining and downstream geographic tasks.

title: GeoLink: Empowering Remote Sensing Foundation Model with OpenStreetMap Data

abstract: In this paper, we address the problem of cost-sensitive hyperparameter optimization (HPO) built upon freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO). Specifically, we assume a scenario where users want to early-stop the HPO process when the expected performance improvement is not satisfactory with respect to the additional computational cost. Motivated by this scenario, we introduce \emph{utility} in the freeze-thaw framework, a function describing the trade-off between the cost and performance that can be estimated from the user's preference data. This utility function, combined with our novel acquisition function and stopping criterion, allows us to dynamically continue training the configuration that we expect to maximally improve the utility in the future, and also automatically stop the HPO process around the maximum utility. Further, we improve the sample efficiency of existing freeze-thaw methods with transfer learning to develop a specialized surrogate model for the cost-sensitive HPO problem. We validate our algorithm on established multi-fidelity HPO benchmarks and show that it outperforms all the previous freeze-thaw BO and transfer-BO baselines we consider, while achieving a significantly better trade-off between the cost and performance.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning can keep consuming computation after its expected benefits have become too small for the user. This paper studies that situation within freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization, where training configurations can be paused and continued. The central objective is to decide both which configuration deserves more training and when the entire search should end.

The method expresses the user’s trade-off between performance and computational cost through a utility function, which can be estimated from preference data. A new acquisition function chooses the configuration expected to deliver the largest future utility improvement. A corresponding stopping rule aims to end the search around its maximum utility, making the stopping decision part of optimization itself.

The authors also use transfer learning to construct a specialized surrogate model that improves sample efficiency. On established benchmarks that evaluate configurations at different training budgets, the algorithm outperforms all freeze-thaw and transfer-based Bayesian optimization baselines considered. The reported benefit is a better cost-performance balance under the specified preference-based objective, rather than simply pursuing the highest possible model performance regardless of expense.
summary.tldr: Preference-based utility guides which hyperparameter trials to continue and when further tuning is no longer worth its computational cost.

title: Cost-Sensitive Freeze-thaw Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Hyperparameter Tuning

abstract: Accurate weather forecasting across time scales is critical for anticipating and mitigating the impacts of climate change. Recent data-driven methods based on deep learning have achieved significant success in the medium range, but struggle at longer subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) horizons due to error accumulation in their autoregressive approach. In this work, we propose OmniCast, a scalable and skillful probabilistic model that unifies weather forecasting across timescales. OmniCast consists of two components: a VAE model that encodes raw weather data into a continuous, lower-dimensional latent space, and a diffusion-based transformer model that generates a sequence of future latent tokens given the initial conditioning tokens. During training, we mask random future tokens and train the transformer to estimate their distribution given conditioning and visible tokens using a per-token diffusion head. During inference, the transformer generates the full sequence of future tokens by iteratively unmasking random subsets of tokens. This joint sampling across space and time mitigates compounding errors from autoregressive approaches. The low-dimensional latent space enables modeling long sequences of future latent states, allowing the transformer to learn weather dynamics beyond initial conditions. OmniCast performs competitively with leading probabilistic methods at the medium-range timescale while being 10× to 20× faster, and achieves state-of-the-art performance at the subseasonal-to-seasonal scale across accuracy, physics-based, and probabilistic metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that OmniCast can generate stable rollouts up to 100 years ahead. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/tung-nd/omnicast.

paragraphs: OmniCast targets probabilistic weather forecasting across both medium-range and subseasonal-to-seasonal horizons. Many forecasting models repeatedly predict the next state from earlier predictions, allowing errors to accumulate over time. OmniCast instead represents and generates a sequence of future states jointly, using a compact representation to make long sequences manageable.

A variational autoencoder compresses raw weather data into continuous latent representations. A diffusion-based transformer learns to estimate randomly hidden future tokens using the initial conditions and visible tokens. At inference, it constructs the future sequence by repeatedly filling randomly chosen subsets of hidden tokens. Joint sampling across space and time mitigates the compounding errors associated with autoregressive forecasting.

That stability result describes long-run model behavior; it is distinct from the forecast-accuracy results at shorter horizons.
summary.tldr: OmniCast jointly generates compressed future weather states, reporting fast medium-range forecasts and state-of-the-art subseasonal-to-seasonal performance.

title: OmniCast: A Masked Latent Diffusion Model for Weather Forecasting Across Time Scales

abstract: Causal discovery in the form of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) for dynamic time series data has been widely studied in various applications. Much of the existing work has focused on observational, offline, and/or stationary settings. In this work, we propose a dynamic DAG discovery algorithm, Meta-D$^2$AG, based on online meta-learning. Meta-D$^2$AG is designed to learn dynamic DAG structures from potentially nonlinear and non-stationary times series datasets, accounting for changes in both parameters and graph structures. Notably, Meta-D$^2$AG explicitly treats data collected at different time points with distribution shifts as distinct domains, which is assumed to occur as a result of external interventions. Moreover, Meta-D$^2$AG contains a new online meta-learning framework to take advantage of the temporal transition among existing domains such that it can quickly adapt to new domains with few measurements. A first-order optimization approach is utilized to efficiently solve the meta-learning framework, and theoretical analysis establishes the identifiability conditions and the convergence of the learning process. We demonstrate the promising performance of our method through better accuracy and sample efficiency on benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Meta-D2AG learns causal graphs from time series whose relationships may change over time. It allows both the parameters of relationships and the graph structure itself to vary, including potentially nonlinear behavior. This addresses a setting beyond the observational, offline, or stationary cases emphasized by much previous work.

The method treats time points associated with distribution shifts as distinct domains and assumes those shifts arise from external interventions. These findings support rapid adaptation of causal structure in changing systems, within a formulation that explicitly links distribution changes to interventions and represents causal relationships using directed acyclic graphs.
summary.tldr: Meta-D2AG uses online meta-learning to adapt causal graphs across changing time-series domains assumed to result from interventions.

title: Meta-D2AG: Causal Graph Learning with Interventional Dynamic Data

abstract: Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) is a popular method for learning a distance metric to be used within a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classifier. A key assumption built into the model is that each point stochastically selects a single neighbor, which makes the model well-justified only for kNN with k=1. However, kNN classifiers with k>1 are more robust and usually preferred in practice. Here we present kNCA, which generalizes NCA by learning distance metrics that are appropriate for kNN with arbitrary k. The main technical contribution is showing how to efficiently compute and optimize the expected accuracy of a kNN classifier. We apply similar ideas in an unsupervised setting to yield kSNE and ktSNE, generalizations of Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (SNE, tSNE) that operate on neighborhoods of size k, which provide an axis of control over embeddings that allow for more homogeneous and interpretable regions. Empirically, we show that kNCA often improves classification accuracy over state of the art methods, produces qualitative differences in the embeddings as k is varied, and is more robust with respect to label noise.

paragraphs: Neighborhood Components Analysis learns a distance measure for nearest-neighbor classification, but its model selects only one neighbor per point. That aligns naturally with a classifier using one neighbor, even though using several neighbors is often preferred for robustness. The paper introduces kNCA to learn distances suited to a classifier with an arbitrary neighborhood size.

The main technical result is an efficient way to compute and optimize the expected classification accuracy of that multi-neighbor classifier. This aligns the learning objective with the neighborhood size used for prediction. The authors also extend the same ideas to unsupervised embedding, producing kSNE and ktSNE as neighborhood-based generalizations of SNE and tSNE.

Neighborhood size becomes a control over the embedding, allowing more homogeneous and interpretable regions. Experiments show that kNCA often improves classification accuracy over leading methods and is more robust to label noise. They also reveal qualitative embedding changes as the neighborhood size varies. These findings support treating neighborhood size as part of the learned representation’s design, with consequences for both prediction and visualization.
summary.tldr: kNCA learns distances for arbitrary-size nearest-neighbor classifiers, with related extensions offering neighborhood-size control over embeddings.

title: Stochastic k-Neighborhood Selection for Supervised and Unsupervised Learning

abstract: We show how options, a class of control structures encompassing primitive and temporally extended actions, can play a valuable role in planning in MDPs with continuous state-spaces. Analyzing the convergence rate of Approximate Value Iteration with options reveals that for pessimistic initial value function estimates, options can speed up convergence compared to planning with only primitive actions even when the temporally extended actions are suboptimal and sparsely scattered throughout the state-space. Our experimental results in an optimal replacement task and a complex inventory management task demonstrate the potential for options to speed up convergence in practice. We show that options induce faster convergence to the optimal value function, which implies deriving better policies with fewer iterations.

Options are control structures that include both primitive actions and actions extending over time. The question is whether these longer actions can help approximate value iteration reach useful value estimates and policies in fewer iterations.

The convergence analysis identifies pessimistic initial value estimates as an important condition. Under that condition, options can speed convergence relative to planning with primitive actions alone, even when the extended actions are suboptimal and available only sparsely across the state space. The result shows that options need not themselves be ideal or widely distributed to provide a planning advantage.

Faster progress toward the optimal value function means better policies can be obtained with fewer iterations. The contribution therefore gives both a conditional theoretical explanation and practical examples of why temporally extended actions can help planning.
summary.tldr: With pessimistic initial value estimates, even suboptimal and sparsely available options can accelerate approximate value iteration.

title: Scaling Up Approximate Value Iteration with Options: Better Policies with Fewer Iterations

abstract: Learning probabilistic models over strings is an important issue for many applications. Spectral methods propose elegant solutions to the problem of inferring weighted automata from finite samples of variable-length strings drawn from an unknown target distribution. These methods rely on a singular value decomposition of a matrix H_S, called the Hankel matrix, that records the frequencies of (some of) the observed strings. The accuracy of the learned distribution depends both on the quantity of information embedded in H_S and on the distance between H_S and its mean H_r. Existing concentration bounds seem to indicate that the concentration over H_r gets looser with its size, suggesting to make a trade-off between the quantity of used information and the size of H_r. We propose new dimension-free concentration bounds for several variants of Hankel matrices. Experiments demonstrate that these bounds are tight and that they significantly improve existing bounds. These results suggest that the concentration rate of the Hankel matrix around its mean does not constitute an argument for limiting its size.

A singular value decomposition of this matrix supports learning a weighted automaton. Accuracy depends both on the information the matrix contains and on how closely its observed values track their expected values.

Earlier concentration bounds appear to worsen as the matrix becomes larger. This suggests a tension: retaining more string information could come with a weaker statistical guarantee. The paper develops dimension-free concentration bounds for several Hankel matrix variants, removing matrix size from this particular source of deterioration in the bounds.

Experiments show that the new bounds are tight and substantially improve on existing ones. The authors conclude that concentration around the mean does not itself provide an argument for restricting Hankel matrix size. This is a focused conclusion about statistical concentration, rather than a claim that every larger matrix necessarily produces a better learned model. It changes how the information-versus-size tradeoff should be interpreted.
summary.tldr: Dimension-free bounds challenge the idea that larger Hankel matrices inherently suffer weaker statistical concentration in spectral learning.

title: Dimension-free Concentration Bounds on Hankel Matrices for Spectral Learning

abstract: Memory efficiency is an important issue in Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms, arising for example in inference of high-dimensional latent variables via Rao-Blackwellized SMC algorithms, where the size of individual particles combined with the required number of particles can stress the main memory. Standard SMC methods have a memory requirement that scales linearly in the number of particles present at all stage of the algorithm. Our contribution is a simple scheme that makes the memory cost of SMC methods depends on the number of distinct particles that survive resampling. We show that this difference has a large empirical impact on the quality of the approximation in realistic scenarios, and also—since memory access is generally slow—on the running time. The method is based on a two pass generation of the particles, which are represented implicitly in the first pass. We parameterize the accuracy of our algorithm with a memory budget rather than with a fixed number of particles. Our algorithm adaptively selects an optimal number of particle to exploit this fixed memory budget. We show that this adaptation does not interfere with the usual consistency guarantees that come with SMC algorithms.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo methods represent uncertainty using collections of particles. Memory becomes a serious concern when individual particles are large and many are needed, as in some high-dimensional latent-variable problems. Standard implementations require memory proportional to the particle count throughout the algorithm.

The authors propose a two-pass particle-generation scheme. During the first pass, particles are represented implicitly. The resulting memory cost depends on how many distinct particles survive resampling. This makes the storage requirement sensitive to the surviving particle collection rather than simply the full number generated.

The method also changes the user-facing resource choice: a memory budget replaces a fixed particle count. The algorithm adaptively selects an optimal number of particles to exploit that budget, and the authors show that this adaptation preserves the usual SMC consistency guarantees. Experiments report a large effect on approximation quality and running time in realistic scenarios. The timing benefit is connected to the cost of memory access, making memory management part of both statistical and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: A two-pass SMC scheme adapts particle counts to a memory budget while preserving consistency and reducing storage demands.

title: Memory (and Time) Efficient Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: We present new algorithms to compute the mean of a set of $N$ empirical probability measures under the optimal transport metric. This mean, known as the Wasserstein barycenter (Agueh and Carlier, 2011; Rabin et al, 2012), is the measure that minimizes the sum of its Wasserstein distances to each element in that set. We argue through a simple example that Wasserstein barycenters have appealing properties that differentiate them from other barycenters proposed recently, which all build on kernel smoothing and/or Bregman divergences. Two original algorithms are proposed that require the repeated computation of primal and dual optimal solutions of transport problems. However direct implementation of these algorithms is too costly as optimal transports are notoriously computationally expensive. Extending the work of Cuturi (2013), we smooth both the primal and dual of the optimal transport problem to recover fast approximations of the primal and dual optimal solutions. We apply these algorithms to the visualization of perturbed images and to a clustering problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to average empirical probability distributions using optimal transport. The resulting Wasserstein barycenter is a distribution that minimizes the sum of its Wasserstein distances to the inputs. Through an example, the authors argue that this kind of average has appealing properties that distinguish it from alternatives based on kernel smoothing or Bregman divergences.

They introduce two algorithms whose steps repeatedly need primal and dual solutions to transport problems. These are complementary optimization formulations of the transport calculation. Computing all of those solutions directly is too expensive, so the central computational challenge is making the repeated transport operations affordable.

The authors smooth both formulations to obtain fast approximations of the needed solutions. This connects the barycenter algorithms to a more efficient computational procedure while retaining optimal transport as the basis for the average. Applications include visualizing perturbed images and solving a clustering problem, showing how the proposed averaging machinery can be used in both settings.
summary.tldr: Two Wasserstein barycenter algorithms use smoothed transport problems to approximate otherwise expensive repeated optimization steps.

title: Fast Computation of Wasserstein Barycenters

abstract: Given a graphical model, one essential problem is MAP inference, that is, finding the most likely configuration of states according to the model. Although this problem is NP-hard, large instances can be solved in practice and it is a major open question is to explain why this is true. We give a natural condition under which we can provably perform MAP inference in polynomial time—we require that the number of fractional vertices in the LP relaxation exceeding the optimal solution is bounded by a polynomial in the problem size. This resolves an open question by Dimakis, Gohari, and Wainwright. In contrast, for general LP relaxations of integer programs, known techniques can only handle a constant number of fractional vertices whose value exceeds the optimal solution. We experimentally verify this condition and demonstrate how efficient various integer programming methods are at removing fractional solutions.

paragraphs: MAP inference seeks the most likely configuration of states in a graphical model. Although this problem is NP-hard in general, large instances can sometimes be solved effectively. This paper offers a sufficient structural condition that helps explain when exact inference can have a polynomial-time guarantee.

The condition concerns a linear-programming relaxation, which admits fractional solutions alongside valid discrete configurations. The authors require that only polynomially many fractional vertices have objective values better than the optimal valid solution. Under that condition, they prove that MAP inference can be performed in polynomial time. The key quantity is therefore the number of fractional competitors that outrank the true optimum.

This resolves an open question identified in the abstract and goes beyond known techniques for general integer-program relaxations, which handle only constantly many such vertices. Experiments verify the proposed condition in the evaluated settings and examine how efficiently integer-programming methods remove fractional solutions. The result provides a conditional explanation of tractability while retaining the problem’s general NP-hardness.
summary.tldr: Exact MAP inference is polynomial-time solvable when only polynomially many fractional relaxation vertices outperform the best valid configuration.

title: Exact MAP Inference by Avoiding Fractional Vertices

abstract: Autoregressive generative models achieve the best results in density estimation tasks involving high dimensional data, such as images or audio. They pose density estimation as a sequence modeling task, where a recurrent neural network (RNN) models the conditional distribution over the next element conditioned on all previous elements. In this paradigm, the bottleneck is the extent to which the RNN can model long-range dependencies, and the most successful approaches rely on causal convolutions. Taking inspiration from recent work in meta reinforcement learning, where dealing with long-range dependencies is also essential, we introduce a new generative model architecture that combines causal convolutions with self attention. In this paper, we describe the resulting model and present state-of-the-art log-likelihood results on heavily benchmarked datasets: CIFAR-10, $32 \times 32$ ImageNet and $64 \times 64$ ImageNet. Our implementation will be made available at \url{https://github.com/neocxi/pixelsnail-public}.

paragraphs: Autoregressive density models treat high-dimensional data as sequences, predicting each element from the elements that precede it. Their effectiveness depends on how well they capture dependencies across that sequence. For images or audio, relevant relationships may extend far beyond nearby elements, making long-range information a central modeling challenge.

PixelSNAIL combines causal convolutions with self-attention in a generative architecture. Causal processing respects the ordering required by autoregressive prediction, while the attention component addresses the need to model relationships across longer ranges. The design draws inspiration from work on long-range dependencies in meta reinforcement learning and applies that architectural motivation to density estimation.

The paper reports state-of-the-art log-likelihood results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet at resolutions of 32 by 32 and 64 by 64. These results concern how well the model assigns probability to data on the evaluated benchmarks. They support the combination of convolution and attention as an effective architecture for autoregressive density estimation in those settings.
summary.tldr: PixelSNAIL combines causal convolutions and self-attention to achieve reported state-of-the-art image log-likelihood results.

title: PixelSNAIL: An Improved Autoregressive Generative Model

abstract: It is important to transfer the knowledge from label-rich source domain to unlabeled target domain due to the expensive cost of manual labeling efforts. Prior domain adaptation methods address this problem through aligning the global distribution statistics between source domain and target domain, but a drawback of prior methods is that they ignore the semantic information contained in samples, e.g., features of backpacks in target domain might be mapped near features of cars in source domain. In this paper, we present moving semantic transfer network, which learn semantic representations for unlabeled target samples by aligning labeled source centroid and pseudo-labeled target centroid. Features in same class but different domains are expected to be mapped nearby, resulting in an improved target classification accuracy. Moving average centroid alignment is cautiously designed to compensate the insufficient categorical information within each mini batch. Experiments testify that our model yields state of the art results on standard datasets.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a source domain with labels to a target domain without labels. Matching the overall feature distributions can help connect the domains, but it can also align examples from different classes. The paper addresses this semantic mismatch: making two distributions look similar does not by itself ensure that corresponding categories are brought together.

The proposed moving semantic transfer network aligns class centroids across domains. Source centroids use known labels, while target centroids use pseudo-labels. By aligning these category-level summaries, the model aims to place examples from the same class near one another even when they come from different domains. This adds class information to the alignment objective.

The method uses moving averages for centroid alignment to compensate for insufficient category information within individual mini-batches. The authors report state-of-the-art results on standard datasets. Their findings support aligning representations at the class level as a way to improve target classification, while using estimated target labels to operate in the unlabeled-domain setting.
summary.tldr: Aligning source and pseudo-labeled target class centroids improves semantic consistency in unsupervised domain adaptation.

title: Learning Semantic Representations for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: We consider the problem of representation learning for graph data. Convolutional neural networks can naturally operate on images, but have significant challenges in dealing with graph data. Given images are special cases of graphs with nodes lie on 2D lattices, graph embedding tasks have a natural correspondence with image pixel-wise prediction tasks such as segmentation. While encoder-decoder architectures like U-Nets have been successfully applied on many image pixel-wise prediction tasks, similar methods are lacking for graph data. This is due to the fact that pooling and up-sampling operations are not natural on graph data. To address these challenges, we propose novel graph pooling (gPool) and unpooling (gUnpool) operations in this work. The gPool layer adaptively selects some nodes to form a smaller graph based on their scalar projection values on a trainable projection vector. We further propose the gUnpool layer as the inverse operation of the gPool layer. The gUnpool layer restores the graph into its original structure using the position information of nodes selected in the corresponding gPool layer. Based on our proposed gPool and gUnpool layers, we develop an encoder-decoder model on graph, known as the graph U-Nets. Our experimental results on node classification and graph classification tasks demonstrate that our methods achieve consistently better performance than previous models.

paragraphs: Image U-Nets use an encoder-decoder structure that reduces spatial resolution and then restores it. Extending that idea to graphs is difficult because graphs lack the regular two-dimensional layout of image pixels. This paper supplies graph-specific pooling and unpooling operations so that a similar architecture can learn representations of graph data.

The pooling operation, gPool, scores nodes using their scalar projections onto a trainable vector. It adaptively selects nodes to construct a smaller graph. The paired gUnpool operation uses the saved positions of those selected nodes to restore the original graph structure. Keeping this positional information connects the reduced representation to the structure from which it came.

Combining these operations produces the graph U-Net encoder-decoder model. The design gives graph networks an explicit mechanism for reducing and restoring structure within the same architecture. Experiments cover both node classification and classification of entire graphs, with consistently better performance than previous models in the reported evaluations. The contribution centers on making the pooling-and-restoration pattern workable for irregular graph inputs.
summary.tldr: Graph U-Nets introduce trainable node pooling and position-based unpooling to bring encoder-decoder architectures to graph learning.

title: Graph U-Nets

abstract: Many reinforcement learning (RL) tasks provide the agent with high-dimensional observations that can be simplified into low-dimensional continuous states. To formalize this process, we introduce the concept of a \texit{DeepMDP}, a parameterized latent space model that is trained via the minimization of two tractable latent space losses: prediction of rewards and prediction of the distribution over next latent states. We show that the optimization of these objectives guarantees (1) the quality of the embedding function as a representation of the state space and (2) the quality of the DeepMDP as a model of the environment. Our theoretical findings are substantiated by the experimental result that a trained DeepMDP recovers the latent structure underlying high-dimensional observations on a synthetic environment. Finally, we show that learning a DeepMDP as an auxiliary task in the Atari 2600 domain leads to large performance improvements over model-free RL.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often receive observations with many dimensions even when the underlying situation admits a much smaller description. DeepMDP formalizes learning such a continuous latent state space. The aim is to produce a compact representation that supports reasoning about the environment through its rewards and future behavior.

A DeepMDP is trained using two tractable losses: one for predicting rewards and another for predicting the distribution of the next latent state. These objectives tie representation learning to quantities that matter for interaction. The authors establish theoretical guarantees connecting their optimization to both the quality of the state embedding and the quality of the learned environment model.

The experiments examine these ideas in two ways. In a synthetic environment, a trained DeepMDP recovers the latent structure behind high-dimensional observations. In Atari 2600 tasks, learning a DeepMDP as an auxiliary objective produces large improvements over model-free reinforcement learning. Together, these findings support using reward and latent-transition prediction to learn useful representations.
summary.tldr: DeepMDP learns compact state representations through reward and latent-transition prediction, with theoretical guarantees and reported reinforcement learning gains.

title: DeepMDP: Learning Continuous Latent Space Models for Representation Learning

abstract: Particle-based variational inference methods (ParVIs) have gained attention in the Bayesian inference literature, for their capacity to yield flexible and accurate approximations. We explore ParVIs from the perspective of Wasserstein gradient flows, and make both theoretical and practical contributions. We unify various finite-particle approximations that existing ParVIs use, and recognize that the approximation is essentially a compulsory smoothing treatment, in either of two equivalent forms. This novel understanding reveals the assumptions and relations of existing ParVIs, and also inspires new ParVIs. We propose an acceleration framework and a principled bandwidth-selection method for general ParVIs; these are based on the developed theory and leverage the geometry of the Wasserstein space. Experimental results show the improved convergence by the acceleration framework and enhanced sample accuracy by the bandwidth-selection method.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference uses a finite collection of particles to construct flexible Bayesian approximations. This paper studies these methods through Wasserstein gradient flows, a perspective that describes how probability distributions move during optimization. The aim is both to explain existing methods and to derive practical improvements from that explanation.

The authors unify several finite-particle approximations and show that their approximation amounts to a necessary smoothing operation, expressible in two equivalent forms. This interpretation exposes relationships and assumptions among existing methods and motivates new ones. It gives apparently different particle procedures a common theoretical description based on how finite representations introduce smoothing.

Building on this theory, the paper proposes an acceleration framework and a principled method for selecting bandwidths for general particle-based variational inference. Both use the geometry of Wasserstein space. Experiments report improved convergence from acceleration and better sample accuracy from bandwidth selection. These results connect the theoretical interpretation to two separate practical concerns: how quickly the particles progress and how accurately their final arrangement represents the target.
summary.tldr: A Wasserstein-flow analysis unifies particle-based variational methods and yields acceleration and bandwidth selection that improve experimental performance.

title: Understanding and Accelerating Particle-Based Variational Inference

abstract: Recent studies on diffusion-based sampling methods have shown that Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) algorithms can be beneficial for non-convex optimization, and rigorous theoretical guarantees have been proven for both asymptotic and finite-time regimes. Algorithmically, LMC-based algorithms resemble the well-known gradient descent (GD) algorithm, where the GD recursion is perturbed by an additive Gaussian noise whose variance has a particular form. Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo (FLMC) is a recently proposed extension of LMC, where the Gaussian noise is replaced by a heavy-tailed $\alpha$-stable noise. As opposed to its Gaussian counterpart, these heavy-tailed perturbations can incur large jumps and it has been empirically demonstrated that the choice of $\alpha$-stable noise can provide several advantages in modern machine learning problems, both in optimization and sampling contexts. However, as opposed to LMC, only asymptotic convergence properties of FLMC have been yet established. In this study, we analyze the non-asymptotic behavior of FLMC for non-convex optimization and prove finite-time bounds for its expected suboptimality. Our results show that the weak-error of FLMC increases faster than LMC, which suggests using smaller step-sizes in FLMC. We finally extend our results to the case where the exact gradients are replaced by stochastic gradients and show that similar results hold in this setting as well.
