paragraphs: Langevin Monte Carlo resembles gradient descent with added Gaussian noise. Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo replaces that noise with a heavy-tailed alpha-stable distribution, allowing occasional large jumps. Earlier empirical work had suggested advantages for optimization and sampling, but the available convergence theory for the fractional method described only its asymptotic behavior.

This paper analyzes what happens within finite time when the fractional method is used for non-convex optimization. The authors prove bounds on expected suboptimality, giving a theoretical description of how far the method’s result can remain from the optimum. This fills the gap between eventual convergence statements and guarantees relevant to a finite run of the algorithm.

The analysis finds that the fractional method’s weak error increases faster than that of ordinary Langevin Monte Carlo, suggesting the use of smaller step sizes. The authors also extend the results to stochastic gradients in place of exact gradients and obtain similar conclusions. The contribution therefore clarifies both finite-time behavior and a step-size implication of using heavy-tailed perturbations.
summary.tldr: Finite-time bounds for fractional Langevin optimization suggest smaller step sizes than for its Gaussian-noise counterpart.

title: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo for Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: The use of black-box optimization for the design of new biological sequences is an emerging research area with potentially revolutionary impact. The cost and latency of wet-lab experiments requires methods that find good sequences in few experimental rounds of large batches of sequences — a setting that off-the-shelf black-box optimization methods are ill-equipped to handle. We find that the performance of existing methods varies drastically across optimization tasks, posing a significant obstacle to real-world applications. To improve robustness, we propose Population-Based Black-Box Optimization (P3BO), which generates batches of sequences by sampling from an ensemble of methods. The number of sequences sampled from any method is proportional to the quality of sequences it previously proposed, allowing P3BO to combine the strengths of individual methods while hedging against their innate brittleness. Adapting the hyper-parameters of each of the methods online using evolutionary optimization further improves performance. Through extensive experiments on in-silico optimization tasks, we show that P3BO outperforms any single method in its population, proposing higher quality sequences as well as more diverse batches. As such, P3BO and Adaptive-P3BO are a crucial step towards deploying ML to real-world sequence design.

paragraphs: Biological sequence design often requires evaluating large batches in only a few experimental rounds because laboratory work is costly and slow. Existing black-box optimization methods vary sharply in performance across tasks, making reliance on a single method fragile. This paper develops a population-based approach designed for that batching constraint and variation in method quality.

P3BO generates each batch by sampling proposals from an ensemble of optimization methods. A method contributes sequences in proportion to the quality of its previous proposals, allowing successful methods to receive more of the batch. An adaptive version also uses evolutionary optimization to tune the methods' hyperparameters online.

Across extensive in-silico optimization experiments, P3BO outperforms every individual method in its population and produces both higher-quality sequences and more diverse batches. Online hyperparameter adaptation improves performance further. These results support combining complementary methods for sequence design, with the stated empirical evidence coming from computational optimization tasks that motivate future real-world deployment.
summary.tldr: P3BO adaptively combines sequence-design optimizers, producing better sequences and more diverse batches than its individual members in computational experiments.

title: Population-Based Black-Box Optimization for Biological Sequence Design

abstract: Online Convex Optimization (OCO) is a powerful framework for sequential prediction, portraying the natural uncertainty inherent in data-streams as though the data were generated by an almost omniscient adversary. However, this view, which is often too pessimistic for real-world data, comes with a price. The complexity of solving many important online tasks in this adversarial framework becomes much worse than that of their offline and even stochastic counterparts. In this work we consider a natural random-order version of the OCO model, in which the adversary can choose the set of loss functions, but does not get to choose the order in which they are supplied to the learner; Instead, they are observed in uniformly random order. Focusing on two important families of online tasks, one in which the cumulative loss function is strongly convex (though individual loss functions may not even be convex), and the other being online $k$-PCA, we show that under standard well-conditioned-data assumptions, standard online gradient descent (OGD) methods become much more efficient in the random-order model. In particular, for the first group of tasks OGD guarantees poly-logarithmic regret. In the case of online $k$-PCA, OGD guarantees sublinear regret using only a rank-$k$ SVD on each iteration and memory linear in the size of the solution.

paragraphs: Online optimization often allows an adversary to choose both the losses a learner faces and their order. This can make sequential learning substantially harder than offline or stochastic alternatives. The paper studies a middle ground: an adversary selects the collection of loss functions, but the learner receives them in uniformly random order.

Under standard well-conditioned-data assumptions, the authors show that ordinary online gradient descent becomes more efficient for two task families. In the first, the cumulative loss is strongly convex even though individual losses may be non-convex. For these tasks, online gradient descent achieves poly-logarithmic regret. The result uses curvature of the cumulative objective rather than requiring convexity of every individual loss.

The second application is online k-PCA. Here, online gradient descent obtains sublinear regret with only a rank-k singular value decomposition per iteration and memory linear in the solution size. Together, the findings show that randomizing presentation order can yield stronger guarantees and efficient computation under the stated data assumptions, even when the collection of losses remains adversarially chosen.
summary.tldr: Uniformly random loss ordering enables stronger regret and efficiency guarantees for online gradient descent under well-conditioned-data assumptions.

title: Online Convex Optimization in the Random Order Model

abstract: We propose a neural information processing system obtained by re-purposing the function of a biological neural circuit model to govern simulated and real-world control tasks. Inspired by the structure of the nervous system of the soil-worm, C. elegans, we introduce ordinary neural circuits (ONCs), defined as the model of biological neural circuits reparameterized for the control of alternative tasks. We first demonstrate that ONCs realize networks with higher maximum flow compared to arbitrary wired networks. We then learn instances of ONCs to control a series of robotic tasks, including the autonomous parking of a real-world rover robot. For reconfiguration of the purpose of the neural circuit, we adopt a search-based optimization algorithm. Ordinary neural circuits perform on par and, in some cases, significantly surpass the performance of contemporary deep learning models. ONC networks are compact, 77% sparser than their counterpart neural controllers, and their neural dynamics are fully interpretable at the cell-level.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether a neural circuit modeled on a biological nervous system can be repurposed as a robot controller. The authors introduce ordinary neural circuits, or ONCs, inspired by the soil worm C. elegans. Their approach keeps a biologically motivated circuit structure while changing its parameters so that it can control alternative tasks.

The authors first show that these circuits have higher maximum network flow than arbitrarily wired networks. They then use a search-based optimization algorithm to configure ONCs for robotic control. The demonstrations include both simulated tasks and autonomous parking by a real rover, connecting the circuit design to physical control behavior.

In the reported comparisons, ONCs match contemporary deep learning controllers and significantly exceed their performance in some cases. They are also 77% sparser than the counterpart controllers, and the authors describe their neural dynamics as fully interpretable at the individual-cell level. Together, these findings suggest that biological circuit structure can provide a useful starting point for compact controllers whose internal dynamics can be examined.
summary.tldr: Biologically inspired neural circuits provide compact, cell-level interpretable controllers that match or sometimes outperform contemporary deep learning models on robotic tasks.

title: A Natural Lottery Ticket Winner: Reinforcement Learning with Ordinary Neural Circuits

abstract: Understanding the dependencies among features of a dataset is at the core of most unsupervised learning tasks. However, a majority of generative modeling approaches are focused solely on the joint distribution $p(x)$ and utilize models where it is intractable to obtain the conditional distribution of some arbitrary subset of features $x_u$ given the rest of the observed covariates $x_o$: $p(x_u \mid x_o)$. Traditional conditional approaches provide a model for a \emph{fixed} set of covariates conditioned on another \emph{fixed} set of observed covariates. Instead, in this work we develop a model that is capable of yielding \emph{all} conditional distributions $p(x_u \mid x_o)$ (for arbitrary $x_u$) via tractable conditional likelihoods. We propose a novel extension of (change of variables based) flow generative models, arbitrary conditioning flow models (ACFlow). ACFlow can be conditioned on arbitrary subsets of observed covariates, which was previously infeasible. We further extend ACFlow to model the joint distributions $p(x)$ and arbitrary marginal distributions $p(x_u)$. We also apply ACFlow to the imputation of features, and develop a unified platform for both multiple and single imputation by introducing an auxiliary objective that provides a principled single “best guess” for flow models. Extensive empirical evaluations show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in modeling arbitrary conditional likelihoods in addition to both single and multiple imputation in synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A generative model may describe how all features vary together yet make it difficult to answer a more specific question: what is the distribution of some features given whichever others happen to be observed? Traditional conditional models typically fix these two groups in advance. ACFlow addresses the need to change the observed and predicted subsets.

The method extends flow models, which construct probability distributions through changes of variables, to provide tractable likelihoods for arbitrary conditional distributions. The authors further extend the framework to represent the full joint distribution and arbitrary marginal distributions. This gives the model several ways to describe feature dependencies within one framework.

The paper applies this flexibility to filling in missing features. It supports multiple imputation, which supplies several possible completions, and adds an auxiliary objective for producing a single best guess. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets report state-of-the-art results for arbitrary conditional likelihood modeling and both forms of imputation.
summary.tldr: ACFlow extends flow models to evaluate arbitrary conditional distributions and supports strong single and multiple missing-feature imputation.

title: ACFlow: Flow Models for Arbitrary Conditional Likelihoods

abstract: Studying the set of exact solutions of a system of polynomial equations largely depends on a single iterative algorithm, known as Buchberger’s algorithm. Optimized versions of this algorithm are crucial for many computer algebra systems (e.g., Mathematica, Maple, Sage). We introduce a new approach to Buchberger’s algorithm that uses reinforcement learning agents to perform S-pair selection, a key step in the algorithm. We then study how the difficulty of the problem depends on the choices of domain and distribution of polynomials, about which little is known. Finally, we train a policy model using proximal policy optimization (PPO) to learn S-pair selection strategies for random systems of binomial equations. In certain domains, the trained model outperforms state-of-the-art selection heuristics in total number of polynomial additions performed, which provides a proof-of-concept that recent developments in machine learning have the potential to improve performance of algorithms in symbolic computation.

paragraphs: Buchberger’s algorithm is central to studying exact solutions of polynomial systems, and optimized implementations matter for computer algebra software. This paper focuses on S-pair selection, a recurring choice within the algorithm. It investigates whether a reinforcement learning policy can make that choice in a way that reduces the amount of symbolic computation.

The authors study how problem difficulty changes with the domain and the distribution from which polynomials are drawn. They then train a policy using proximal policy optimization on random systems of binomial equations. Learning targets the selection strategy inside the existing algorithm, making a specific algorithmic decision the point of intervention.

In certain domains, the learned policy uses fewer total polynomial additions than state-of-the-art selection heuristics. That qualification matters: the reported advantage is domain-dependent and measured in polynomial additions. The result serves as a proof of concept that reinforcement learning can improve a component of a symbolic computation algorithm. It also emphasizes that the distribution of mathematical inputs is relevant when evaluating learned selection rules.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning policy reduces polynomial additions in Buchberger’s algorithm relative to leading selection heuristics in certain domains.

title: Learning Selection Strategies in Buchberger’s Algorithm

abstract: Efficient optimisation of black-box problems that comprise both continuous and categorical inputs is important, yet poses significant challenges. Current approaches, like one-hot encoding, severely increase the dimension of the search space, while separate modelling of category-specific data is sample-inefficient. Both frameworks are not scalable to practical applications involving multiple categorical variables, each with multiple possible values. We propose a new approach, Continuous and Categorical Bayesian Optimisation (CoCaBO), which combines the strengths of multi-armed bandits and Bayesian optimisation to select values for both categorical and continuous inputs. We model this mixed-type space using a Gaussian Process kernel, designed to allow sharing of information across multiple categorical variables; this allows CoCaBO to leverage all available data efficiently. We extend our method to the batch setting and propose an efficient selection procedure that dynamically balances exploration and exploitation whilst encouraging batch diversity. We demonstrate empirically that our method outperforms existing approaches on both synthetic and real-world optimisation tasks with continuous and categorical inputs.

paragraphs: Many black-box optimization problems involve both numerical settings and categorical choices. Existing approaches can struggle when several categorical variables each have many possible values. One-hot encoding expands the search space, while building separate models for different categories uses observations inefficiently because information is divided across those models.

The proposed method, CoCaBO, combines multi-armed bandits with Bayesian optimization to choose categorical and continuous inputs. A Gaussian process kernel models the mixed input space and allows information to be shared across multiple categorical variables. This sharing is central to the approach: available observations can inform the search without requiring a separate, isolated model for every categorical configuration.

The authors also extend CoCaBO to select batches of evaluations. Their selection procedure adjusts the balance between exploring uncertain choices and exploiting promising ones while encouraging diversity within a batch. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show better performance than existing approaches in the tested settings. The findings support treating mixed inputs jointly and sharing information across categories as a practical route to more efficient optimization.
summary.tldr: CoCaBO combines bandits and Bayesian optimization to search mixed categorical and continuous spaces while sharing information across categorical choices.

title: Bayesian Optimisation over Multiple Continuous and Categorical Inputs

abstract: Most of the recent deep reinforcement learning advances take an RL-centric perspective and focus on refinements of the training objective. We diverge from this view and show we can recover the performance of these developments not by changing the objective, but by regularising the value-function estimator. Constraining the Lipschitz constant of a single layer using spectral normalisation is sufficient to elevate the performance of a Categorical-DQN agent to that of a more elaborated agent on the challenging Atari domain. We conduct ablation studies to disentangle the various effects normalisation has on the learning dynamics and show that is sufficient to modulate the parameter updates to recover most of the performance of spectral normalisation. These findings hint towards the need to also focus on the neural component and its learning dynamics to tackle the peculiarities of Deep Reinforcement Learning.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning improvements often come from changing the training objective. This paper investigates the value-function network itself, asking how much performance can improve through regularization and changes to learning dynamics. The focus is on how the neural estimator is optimized within an existing reinforcement learning method.

The authors apply spectral normalization to constrain the Lipschitz constant of a single layer. In their Atari experiments, this change is sufficient to bring a Categorical-DQN agent to the performance level of a more elaborate agent. The result shows that modifying one aspect of the estimator can have a substantial effect without redesigning the objective.

Ablation studies then examine which effects of normalization explain the improvement. They find that modulating parameter updates is enough to recover most of spectral normalization’s performance gain. This points toward optimization dynamics as a major part of the observed benefit. The findings encourage attention to the neural network and its updates when developing deep RL methods, alongside the choice of reinforcement learning objective.
summary.tldr: Normalizing one value-network layer improves Categorical-DQN on Atari, and update modulation recovers most of the reported benefit.

title: Spectral Normalisation for Deep Reinforcement Learning: An Optimisation Perspective

abstract: We consider the decision-making framework of online convex optimization with a very large number of experts. This setting is ubiquitous in contextual and reinforcement learning problems, where the size of the policy class renders enumeration and search within the policy class infeasible. Instead, we consider generalizing the methodology of online boosting. We define a weak learning algorithm as a mechanism that guarantees multiplicatively approximate regret against a base class of experts. In this access model, we give an efficient boosting algorithm that guarantees near-optimal regret against the convex hull of the base class. We consider both full and partial (a.k.a. bandit) information feedback models. We also give an analogous efficient boosting algorithm for the i.i.d. statistical setting. Our results simultaneously generalize online boosting and gradient boosting guarantees to contextual learning model, online convex optimization and bandit linear optimization settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making when the available collection of experts is too large to search directly. This situation arises in contextual and reinforcement learning, where experts can represent candidate policies. The aim is to compete with a powerful reference class without needing to enumerate every policy it contains.

The authors approach this through boosting: building a stronger learner from a weaker learning mechanism. They define the weaker mechanism through a multiplicative approximation guarantee on regret, which measures accumulated loss relative to a comparator. Given this access, their efficient algorithm achieves near-optimal regret against the convex hull of the base experts, meaning combinations of those experts.

The results cover both full feedback and partial, bandit feedback, where the learner receives more restricted information about its decisions. An analogous algorithm handles independently sampled statistical data. Together, these guarantees extend online and gradient boosting ideas across several learning settings, with the weak learner’s stated guarantee providing the foundation for the stronger result.
summary.tldr: An efficient boosting method turns weak regret guarantees into near-optimal guarantees over combinations of experts, including under bandit feedback.

title: Boosting for Online Convex Optimization

abstract: Efficient exploration in bandits is a fundamental online learning problem. We propose a variant of Thompson sampling that learns to explore better as it interacts with bandit instances drawn from an unknown prior. The algorithm meta-learns the prior and thus we call it MetaTS. We propose several efficient implementations of MetaTS and analyze it in Gaussian bandits. Our analysis shows the benefit of meta-learning and is of a broader interest, because we derive a novel prior-dependent Bayes regret bound for Thompson sampling. Our theory is complemented by empirical evaluation, which shows that MetaTS quickly adapts to the unknown prior.

The algorithm meta-learns the prior and thus we call it MetaTS. We propose several efficient implementations of MetaTS and analyze it in Gaussian bandits. Our analysis shows the benefit of meta-learning and is of a broader interest, because we derive a novel prior-dependent Bayes regret bound for Thompson sampling. Our theory is complemented by empirical evaluation, which shows that MetaTS quickly adapts to the unknown prior.

paragraphs: Bandit learning requires choosing actions while gathering information about their rewards. This paper considers repeated encounters with bandit instances drawn from a shared but unknown prior. The opportunity is to learn across instances, using earlier interactions to improve exploration on later ones rather than treating every instance as an unrelated problem.

Meta-Thompson Sampling, or MetaTS, adapts Thompson sampling by learning that prior. The authors propose several efficient implementations and analyze the method for Gaussian bandits. Their analysis establishes a benefit from meta-learning and derives a new Bayes regret bound for Thompson sampling that depends on the prior, making the role of prior information explicit.

Empirical evaluation shows that MetaTS adapts quickly to the unknown prior. The theoretical result and experiments address complementary aspects of the approach: why learning the shared prior can help, and how rapidly adaptation occurs in the evaluated settings. The main contribution is to make exploration itself improve through experience across related bandit instances, with Gaussian bandits providing the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: MetaTS learns the shared prior across bandit instances so Thompson sampling can improve its exploration through experience.

title: Meta-Thompson Sampling

abstract: This paper quantifies the uncertainty of prediction risk for the min-norm least squares estimator in high-dimensional linear regression models. We establish the asymptotic normality of prediction risk when both the sample size and the number of features tend to infinity. Based on the newly established central limit theorems(CLTs), we derive the confidence intervals of the prediction risk under various scenarios. Our results demonstrate the sample-wise non-monotonicity of the prediction risk and confirm “more data hurt" phenomenon. Furthermore, the width of confidence intervals indicates that over-parameterization would enlarge the randomness of prediction performance.

paragraphs: Prediction risk describes how well a fitted model is expected to predict, but that risk can itself vary with the training sample. This paper studies such uncertainty for the minimum-norm least squares estimator in high-dimensional linear regression. Its focus is the variability of prediction performance, rather than only a single value summarizing that performance.

The authors establish asymptotic normality as both the number of observations and the number of features grow. Their central limit theorems describe the limiting fluctuations of prediction risk and provide the basis for confidence intervals under several scenarios. These intervals make uncertainty in the risk estimate explicit within the high-dimensional regimes analyzed.

The results show sample-wise nonmonotonicity: adding data can sometimes worsen prediction risk, confirming a possible “more data hurt” effect. They also find that confidence interval widths indicate greater randomness in prediction performance with overparameterization. The findings therefore concern both changes in risk and its variability; they do not say that additional data always harms prediction or that every overparameterized fit performs poorly.
summary.tldr: New central limit theorems quantify uncertainty in minimum-norm regression risk and show that more data can sometimes worsen prediction performance.

title: Asymptotic Normality and Confidence Intervals for Prediction Risk of the Min-Norm Least Squares Estimator

abstract: Choosing the optimizer is considered to be among the most crucial design decisions in deep learning, and it is not an easy one. The growing literature now lists hundreds of optimization methods. In the absence of clear theoretical guidance and conclusive empirical evidence, the decision is often made based on anecdotes. In this work, we aim to replace these anecdotes, if not with a conclusive ranking, then at least with evidence-backed heuristics. To do so, we perform an extensive, standardized benchmark of fifteen particularly popular deep learning optimizers while giving a concise overview of the wide range of possible choices. Analyzing more than 50,000 individual runs, we contribute the following three points: (i) Optimizer performance varies greatly across tasks. (ii) We observe that evaluating multiple optimizers with default parameters works approximately as well as tuning the hyperparameters of a single, fixed optimizer. (iii) While we cannot discern an optimization method clearly dominating across all tested tasks, we identify a significantly reduced subset of specific optimizers and parameter choices that generally lead to competitive results in our experiments: Adam remains a strong contender, with newer methods failing to significantly and consistently outperform it. Our open-sourced results are available as challenging and well-tuned baselines for more meaningful evaluations of novel optimization methods without requiring any further computational efforts.

paragraphs: Choosing an optimizer means choosing how a neural network updates its parameters during training. With hundreds of proposed methods and limited decisive guidance, that choice often rests on anecdotes. This paper replaces some of that guesswork with a standardized comparison of fifteen popular optimizers, covering more than 50,000 individual runs.

The results show substantial variation across tasks, with no optimizer clearly dominating every tested setting. One useful practical finding is that trying several optimizers with their default settings worked approximately as well as tuning the hyperparameters of one fixed optimizer. In these experiments, exploring the optimizer choice itself was therefore a competitive use of search effort.

The authors identify a smaller collection of optimizer and parameter choices that generally produced competitive results. Adam remains strong: newer methods did not significantly and consistently outperform it. These are evidence-backed heuristics from the tested tasks, not a universal ranking. The released results also provide well-tuned reference points for evaluating new optimization methods without repeating the full benchmark.
summary.tldr: A large standardized benchmark finds task-dependent optimizer performance, with Adam competitive and default-setting optimizer searches approximately matching single-optimizer tuning.

title: Descending through a Crowded Valley - Benchmarking Deep Learning Optimizers

abstract: This paper introduces Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting (SGLB) - a powerful and efficient machine learning framework that may deal with a wide range of loss functions and has provable generalization guarantees. The method is based on a special form of the Langevin diffusion equation specifically designed for gradient boosting. This allows us to theoretically guarantee the global convergence even for multimodal loss functions, while standard gradient boosting algorithms can guarantee only local optimum. We also empirically show that SGLB outperforms classic gradient boosting when applied to classification tasks with 0-1 loss function, which is known to be multimodal.

The method is based on a special form of the Langevin diffusion equation specifically designed for gradient boosting. This allows us to theoretically guarantee the global convergence even for multimodal loss functions, while standard gradient boosting algorithms can guarantee only local optimum. We also empirically show that SGLB outperforms classic gradient boosting when applied to classification tasks with 0-1 loss function, which is known to be multimodal.

paragraphs: Gradient boosting can encounter loss functions with multiple modes, where reaching a local optimum does not establish that the best solution has been found. This paper introduces Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting to address that optimization difficulty. It presents the method as an efficient framework that may handle a broad range of losses.

SGLB is built from a form of the Langevin diffusion equation designed specifically for gradient boosting. This construction supports a theoretical guarantee of global convergence even for multimodal losses. The authors also provide generalization guarantees, addressing how the learned model performs beyond the optimization objective on its training data. These are distinct theoretical aspects of the proposed framework.

The empirical study considers classification with the 0-1 loss, which counts incorrect predictions and is multimodal in the setting described. SGLB outperforms classic gradient boosting in those experiments. The findings pair a theoretical treatment of global convergence with evidence on a classification loss that exhibits the optimization difficulty motivating the method.
summary.tldr: SGLB adapts Langevin diffusion to gradient boosting, providing global convergence guarantees and improved reported performance on 0-1-loss classification.

title: SGLB: Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting

abstract: We propose Compressed Vertical Federated Learning (C-VFL) for communication-efficient training on vertically partitioned data. In C-VFL, a server and multiple parties collaboratively train a model on their respective features utilizing several local iterations and sharing compressed intermediate results periodically. Our work provides the first theoretical analysis of the effect message compression has on distributed training over vertically partitioned data. We prove convergence of non-convex objectives at a rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ when the compression error is bounded over the course of training. We provide specific requirements for convergence with common compression techniques, such as quantization and top-$k$ sparsification. Finally, we experimentally show compression can reduce communication by over $90%$ without a significant decrease in accuracy over VFL without compression.

This paper introduces Compressed Vertical Federated Learning, or C-VFL, to reduce the amount of information sent during training.

The server and participating parties perform several local iterations and periodically share compressed intermediate results. The analysis examines how errors introduced by compression affect learning. For non-convex objectives, the authors prove a convergence rate of O(1/√T), provided compression error remains bounded throughout training. They also give convergence requirements for common techniques, including quantization and top-k sparsification.

This supports compression as a practical way to reduce coordination costs in the evaluated settings. The theoretical contribution explains when this saving remains compatible with convergence, tying the behavior of the training procedure to explicit control of compression error.
summary.tldr: C-VFL compresses exchanged training results, reducing communication by over 90% in experiments while providing convergence guarantees under bounded compression error.

title: Compressed-VFL: Communication-Efficient Learning with Vertically Partitioned Data

abstract: The invariance to permutations of the adjacency matrix, i.e., graph isomorphism, is an overarching requirement for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Conventionally, this prerequisite can be satisfied by the invariant operations over node permutations when aggregating messages. However, such an invariant manner may ignore the relationships among neighboring nodes, thereby hindering the expressivity of GNNs. In this work, we devise an efficient permutation-sensitive aggregation mechanism via permutation groups, capturing pairwise correlations between neighboring nodes. We prove that our approach is strictly more powerful than the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (2-WL) graph isomorphism test and not less powerful than the 3-WL test. Moreover, we prove that our approach achieves the linear sampling complexity. Comprehensive experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our model.

paragraphs: A graph's meaning should not depend on how its nodes are numbered or its adjacency matrix is ordered. Graph neural networks commonly enforce this through permutation-invariant message aggregation. However, such aggregation can overlook relationships between neighboring nodes, reducing the structural information available to the network.

This paper introduces an efficient permutation-sensitive aggregation mechanism built using permutation groups. The mechanism captures pairwise correlations among neighbors while addressing the overarching requirement of graph-isomorphism invariance. The key distinction is between preserving the identity of the graph under relabeling and retaining useful relationships within a node's neighborhood.

The authors prove that their approach has strictly greater distinguishing power than the two-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman test and at least the power of the three-dimensional test. They also establish linear sampling complexity. Experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the model's superiority in the reported evaluations. The theoretical and empirical results together support capturing neighbor relationships as a way to improve graph representations without requiring an inefficient sampling mechanism.
summary.tldr: Permutation-group aggregation captures relationships among graph neighbors with proven expressive power at least matching the 3-WL test.

title: Going Deeper into Permutation-Sensitive Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance on graph-based tasks. The key idea for GNNs is to obtain informative representation through aggregating information from local neighborhoods. However, it remains an open question whether the neighborhood information is adequately aggregated for learning representations of nodes with few neighbors. To address this, we propose a simple and efficient data augmentation strategy, local augmentation, to learn the distribution of the node representations of the neighbors conditioned on the central node’s representation and enhance GNN’s expressive power with generated features. Local augmentation is a general framework that can be applied to any GNN model in a plug-and-play manner. It samples feature vectors associated with each node from the learned conditional distribution as additional input for the backbone model at each training iteration. Extensive experiments and analyses show that local augmentation consistently yields performance improvement when applied to various GNN architectures across a diverse set of benchmarks. For example, experiments show that plugging in local augmentation to GCN and GAT improves by an average of 3.4% and 1.6% in terms of test accuracy on Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed. Besides, our experimental results on large graphs (OGB) show that our model consistently improves performance over backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/SongtaoLiu0823/LAGNN.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks build node representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes. For a node with few neighbors, that process has relatively little local information available. This paper asks whether the neighborhood input is sufficient and proposes local augmentation as a way to enrich what an existing graph neural network receives.

The method learns a distribution of neighbor representations conditioned on the central node's representation. During each training iteration, it samples additional feature vectors from that distribution and supplies them to the backbone network. The generated inputs therefore reflect a learned relationship to the central node. The authors present the procedure as a general, plug-in framework for graph neural networks.

Experiments across several architectures and benchmarks consistently show improvements. On Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed, the reported average test-accuracy improvements are 3.4% for GCN and 1.6% for GAT. Evaluations on larger OGB graphs also improve on the backbone models. Together, these results support learned local feature generation as a practical way to strengthen neighborhood-based representation learning.
summary.tldr: Local augmentation supplies graph neural networks with generated neighbor features, improving the tested backbones across small and large graph benchmarks.

title: Local Augmentation for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We investigate quantum circuits for graph representation learning, and propose equivariant quantum graph circuits (EQGCs), as a class of parameterized quantum circuits with strong relational inductive bias for learning over graph-structured data. Conceptually, EQGCs serve as a unifying framework for quantum graph representation learning, allowing us to define several interesting subclasses which subsume existing proposals. In terms of the representation power, we prove that the studied subclasses of EQGCs are universal approximators for functions over the bounded graph domain. This theoretical perspective on quantum graph machine learning methods opens many directions for further work, and could lead to models with capabilities beyond those of classical approaches. We empirically verify the expressive power of EQGCs through a dedicated experiment on synthetic data, and additionally observe that the performance of EQGCs scales well with the depth of the model and does not suffer from barren plateu issues.

paragraphs: The paper investigates quantum circuits that learn representations of graphs. It introduces equivariant quantum graph circuits, or EQGCs, whose design incorporates the relational structure of graph data. The framework organizes several circuit subclasses and includes existing proposals within a common mathematical description.

The authors prove that the studied subclasses can universally approximate functions over a bounded graph domain. This establishes a broad representational capability within that domain. It also supplies a theoretical basis for investigating quantum graph-learning models, including the possibility of capabilities beyond classical approaches. That possible advantage remains a direction suggested by the framework.

A dedicated synthetic-data experiment supports the expressive-power results. The authors also observe that performance scales well with circuit depth and that the tested models do not encounter barren plateau issues. These observations concern the evaluated setting, while the approximation theorem concerns representational power. Together, they provide complementary reasons to investigate EQGCs: a unified architecture family, a formal expressiveness result, and encouraging empirical behavior.
summary.tldr: Equivariant quantum graph circuits unify graph-learning architectures and offer universal approximation results on bounded graph domains.

title: Equivariant Quantum Graph Circuits

abstract: Conformer has proven to be effective in many speech processing tasks. It combines the benefits of extracting local dependencies using convolutions and global dependencies using self-attention. Inspired by this, we propose a more flexible, interpretable and customizable encoder alternative, Branchformer, with parallel branches for modeling various ranged dependencies in end-to-end speech processing. In each encoder layer, one branch employs self-attention or its variant to capture long-range dependencies, while the other branch utilizes an MLP module with convolutional gating (cgMLP) to extract local relationships. We conduct experiments on several speech recognition and spoken language understanding benchmarks. Results show that our model outperforms both Transformer and cgMLP. It also matches with or outperforms state-of-the-art results achieved by Conformer. Furthermore, we show various strategies to reduce computation thanks to the two-branch architecture, including the ability to have variable inference complexity in a single trained model. The weights learned for merging branches indicate how local and global dependencies are utilized in different layers, which benefits model designing.

paragraphs: Speech processing benefits from both nearby relationships and connections across a longer sequence. Branchformer builds an encoder that handles these ranges through parallel branches within each layer. The design follows the motivation behind Conformer, which combines local convolutional processing with global self-attention, while making the two forms of processing more explicitly separable.

One branch uses self-attention or a related mechanism to capture long-range dependencies. The other uses a multilayer perceptron with convolutional gating to model local relationships. Learned merging weights indicate how the model combines these branches at different layers. Those weights provide information about the use of local and global context that can help guide architecture design.

Across the reported speech recognition and spoken language understanding benchmarks, Branchformer outperforms Transformer and the convolutionally gated MLP model. It also matches or exceeds the reported state-of-the-art Conformer results. The parallel structure supports several ways to reduce computation, including varying inference complexity within one trained model. This makes the architecture relevant to both prediction quality and computational flexibility.
summary.tldr: Branchformer combines parallel local and global speech-processing branches, achieving strong benchmark results with flexible inference computation.

title: Branchformer: Parallel MLP-Attention Architectures to Capture Local and Global Context for Speech Recognition and Understanding

abstract: k-means clustering is an important problem in machine learning and statistics. The k-means++ initialization algorithm has driven new acceleration strategies and theoretical analysis for solving the k-means clustering problem. The state-of-the-art variant, called LocalSearch++, adds extra local search steps upon k-means++ to achieve constant approximation error in expectation. In this paper, we propose a new variant named LSDS++, which improves the sampling efficiency of LocalSearch++ via a strategy called dual sampling. By defining a new capture graph based on the concept of coreset, we show that the proposed LSDS++ is able to achieve the same expected constant error with reduced complexity. Experiments are conducted to justify the benefit of LSDS++ in practice.

paragraphs: The quality of the starting centers is important in k-means clustering, and k-means++ provides an initialization procedure that has motivated further algorithmic improvements. One extension, LocalSearch++, adds local search steps to obtain a constant-factor approximation guarantee in expectation. This paper asks whether that guarantee can be retained with less computational work.

The proposed algorithm, LSDS++, changes how LocalSearch++ samples through a strategy called dual sampling. Its main target is sampling efficiency within the existing local-search approach. To analyze the change, the authors introduce a capture graph built around the concept of a coreset. This provides the structure needed to relate the more efficient sampling procedure to the approximation guarantee.

The theoretical result preserves the same expected constant approximation error while reducing complexity. The expectation qualifier matters: the claim concerns expected approximation quality rather than an identical outcome on every run. Experiments also support practical benefits for LSDS++. Together, the analysis and evaluation present more efficient sampling as a way to accelerate this clustering approach without weakening its stated expected guarantee.
summary.tldr: LSDS++ improves LocalSearch++ sampling efficiency while retaining its expected constant-factor approximation guarantee for k-means.

title: LSDS++ : Dual Sampling for Accelerated k-means++

abstract: We study streaming algorithms in the white-box adversarial stream model, where the internal state of the streaming algorithm is revealed to an adversary who adaptively generates the stream updates, but the algorithm obtains fresh randomness unknown to the adversary at each time step. We incorporate cryptographic assumptions to construct robust algorithms against such adversaries. We propose efficient algorithms for sparse recovery of vectors, low rank recovery of matrices and tensors, as well as low rank plus sparse recovery of matrices, i.e., robust PCA. Unlike deterministic algorithms, our algorithms can report when the input is not sparse or low rank even in the presence of such an adversary. We use these recovery algorithms to improve upon and solve new problems in numerical linear algebra and combinatorial optimization on white-box adversarial streams. For example, we give the first efficient algorithm for outputting a matching in a graph with insertions and deletions to its edges provided the matching size is small, and otherwise we declare the matching size is large. We also improve the approximation versus memory tradeoff of previous work for estimating the number of non-zero elements in a vector and computing the matrix rank.

paragraphs: A streaming algorithm processes updates while maintaining an internal summary. This paper considers an adversary that can inspect that internal state and adapt future updates accordingly. The algorithm still receives fresh randomness at each step that the adversary does not know. Under cryptographic assumptions, the authors construct algorithms robust to this demanding information model.

Their methods recover sparse vectors, low-rank matrices and tensors, and matrices decomposable into low-rank and sparse parts. The last task corresponds to robust PCA. A key feature is that the algorithms can report when an input lacks the assumed sparsity or low rank, even under adaptive interference. The abstract contrasts this capability with deterministic algorithms.

These recovery tools lead to applications in numerical linear algebra and combinatorial optimization. One algorithm outputs a graph matching when the matching size is small, or declares the size large, while supporting edge insertions and deletions. Other results improve the tradeoff between memory and approximation for counting nonzero vector entries and computing matrix rank.
summary.tldr: Using cryptographic assumptions and fresh randomness, the paper improves streaming recovery and optimization against adversaries that can inspect algorithm state.

title: Improved Algorithms for White-Box Adversarial Streams

abstract: The development of largely human-annotated benchmarks has driven the success of deep neural networks in various NLP tasks. To enhance the effectiveness of existing benchmarks, collecting new additional input-output pairs is often too costly and challenging, particularly considering their marginal impact on improving the current model accuracy. Instead, additional or complementary annotations on the existing input texts in the benchmarks can be preferable as an efficient way to pay the additional human cost. In this paper, we investigate task-specific preferences between pairs of input texts as a new alternative way for such auxiliary data annotation. From pair-wise comparisons with respect to the task, the auxiliary preference learning enables the model to learn an additional informative training signal that cannot be captured with instance-wise task labels. To this end, we propose a novel multi-task learning framework, called prefer-to-classify (P2C), which can enjoy the cooperative effect of learning both the given classification task and the auxiliary preferences. Here, we provide three different ways to collect preference signals in practice: (a) implicitly extracting from annotation records (for free, but often unavailable), (b) collecting explicitly from crowd workers (high paid), or (c) pre-trained large language models such as GPT-3 (low paid). Given existing classification NLP benchmarks, we demonstrate that the proposed auxiliary preference learning via P2C on them is effective in improving text classifiers. Our codes are publicly available.

paragraphs: Improving a text classifier by collecting more labeled examples can be costly, particularly when the accuracy gains are small. This paper explores adding a different kind of annotation to texts already in a benchmark. It asks for task-specific preferences between pairs of texts, supplying relational information alongside the existing classification labels.

The proposed prefer-to-classify framework, P2C, trains classification and preference prediction together. Individual labels describe each example separately, while pairwise comparisons provide an additional training signal about the relationship between examples. The multi-task setup aims to make these two kinds of supervision cooperate, extracting more useful information from an existing collection of texts.

The authors describe three practical sources of preferences: existing annotation records, explicit judgments from crowd workers, and pretrained language models such as GPT-3. Existing records can supply signals without additional annotation cost but are often unavailable; crowd and language-model annotation have different stated costs. Experiments on existing NLP classification benchmarks show that auxiliary preference learning improves the classifiers, supporting complementary annotation as a useful way to strengthen established datasets.
summary.tldr: P2C improves text classifiers by jointly learning classification labels and task-specific pairwise preferences over existing texts.

title: Prefer to Classify: Improving Text Classifiers via Auxiliary Preference Learning

abstract: Transformer models have achieved remarkable results in various natural language tasks, but they are often prohibitively large, requiring massive memories and computational resources. To re- duce the size and complexity of these models, we propose LoSparse (Low-Rank and Sparse ap- proximation), a novel model compression tech- nique that approximates a weight matrix by the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix. Our method combines the advantages of both low- rank approximations and pruning, while avoid- ing their limitations. Low-rank approximation compresses the coherent and expressive parts in neurons, while pruning removes the incoherent and non-expressive parts in neurons. Pruning enhances the diversity of low-rank approxima- tions, and low-rank approximation prevents prun- ing from losing too many expressive neurons. We evaluate our method on natural language under- standing, question answering, and natural lan- guage generation tasks. We show that it signif- icantly outperforms existing compression meth- ods. Our code is publicly available at https: //github.com/yxli2123/LoSparse

paragraphs: Large transformer models can demand substantial memory and computation, motivating methods that compress their learned weights. LoSparse approximates a weight matrix as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix. This combines two compression strategies within a single representation, allowing each component to preserve a different aspect of the original weights.

The low-rank component compresses coherent, expressive structure across neurons. Pruning removes incoherent, less expressive portions, while the retained sparse component contributes diversity beyond the low-rank approximation. The authors describe these roles as complementary: low-rank approximation helps prevent excessive loss of expressive neurons, and pruning enriches what can be represented alongside the low-rank structure.

The method is evaluated on natural-language understanding, question answering, and language generation tasks. The paper reports significant improvements over existing compression methods across these evaluations. The findings support combining shared structure and sparse retained information when compressing transformers. The central contribution is the joint approximation itself and the way its two parts are designed to compensate for weaknesses of using either strategy alone.
summary.tldr: LoSparse compresses transformer weights with complementary low-rank and sparse components, outperforming existing compression methods in the reported language-task evaluations.

title: LoSparse: Structured Compression of Large Language Models based on Low-Rank and Sparse Approximation

abstract: Human brains respond to semantic features of presented stimuli with different neurons. This raises the question of whether deep neural networks admit a similar behavior pattern. To investigate this phenomenon, this paper identifies a small cluster of neurons associated with a specific subject in a diffusion model. We call those neurons the concept neurons. They can be identified by statistics of network gradients to a stimulation connected with the given subject. The concept neurons demonstrate magnetic properties in interpreting and manipulating generation results. Shutting them can directly yield the related subject contextualized in different scenes. Concatenating multiple clusters of concept neurons can vividly generate all related concepts in a single image. Our method attains impressive performance for multi-subject customization, even four or more subjects. For large-scale applications, the concept neurons are environmentally friendly as we only need to store a sparse cluster of int index instead of dense float32 parameter values, reducing storage consumption by 90% compared with previous customized generation methods. Extensive qualitative and quantitative studies on diverse scenarios show the superiority of our method in interpreting and manipulating diffusion models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a diffusion model contains small groups of neurons associated with particular subjects. The authors call these groups concept neurons and identify them through statistics of network gradients produced by stimulation connected to a subject. The aim is both to interpret how subjects are represented and to control their appearance in generated images.

The identified neurons provide a direct handle for customization. The authors report that shutting off a subject’s concept neurons can produce that subject in different scenes. Combining several clusters can bring their associated subjects into a single image, with reported success on customization involving four or more subjects.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across diverse scenarios support the approach’s usefulness for interpreting diffusion models and manipulating their outputs.
summary.tldr: Cones identifies small neuron clusters that support subject-specific diffusion customization and multi-subject generation while substantially reducing storage.

title: Cones: Concept Neurons in Diffusion Models for Customized Generation

abstract: Data valuation—quantifying the contribution of individual data sources to certain predictive behaviors of a model—is of great importance to enhancing the transparency of machine learning and designing incentive systems for data sharing. Existing work has focused on evaluating data sources with the shared feature or sample space. How to valuate fragmented data sources of which each only contains partial features and samples remains an open question. We start by presenting a method to calculate the counterfactual of removing a fragment from the aggregated data matrix. Based on the counterfactual calculation, we further propose 2D-Shapley, a theoretical framework for fragmented data valuation that uniquely satisfies some appealing axioms in the fragmented data context. 2D-Shapley empowers a range of new use cases, such as selecting useful data fragments, providing interpretation for sample-wise data values, and fine-grained data issue diagnosis.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks how much a data source contributes to a model’s predictive behavior. Existing approaches typically assume that sources share either the same features or the same samples. This paper addresses a more fragmented situation: each source may provide only some features for some samples, so its contribution occupies only part of the combined data matrix.

The authors first develop a way to calculate the counterfactual outcome of removing one such fragment. This gives a basis for assessing what that fragment contributes when combined with other available data. They then introduce 2D-Shapley, a valuation framework that uniquely satisfies a specified set of axioms for this fragmented setting.

The framework makes it possible to evaluate contributions at a finer level than an entire sample or source. Its stated uses include choosing useful fragments, explaining sample-level valuations, and locating data problems more precisely. The theoretical uniqueness claim is tied to the framework’s axioms, giving a principled basis for valuation within that formulation.
summary.tldr: 2D-Shapley provides an axiomatic way to value data sources that contain only partial sets of both samples and features.

title: 2D-Shapley: A Framework for Fragmented Data Valuation

abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), independent learning (IL) often shows remarkable performance and easily scales with the number of agents. Yet, using IL can be inefficient and runs the risk of failing to successfully train, particularly in scenarios that require agents to coordinate their actions. Using centralised learning (CL) enables MARL agents to quickly learn how to coordinate their behaviour but employing CL everywhere is often prohibitively expensive in real-world applications. Besides, using CL in value-based methods often needs strong representational constraints (e.g. individual-global-max condition) that can lead to poor performance if violated. In this paper, we introduce a novel plug & play IL framework named Multi-Agent Network Selection Algorithm (MANSA) which selectively employs CL only at states that require coordination. At its core, MANSA has an additional agent that uses switching controls to quickly learn the best states to activate CL during training, using CL only where necessary and vastly reducing the computational burden of CL. Our theory proves MANSA preserves cooperative MARL convergence properties, boosts IL performance and can optimally make use of a fixed budget on the number CL calls. We show empirically in Level-based Foraging (LBF) and StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge (SMAC) that MANSA achieves fast, superior and more reliable performance while making 40% fewer CL calls in SMAC and using CL at only 1% CL calls in LBF.

Value-based centralized approaches can also require restrictive representational conditions that harm performance when violated.

MANSA combines independent learning with selective centralized assistance. An additional agent learns when to activate centralized learning using switching controls. Its task is to identify states where coordination assistance is needed, concentrating centralized computation there. The framework is designed to plug into independent learning rather than require centralized learning at every state.

The theoretical results preserve cooperative learning convergence properties, improve independent learning performance, and support optimal use of a fixed budget of centralized calls. Experiments in Level-based Foraging and the StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge report faster, stronger, and more reliable performance. Reported usage includes 40% fewer centralized calls in StarCraft and centralized learning at only 1% of calls in Level-based Foraging.
summary.tldr: MANSA learns when to activate centralized training, improving multi-agent coordination while substantially reducing centralized learning calls.

title: MANSA: Learning Fast and Slow in Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: We study the problem of temporal-difference-based policy evaluation in reinforcement learning. In particular, we analyse the use of a distributional reinforcement learning algorithm, quantile temporal-difference learning (QTD), for this task. We reach the surprising conclusion that even if a practitioner has no interest in the return distribution beyond the mean, QTD (which learns predictions about the full distribution of returns) may offer performance superior to approaches such as classical TD learning, which predict only the mean return, even in the tabular setting.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation in reinforcement learning asks how much return a given policy is expected to produce. Classical temporal-difference learning focuses directly on this mean return. Quantile temporal-difference learning takes a richer route, learning predictions about the distribution of possible returns. This paper studies whether that additional distributional information can help even when the final quantity of interest is only the mean.

The authors analyze quantile temporal-difference learning for temporal-difference-based policy evaluation. Their conclusion is that learning the return distribution may produce better value estimates than approaches that predict only its mean. The important distinction is between the information represented during learning and the information ultimately requested: a richer prediction target can be useful even when the user wants a single expected value.

The stated benefit can arise in the tabular setting, so it is not presented solely as a consequence of using a complex neural representation. The claim remains a possibility rather than a universal ranking of algorithms. It gives a statistical reason to consider distributional learning for ordinary value estimation, beyond applications that explicitly need the full distribution of outcomes.
summary.tldr: Learning return quantiles may improve mean-value estimation over classical temporal-difference learning, even in tabular policy evaluation.

title: The Statistical Benefits of Quantile Temporal-Difference Learning for Value Estimation

abstract: Despite the significant recent progress in deep generative models, the underlying structure of their latent spaces is still poorly understood, thereby making the task of performing semantically meaningful latent traversals an open research challenge. Most prior work has aimed to solve this challenge by modeling latent structures linearly, and finding corresponding linear directions which result in ‘disentangled’ generations. In this work, we instead propose to model latent structures with a learned dynamic potential landscape, thereby performing latent traversals as the flow of samples down the landscape’s gradient. Inspired by physics, optimal transport, and neuroscience, these potential landscapes are learned as physically realistic partial differential equations, thereby allowing them to flexibly vary over both space and time. To achieve disentanglement, multiple potentials are learned simultaneously, and are constrained by a classifier to be distinct and semantically self-consistent. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our method achieves both more qualitatively and quantitatively disentangled trajectories than state-of-the-art baselines. Further, we demonstrate that our method can be integrated as a regularization term during training, thereby acting as an inductive bias towards the learning of structured representations, ultimately improving model likelihood on similarly structured data. Code is available at https://github.com/KingJamesSong/PDETraversal.

paragraphs: A meaningful latent traversal changes a generative model’s internal representation so that its output changes in an understandable way. Many approaches seek straight-line directions associated with distinct semantic changes. This paper instead learns a dynamic potential landscape and moves samples along its downhill gradients, allowing traversal directions to vary with position and time.

The potential landscapes are learned as physically realistic partial differential equations. Multiple potentials are trained together, with a classifier constraining them to be distinct and semantically self-consistent. This structure aims to produce separate kinds of meaningful change even when the corresponding paths through latent space are more complex than straight lines.

Experiments report better qualitative and quantitative disentanglement of trajectories than state-of-the-art baselines. The authors also use the method as a regularization term while training a generative model. In that role, it encourages structured representations and improves model likelihood on similarly structured data. The contribution thus covers both navigating learned latent spaces and influencing their structure during training.
summary.tldr: Learned dynamic potential fields guide nonlinear latent traversals and can encourage more structured generative representations during training.

title: Latent Traversals in Generative Models as Potential Flows

abstract: We introduce Masked Trajectory Models (MTM) as a generic abstraction for sequential decision making. MTM takes a trajectory, such as a state-action sequence, and aims to reconstruct the trajectory conditioned on random subsets of the same trajectory. By training with a highly randomized masking pattern, MTM learns versatile networks that can take on different roles or capabilities, by simply choosing appropriate masks at inference time. For example, the same MTM network can be used as a forward dynamics model, inverse dynamics model, or even an offline RL agent. Through extensive experiments in several continuous control tasks, we show that the same MTM network – i.e. same weights – can match or outperform specialized networks trained for the aforementioned capabilities. Additionally, we find that state representations learned by MTM can significantly accelerate the learning speed of traditional RL algorithms. Finally, in offline RL benchmarks, we find that MTM is competitive with specialized offline RL algorithms, despite MTM being a generic self-supervised learning method without any explicit RL components. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/mtm.

paragraphs: Masked Trajectory Models learn by reconstructing a trajectory from randomly selected visible parts of that same trajectory. A trajectory can contain states and actions, so the missing information can correspond to different sequential decision-making questions. Highly varied masking during training encourages one network to handle multiple kinds of reconstruction.

At inference time, choosing a mask determines the network's role. The same learned weights can serve as a forward dynamics model, an inverse dynamics model, or an offline reinforcement-learning agent. The approach makes these capabilities different uses of a shared model rather than requiring a separately trained network for each function.

Experiments on several continuous-control tasks show that the same MTM network can match or outperform specialized networks for these roles. Its learned state representations also significantly accelerate traditional reinforcement-learning algorithms in the reported experiments. On offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks, MTM is competitive with specialized algorithms despite using a generic self-supervised objective without explicit reinforcement-learning components. The findings support masked reconstruction as a versatile source of decision-making capabilities.
summary.tldr: MTM learns multiple prediction and control capabilities through masked trajectory reconstruction, selecting each role with an inference-time mask.

title: Masked Trajectory Models for Prediction, Representation, and Control

abstract: We first propose a decentralized proximal stochastic gradient tracking method (DProxSGT) for nonconvex stochastic composite problems, with data heterogeneously distributed on multiple workers in a decentralized connected network. To save communication cost, we then extend DProxSGT to a compressed method by compressing the communicated information. Both methods need only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ samples per worker for each proximal update, which is important to achieve good generalization performance on training deep neural networks. With a smoothness condition on the expected loss function (but not on each sample function), the proposed methods can achieve an optimal sample complexity result to produce a near-stationary point. Numerical experiments on training neural networks demonstrate the significantly better generalization performance of our methods over large-batch training methods and momentum variance-reduction methods and also, the ability of handling heterogeneous data by the gradient tracking scheme.

paragraphs: This paper studies training across workers connected through a decentralized network, where different workers hold different data distributions. The optimization problems are nonconvex and composite, requiring more than a plain gradient update. The goal is to handle this heterogeneity while keeping both data use per update and communication costs manageable.

The authors introduce DProxSGT, a proximal stochastic method with gradient tracking, and a compressed version that reduces the information exchanged between workers. Both use only a constant number of samples per worker for each proximal update. Gradient tracking provides the mechanism for handling differences in the data held across the network.

Under a smoothness condition on the expected loss, without requiring that condition for every sample loss, the methods achieve optimal sample complexity for reaching a near-stationary point. This is a stationarity guarantee, not a global-optimum claim. Neural-network experiments report better generalization than large-batch and momentum variance-reduction methods, alongside evidence that gradient tracking handles heterogeneous data.
summary.tldr: Decentralized gradient tracking with optional communication compression supports small-sample updates and provable convergence for heterogeneous nonconvex training.

title: Compressed Decentralized Proximal Stochastic Gradient Method for Nonconvex Composite Problems with Heterogeneous Data

abstract: Adversarial attacks in Natural Language Processing apply perturbations in the character or token levels. Token-level attacks, gaining prominence for their use of gradient-based methods, are susceptible to altering sentence semantics, leading to invalid adversarial examples. While character-level attacks easily maintain semantics, they have received less attention as they cannot easily adopt popular gradient-based methods, and are thought to be easy to defend. Challenging these beliefs, we introduce Charmer, an efficient query-based adversarial attack capable of achieving high attack success rate (ASR) while generating highly similar adversarial examples. Our method successfully targets both small (BERT) and large (Llama 2) models. Specifically, on BERT with SST-2, Charmer improves the ASR in $4.84$% points and the USE similarity in $8$% points with respect to the previous art. Our implementation is available in https://github.com/LIONS-EPFL/Charmer.

Challenging these beliefs, we introduce Charmer, an efficient query-based adversarial attack capable of achieving high attack success rate (ASR) while generating highly similar adversarial examples. paragraphs: Adversarial text attacks seek small input changes that cause a model to behave incorrectly. Changing whole tokens can inadvertently alter a sentence’s meaning, weakening the validity of the attack example. Character-level edits can more easily preserve meaning, but they have received less attention because gradient-based methods are difficult to apply and these attacks have been considered easy to defend.

The paper introduces Charmer, an efficient query-based character attack. It aims to achieve both a high attack success rate and high similarity between the original and modified text. Considering both outcomes matters: an attack is more informative when it changes model behavior while leaving the input closely related to what the model originally received.

Charmer successfully attacks both BERT and Llama 2. On BERT with SST-2, it improves attack success by 4.84 percentage points and USE similarity by eight percentage points relative to prior work. These results challenge the view that character-level perturbations are a weak threat and demonstrate that successful attacks can remain highly similar to the original examples.
summary.tldr: Charmer uses character-level queries to attack language models while preserving high similarity to the original text.

title: Revisiting Character-level Adversarial Attacks for Language Models

abstract: Sampling-based methods, e.g., Deep Ensembles and Bayesian Neural Nets have become promising approaches to improve the quality of uncertainty estimation and robust generalization. However, they suffer from a large model size and high latency at test time, which limits the scalability needed for low-resource devices and real-time applications. To resolve these computational issues, we propose Density-Softmax, a sampling-free deterministic framework via combining a density function built on a Lipschitz-constrained feature extractor with the softmax layer. Theoretically, we show that our model is the solution of minimax uncertainty risk and is distance-aware on feature space, thus reducing the over-confidence of the standard softmax under distribution shifts. Empirically, our method enjoys competitive results with state-of-the-art techniques in terms of uncertainty and robustness, while having a lower number of model parameters and a lower latency at test time.

paragraphs: Methods such as deep ensembles and Bayesian neural networks can improve uncertainty estimates, but their model size and prediction latency can make deployment expensive. Density-Softmax addresses this computational problem with a deterministic framework that does not require sampling at test time. The goal is useful uncertainty estimation and robustness with a smaller prediction-time burden.

The framework combines softmax with a density function built on a Lipschitz-constrained feature extractor. This construction makes predictions sensitive to distance in the learned feature space. The authors theoretically characterize the model as a solution to a minimax uncertainty-risk problem and show how its distance awareness reduces standard softmax’s overconfidence under distribution shifts.

Experiments report uncertainty and robustness results competitive with state-of-the-art techniques, alongside fewer model parameters and lower test-time latency. These findings support the framework’s relevance to resource-constrained devices and real-time applications. The stated result is competitive empirical performance with greater efficiency, rather than a claim that the method surpasses every alternative on every measure.
summary.tldr: Density-Softmax combines feature-space density with softmax to deliver competitive uncertainty and robustness with lower test-time cost.

title: Density-Softmax: Efficient Test-time Model for Uncertainty Estimation and Robustness under Distribution Shifts

abstract: Editing signals using large pre-trained models, in a zero-shot manner, has recently seen rapid advancements in the image domain. However, this wave has yet to reach the audio domain. In this paper, we explore two zero-shot editing techniques for audio signals, which use DDPM inversion with pre-trained diffusion models. The first, which we coin ZEro-shot Text-based Audio (ZETA) editing, is adopted from the image domain. The second, named ZEro-shot UnSupervized (ZEUS) editing, is a novel approach for discovering semantically meaningful editing directions without supervision. When applied to music signals, this method exposes a range of musically interesting modifications, from controlling the participation of specific instruments to improvisations on the melody. Samples and code can be found on our examples page.
