paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models have enabled zero-shot editing of images, and this paper explores corresponding techniques for audio. Both proposed techniques use DDPM inversion with pretrained diffusion models. The shared goal is to edit an existing audio signal using capabilities already present in the model.

The first technique, ZETA, adapts a text-based editing approach from the image domain. Text provides a way to specify the desired change. The second, ZEUS, discovers semantically meaningful editing directions without supervision. Its focus is finding modifications within the model that correspond to recognizable changes in the audio, rather than requiring a supervised description of those directions.

Applied to music, ZEUS exposes changes ranging from altering the participation of particular instruments to improvising on a melody. These examples indicate that the discovered directions can affect musically meaningful aspects of a signal. The paper’s contribution is the exploration of two complementary zero-shot routes to audio editing: describing changes through language and discovering useful changes without supervision.
summary.tldr: ZETA and ZEUS use pretrained diffusion models for zero-shot audio editing through text guidance or unsupervised discovery of meaningful changes.

title: Zero-Shot Unsupervised and Text-Based Audio Editing Using DDPM Inversion

abstract: Surrogate neural network-based partial differential equation (PDE) solvers have the potential to solve PDEs in an accelerated manner, but they are largely limited to systems featuring fixed domain sizes, geometric layouts, and boundary conditions. We propose Specialized Neural Accelerator-Powered Domain Decomposition Methods (SNAP-DDM), a DDM-based approach to PDE solving in which subdomain problems containing arbitrary boundary conditions and geometric parameters are accurately solved using an ensemble of specialized neural operators. We tailor SNAP-DDM to 2D electromagnetics and fluidic flow problems and show how innovations in network architecture and loss function engineering can produce specialized surrogate subdomain solvers with near unity accuracy. We utilize these solvers with standard DDM algorithms to accurately solve freeform electromagnetics and fluids problems featuring a wide range of domain sizes.

We propose Specialized Neural Accelerator-Powered Domain Decomposition Methods (SNAP-DDM), a DDM-based approach to PDE solving in which subdomain problems containing arbitrary boundary conditions and geometric parameters are accurately solved using an ensemble of specialized neural operators. paragraphs: Neural surrogate solvers can accelerate partial differential equation calculations, but many are tied to fixed domain sizes, geometries, and boundary conditions. This paper proposes SNAP-DDM, which combines specialized neural solvers with domain decomposition. The aim is to reuse accurate solvers for smaller subproblems when solving larger problems with varied layouts.

The approach uses an ensemble of specialized neural operators to solve subdomain problems containing arbitrary boundary conditions and geometric parameters. These operators are incorporated into standard domain-decomposition algorithms. The overall construction connects learned local solution capabilities with an established method for assembling solutions across a larger domain.

The authors tailor the system to two-dimensional electromagnetics and fluid-flow problems. Changes to network architecture and loss design produce specialized subdomain solvers with accuracy described as near unity. Used within domain decomposition, these solvers accurately handle freeform electromagnetics and fluid problems across a wide range of domain sizes. The findings support specialization at the subdomain level as a route toward more flexible neural PDE solving in the demonstrated settings.
summary.tldr: SNAP-DDM combines specialized neural subdomain solvers with domain decomposition to solve varied two-dimensional electromagnetic and fluid problems.

title: Towards General Neural Surrogate Solvers with Specialized Neural Accelerators

abstract: We develop universal gradient methods for Stochastic Convex Optimization (SCO). Our algorithms automatically adapt not only to the oracle’s noise but also to the Hölder smoothness of the objective function without a priori knowledge of the particular setting. The key ingredient is a novel strategy for adjusting step-size coefficients in the Stochastic Gradient Method (SGD). Unlike AdaGrad, which accumulates gradient norms, our Universal Gradient Method accumulates appropriate combinations of gradientand iterate differences. The resulting algorithm has state-of-the-art worst-case convergence rate guarantees for the entire Hölder class including, in particular, both nonsmooth functions and those with Lipschitz continuous gradient. We also present the Universal Fast Gradient Method for SCO enjoying optimal efficiency estimates.

The resulting algorithm has state-of-the-art worst-case convergence rate guarantees for the entire Hölder class including, in particular, both nonsmooth functions and those with Lipschitz continuous gradient. paragraphs: Choosing a step-size schedule for stochastic optimization often requires knowing both how noisy gradients are and how smooth the objective is. This paper develops methods that adapt to those properties without prior knowledge. The setting is convex optimization across the full Hölder smoothness class, including nonsmooth objectives.

The Universal Gradient Method adjusts step-size coefficients using combinations of gradient differences and iterate differences. This differs from accumulating gradient norms as in AdaGrad. The update rule uses information about how the optimization process changes locally to adapt its behavior to the objective and the stochastic oracle.

The resulting guarantees match state-of-the-art worst-case convergence rates throughout the studied smoothness class. The authors also introduce a Universal Fast Gradient Method with optimal efficiency estimates. The contribution is adaptive optimization with broad theoretical coverage; those guarantees rely on convexity and the stated oracle setting, rather than extending automatically to arbitrary nonconvex neural-network training.
summary.tldr: Universal gradient methods adapt to unknown noise and Hölder smoothness while retaining strong stochastic convex-optimization guarantees.

title: Universal Gradient Methods for Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: Monotonic Linear Interpolation (MLI) refers to the peculiar phenomenon that the error between the initial and converged model monotonically decreases along the linear interpolation, i.e., $(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{\theta}_0 + \alpha \boldsymbol{\theta}_F$. Previous works focus on paired initial and converged points, relating MLI to the smoothness of the optimization trajectory. In this paper, we find a shocking fact that the error curves still exhibit a monotonic decrease when $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ is replaced with noise or even zero values, implying that the decreasing curve may be primarily related to the property of the converged model rather than the optimization trajectory. We further explore the relationship between $\alpha\boldsymbol{\theta}_F$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_F$ and propose scale invariance properties in various cases, including Generalized Scale Invariance (GSI), Rectified Scale Invariance (RSI), and Normalized Scale Invariance (NSI). From an inverse perspective, the MLI formula is essentially an equation that adds varying levels of noise (i.e., $(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$) to a nearly scale-invariant network (i.e., $\alpha \boldsymbol{\theta}_F$), resulting in a monotonically increasing error as the noise level rises. MLI is a special case where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ is equal to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$.
originalAbstract: Monotonic Linear Interpolation (MLI) refers to the peculiar phenomenon that the error between the initial and converged model monotonically decreases along the linear interpolation, i.e., $(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{\theta}_0 + \alpha \boldsymbol{\theta}_F$. Previous works focus on paired initial and converged points, relating MLI to the smoothness of the optimization trajectory. We further explore the relationship between $\alpha\boldsymbol{\theta}_F$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_F$ and propose scale invariance properties in various cases, including Generalized Scale Invariance (GSI), Rectified Scale Invariance (RSI), and Normalized Scale Invariance (NSI). From an inverse perspective, the MLI formula is essentially an equation that adds varying levels of noise (i.e., $(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$) to a nearly scale-invariant network (i.e., $\alpha \boldsymbol{\theta}_F$), resulting in a monotonically increasing error as the noise level rises. MLI is a special case where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ is equal to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$.

paragraphs: Monotonic linear interpolation describes an observation about model parameters: error can decrease steadily along the straight line from initialization to a trained solution. Earlier explanations connected this behavior to the smoothness of the optimization trajectory. This paper tests whether the original initialization is actually central to the observed pattern.

The authors find that error curves can still decrease monotonically when the initial parameters are replaced by noise or even zeros. This suggests that the pattern may depend primarily on properties of the converged model. They investigate how a scaled version of that model relates to the original and introduce generalized, rectified, and normalized forms of scale invariance for different cases.

Their interpretation rewrites interpolation as a nearly scale-invariant trained network plus a noise term whose magnitude changes. Viewed in reverse, increasing the noise raises error monotonically. Interpolation from the actual initialization becomes a special case in which that initialization supplies the noise term. This reframing shifts attention toward the endpoint’s properties without establishing that optimization trajectories are universally irrelevant.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets monotonic interpolation through near scale invariance and changing noise, suggesting trained-model properties may explain much of the phenomenon.

title: MLI Formula: A Nearly Scale-Invariant Solution with Noise Perturbation

abstract: The advent of generative AI (GenAI) technology produces a transformative impact on the content creation landscape, offering alternative approaches to produce diverse, good-quality content across media, thereby reshaping online ecosystems but also raising concerns about market over-saturation and the potential marginalization of human creativity. Our work introduces a competition model generalized from the Tullock contest to analyze the tension between human creators and GenAI. Our theory and simulations suggest that despite challenges, a stable equilibrium between human and AI-generated content is possible. Our work contributes to understanding the competitive dynamics in the content creation industry, offering insights into the future interplay between human creativity and technological advancements in GenAI.
originalAbstract: The advent of generative AI (GenAI) technology produces a transformative impact on the content creation landscape, offering alternative approaches to produce diverse, good-quality content across media, thereby reshaping online ecosystems but also raising concerns about market over-saturation and the potential marginalization of human creativity. Our work introduces a competition model generalized from the Tullock contest to analyze the tension between human creators and GenAI. Our theory and simulations suggest that despite challenges, a stable equilibrium between human and AI-generated content is possible. Our work contributes to understanding the competitive dynamics in the content creation industry, offering insights into the future interplay between human creativity and technological advancements in GenAI.

paragraphs: Generative AI offers another way to produce diverse, good-quality content across media. That changes the competitive environment for human creators and raises concerns about oversaturated markets and the marginalization of human creativity. This paper studies the tension through a formal competition model.

The authors generalize the Tullock contest to represent competition involving human creators and generative AI. They use both theory and simulations to investigate the resulting dynamics. This approach puts the relationship between the two sources of content into an explicit analytical framework, allowing the possibility of coexistence to be examined as a competitive outcome.

The analysis and simulations suggest that a stable equilibrium between human and AI-generated content is possible despite the challenges. This is a claim about a possible outcome of the model, rather than a prediction that every content market will settle into coexistence. The paper's contribution is a framework for reasoning about that possibility and the competitive interplay between human creativity and generative technology.
summary.tldr: A competition model and simulations suggest that stable coexistence between human and AI-generated content is possible.

title: Human vs. Generative AI in Content Creation Competition: Symbiosis or Conflict?

abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal large language models have driven breakthroughs in visual question answering. Yet, a critical gap persists, ‘conceptualization’—the ability to recognize and reason about the same concept despite variations in visual form, a basic ability of human reasoning. To address this challenge, we introduce the Visual Graph Arena (VGA), a dataset featuring six graph-based tasks designed to evaluate and improve AI systems’ capacity for visual abstraction. VGA uses diverse graph layouts (e.g., Kamada-Kawai vs. planar) to test reasoning independent of visual form. Experiments with state-of-the-art vision models and multimodal LLMs reveal a striking divide: humans achieved near-perfect accuracy across tasks, while models totally failed on isomorphism detection and showed limited success in path/cycle tasks. We further identify behavioral anomalies suggesting pseudo-intelligent pattern matching rather than genuine understanding. These findings underscore fundamental limitations in current AI models for visual understanding. By isolating the challenge of representation-invariant reasoning, the VGA provides a framework to drive progress toward human-like conceptualization in AI visual models. The Visual Graph Arena is available at: https://vga.csail.mit.edu/.

paragraphs: Recognizing the same underlying structure across different drawings is a basic test of visual abstraction. Visual Graph Arena targets this ability with six graph-based tasks. By presenting graphs through different layouts, the benchmark examines whether a system can reason about the represented relationships even when their visual arrangement changes.

summary.tldr: Visual Graph Arena exposes large gaps between humans and tested models in recognizing graph structure across changing visual layouts.

title: Visual Graph Arena: Evaluating Visual Conceptualization of Vision and Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Language model alignment is a critical step in training modern generative language models. Alignment targets to improve win rate of a sample from the aligned model against the base model. Today, we are increasingly using inference-time algorithms (e.g., Best-of-$N$ , controlled decoding, tree search) to decode from language models rather than standard sampling. We show that this train/test mismatch makes standard RLHF framework sub-optimal in view of such inference-time methods. To this end, we propose a framework for inference-aware alignment (InfAlign), which aims to optimize inference-time win rate of the aligned policy against the base model. We prove that for any inference-time decoding procedure, the optimal aligned policy is the solution to the standard RLHF problem with a transformation of the reward. This motivates us to provide the calibrate-and-transform RL (InfAlign-CTRL) algorithm to solve this problem, which involves a reward calibration step and a KL-regularized reward maximization step with a transformation of the calibrated reward. For best-of-$N$ sampling and best-of-$N$ jailbreaking, we propose specific transformations offering up to 3-8% improvement on inference-time win rates. Finally, we also show that our proposed reward calibration method is a strong baseline for optimizing standard win rate.

Deployment increasingly uses procedures such as best-of-N sampling, controlled decoding, or tree search. The paper shows that optimizing for standard sampling can be suboptimal when a different inference procedure determines which answer reaches the user.

InfAlign targets win rate after the inference procedure has been applied. The authors prove that, for any inference-time decoding procedure, the optimal aligned policy can be obtained through a standard RLHF problem with a transformed reward. The results connect alignment objectives to deployment behavior, showing that the answer-selection procedure belongs in the training objective.
summary.tldr: InfAlign transforms alignment rewards to account for deployment-time decoding, improving reported win rates for best-of-N procedures.

title: InfAlign: Inference-aware language model alignment

abstract: Quadratic programming (QP) is the most widely applied category of problems in nonlinear programming. Many applications require real-time/fast solutions, though not necessarily with high precision. Existing methods either involve matrix decomposition or use the preconditioned conjugate gradient method. For relatively large instances, these methods cannot achieve the real-time requirement unless there is an effective preconditioner. Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) opened new possibilities for QP. Some promising empirical studies of applying GNNs for QP tasks show that GNNs can capture key characteristics of an optimization instance and provide adaptive guidance accordingly to crucial configurations during the solving process, or directly provide an approximate solution. However, the theoretical understanding of GNNs in this context remains limited. Specifically, it is unclear what GNNs can and cannot achieve for QP tasks in theory. This work addresses this gap in the context of linearly constrained QP tasks. In the continuous setting, we prove that message-passing GNNs can universally represent fundamental properties of quadratic programs, including feasibility, optimal objective values, and optimal solutions. In the more challenging mixed-integer setting, while GNNs are not universal approximators, we identify a subclass of QP problems that GNNs can reliably represent.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks have shown promise for guiding quadratic-program solvers and directly predicting approximate solutions. This paper asks a more fundamental question: which properties of these optimization problems can such networks represent at all? It studies quadratic programs with linear constraints, separating problems with continuous variables from those that also impose integer requirements.

In the continuous setting, the authors prove that message-passing graph neural networks can universally represent several central properties. These include feasibility, the optimal objective value, and optimal solutions. The result provides a theoretical basis for using these networks to capture information that is directly relevant to solving a quadratic program.

The mixed-integer setting has a different answer. Here, graph neural networks are not universal approximators, although the authors identify a subclass of problems that they can reliably represent. This distinction matters when interpreting successful applications: expressive capacity depends on the problem class. The paper's contribution concerns what the networks can represent in theory, rather than an empirical claim that every representable problem can be learned or solved quickly.
summary.tldr: Message-passing GNNs can universally represent key properties of continuous linearly constrained quadratic programs, but have expressiveness limits in the mixed-integer setting.

title: Expressive Power of Graph Neural Networks for (Mixed-Integer) Quadratic Programs

abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) are gaining attention as an efficient alternative to Transformers due to their constant memory complexity and comparable performance. Yet, deploying large-scale SSMs on cloud-based services or resource-constrained devices faces challenges. To address this, quantizing SSMs using low bit-width data types is proposed to reduce model size and leverage hardware acceleration. Given that SSMs are sensitive to quantization errors, recent advancements focus on quantizing a specific model or bit-width to improve their efficiency while maintaining performance. However, different bit-width configurations, such as W4A8 for cloud service throughput and W4A16 for improving question-answering on personal devices, are necessary for specific scenarios. To this end, we present Quamba2, compatible with W8A8, W4A8, and W4A16 for both Mamba and Mamba2, addressing the rising demand for SSM deployment across various platforms. We propose an offline approach to quantize inputs of a linear recurrence in 8-bit by sorting and clustering for $x$, combined with a per-state-group quantization for $B$ and $C$. To ensure compute-invariance in the SSM output, we offline rearrange weights according to the clustering sequence. The experiments show Quamba2-8B outperforms several state-of-the-art SSMs quantization methods and delivers 1.3$\times$ and 3$\times$ speedup in the pre-filling and generation stages and 4$\times$ memory reduction with only a $1.6$% accuracy drop on average. paragraphs: Low-bit quantization can reduce the size and computational demands of state space models, but these models are sensitive to quantization errors. Deployment also calls for different weight and activation precisions across platforms. Quamba2 supports Mamba and Mamba2 with W8A8, W4A8, and W4A16 configurations, covering several such requirements.

The framework sorts and clusters the recurrence input x offline for 8-bit quantization, and applies quantization by state groups to B and C. It also rearranges weights offline according to the clustering order so that the rearrangement preserves the SSM’s computation. These coordinated changes address quantization within the recurrence rather than treating every internal quantity identically.

Experiments report that Quamba2-8B outperforms several state-of-the-art SSM quantization methods. The reported outcomes include 1.3× faster pre-filling, 3× faster generation, and a fourfold memory reduction, with an average accuracy drop of 1.6%. These measurements demonstrate a practical efficiency–accuracy trade-off in the evaluated setting, while the supported precision configurations broaden the framework’s deployment applicability.
summary.tldr: Quamba2 supports multiple low-bit Mamba configurations using coordinated recurrence quantization, delivering reported speed and memory gains.

title: Quamba2: A Robust and Scalable Post-training Quantization Framework for Selective State Space Models

abstract: Though Rectified Flows (ReFlows) with distillation offer a promising way for fast sampling, its fast inversion transforms images back to structured noise for recovery and following editing remains unsolved. This paper introduces FireFlow, an embarrassingly simple yet effective zero-shot approach that inherits the startling capacity of ReFlow-based models (such as FLUX) in generation while extending its capabilities to accurate inversion and editing in 8 steps. We first demonstrate that a carefully designed numerical solver is pivotal for ReFlow inversion, enabling accurate inversion and reconstruction with the precision of a second-order solver while maintaining the practical efficiency of a first-order Euler method. This solver achieves a $3\times$ runtime speedup compared to state-of-the-art ReFlow inversion and editing techniques while delivering smaller reconstruction errors and superior editing results in a training-free mode. The code is available at this-URL.

paragraphs: Rectified-flow models can generate images quickly, but editing an existing image also requires an effective reverse operation. Inversion maps the image back to structured noise, providing a starting point for reconstruction and subsequent changes. FireFlow addresses fast, accurate inversion and semantic editing without additional training.

The method centers on a carefully designed numerical solver for rectified-flow inversion. The authors report accuracy associated with a second-order solver while retaining the practical efficiency of a first-order Euler method. This matters because errors in the inversion affect how accurately the original image can be reconstructed before an edit is applied.

FireFlow extends models such as FLUX to inversion and editing in eight steps. Compared with state-of-the-art rectified-flow inversion and editing techniques, the solver delivers a threefold runtime speedup, smaller reconstruction errors, and better editing results in the reported evaluation. The contribution shows how changing the numerical procedure can improve both speed and reconstruction quality while using the existing model’s capabilities in a zero-shot, training-free setting.
summary.tldr: FireFlow enables training-free rectified-flow inversion and image editing in eight steps, with reported improvements in speed, reconstruction, and editing quality.

title: FireFlow: Fast Inversion of Rectified Flow for Image Semantic Editing

abstract: Accurately modeling chemical reactions using Artificial Intelligence (AI) can accelerate discovery and development, especially in fields like drug design and material science. Although AI has made remarkable advancements in single molecule recognition, such as predicting molecular properties, the study of interactions between molecules, particularly chemical reactions, has been relatively overlooked. In this paper, we introduce Reaction Graph (RG), a unified graph representation that encapsulates the 3D molecular structures within chemical reactions. RG integrates the molecular graphs of reactants and products into a cohesive framework, effectively capturing the interatomic relationships pertinent to the reaction process. Additionally, it incorporates the 3D structure information of molecules in a simple yet effective manner. We conduct experiments on a range of tasks, including chemical reaction classification, condition prediction, and yield prediction. RG achieves the highest accuracy across six datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness. The code is available at https://github.com/Shadow-Dream/Reaction-Graph.

paragraphs: Reaction Graph addresses chemical reactions as a modeling problem involving relationships across molecules. The paper contrasts this with the stronger attention given to recognizing individual molecules and predicting their properties. Its aim is to provide a representation that brings the participants in a reaction and their three-dimensional structures into one framework.

The representation combines the molecular graphs of reactants and products into a unified graph. It captures interatomic relationships relevant to the reaction and incorporates molecular geometry. This gives the model a shared structure for reasoning about the reaction as a whole, with both molecular connections and three-dimensional information available in the representation.

The authors evaluate Reaction Graph on reaction classification, condition prediction, and yield prediction. It achieves the highest accuracy across six datasets in their experiments. These results support the usefulness of a common reaction-level representation across several predictive tasks. The broader motivation is to improve AI modeling of chemistry for discovery in areas such as drug design and materials science, with the reported evidence coming from those prediction benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Reaction Graph unifies reactant and product graphs with 3D molecular information, achieving the highest reported accuracy across six reaction datasets.

title: Reaction Graph: Towards Reaction-Level Modeling for Chemical Reactions with 3D Structures

abstract: The next-coordinate prediction paradigm has emerged as the de facto standard in current auto-regressive mesh generation methods. Despite their effectiveness, there is no efficient measurement for the various tokenizers that serialize meshes into sequences. In this paper, we introduce a new metric Per-Token-Mesh-Entropy (PTME) to evaluate the existing mesh tokenizers theoretically without any training. Building upon PTME, we propose a plug-and-play tokenization technique called coordinate merging. It further improves the compression ratios of existing tokenizers by rearranging and merging the most frequent patterns of coordinates. Through experiments on various tokenization methods like MeshXL, MeshAnything V2, and Edgerunner, we further validate the performance of our method. We hope that the proposed PTME and coordinate merging can enhance the existing mesh tokenizers and guide the further development of native mesh generation.

paragraphs: Autoregressive mesh generators represent a mesh as a sequence and predict its coordinates progressively. The tokenizer determines how that geometry becomes a sequence, making its representation an important part of the generation pipeline. This paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating different mesh tokenizers efficiently, without first training a model for each candidate.

The authors introduce Per-Token-Mesh-Entropy, or PTME, as a theoretical metric that can evaluate existing tokenizers without training. Building on this metric, they propose coordinate merging: a technique that rearranges and combines frequently occurring coordinate patterns. It is designed to plug into existing tokenizers and increase their compression ratios, improving how compactly mesh information is represented.

Experiments with MeshXL, MeshAnything V2, and Edgerunner validate the proposed method across several tokenization approaches. The contribution therefore has two linked parts: a way to assess tokenizers and a practical modification informed by that assessment. The authors position both as tools for improving existing representations and guiding future mesh-generation development, rather than presenting that future impact as established.
summary.tldr: FreeMesh introduces a training-free metric for mesh tokenizers and a coordinate-merging technique that improves their compression ratios.

title: FreeMesh: Boosting Mesh Generation with Coordinates Merging

abstract: Recently, spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks have achieved dominant performance in spatiotemporal prediction tasks. However, most models relying on node-to-node messaging interaction exhibit sensitivity to spatiotemporal shifts, encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) challenges. To address these issues, we introduce Spatio-Temporal OOD Processor (STOP), which employs a centralized messaging mechanism along with a message perturbation mechanism to facilitate robust spatiotemporal interactions. Specifically, the centralized messaging mechanism integrates Context-Aware Units for coarse-grained spatiotemporal feature interactions with nodes, effectively blocking traditional node-to-node messages. We also implement a message perturbation mechanism to disrupt this messaging process, compelling the model to extract generalizable contextual features from generated variant environments. Finally, we customize a spatiotemporal distributionally robust optimization approach that exposes the model to challenging environments, thereby further enhancing its generalization capabilities. Compared with 14 baselines across six datasets, STOP achieves up to 17.01% improvement in generalization performance and 18.44% improvement in inductive learning performance. The code is available at https://github.com/PoorOtterBob/STOP.

paragraphs: Spatiotemporal graph models predict patterns that vary across both connected locations and time. The paper identifies a weakness in conventional node-to-node messaging: predictions can become sensitive to shifts in those spatial and temporal patterns. STOP addresses this by changing how information moves through the model and how training environments are constructed.

Its centralized messaging mechanism uses Context-Aware Units to exchange coarse-grained spatiotemporal features with nodes, blocking conventional direct node-to-node messages. These are reported maxima, rather than uniform gains across all evaluations. The results support combining centralized interaction, message variation, and robust optimization to improve prediction under distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: STOP combines centralized messages, message perturbations, and robust optimization to improve spatiotemporal prediction under distribution shifts.

title: Robust Spatio-Temporal Centralized Interaction for OOD Learning

abstract: The development of Generalist Virtual Agents (GVAs) has shown significant promise in autonomous task execution. However, current training paradigms face critical limitations, including reliance on outcome supervision and labor-intensive human annotations. To address these challenges, we propose Similar, a step-wise multi-dimensional generalist reward model, which offers fine-grained signals for agent training and can choose better actions for inference-time scaling. Specifically, we begin by systematically defining five dimensions for evaluating agent actions. Building on this framework, we design an MCTS-P algorithm to automatically collect and annotate step-wise, five-dimensional agent execution data. Using this data, we train Similar with our crafted Triple-M strategy. Furthermore, we introduce the first benchmark in the virtual agent domain for step-wise, multi-dimensional reward model training and evaluation, named SRM. This benchmark consists of two components: SRMTrain, which serves as the training set for Similar, and SRMEval, a manually selected test set for evaluating the reward model. Experimental results demonstrate that Similar, through its step-wise, multi-dimensional assessment and synergistic gain, provides GVAs with effective intermediate signals during both training and inference-time scaling. The code is available at https://github.com/antgroup/Similar.

paragraphs: Virtual agents need feedback that helps them improve the actions taken along the way to a goal. Supervision based only on the final outcome provides limited guidance about intermediate decisions, while human annotation requires substantial effort. This paper introduces Similar, a reward model designed to evaluate individual agent actions across five dimensions.

The authors first define those evaluation dimensions, then use an algorithm called MCTS-P to collect and annotate execution data automatically. They train Similar on this data using their Triple-M strategy. They also introduce SRM, a benchmark for training and evaluating reward models with this step-level, multidimensional perspective. SRMTrain supplies training data, while SRMEval is a manually selected test set.

Experiments show that Similar provides useful intermediate signals during agent training and can help select better actions when additional computation is used at inference time. Its contribution is a shared approach to evaluating actions throughout execution, supported by both a data collection method and a benchmark for assessing the reward model itself.
summary.tldr: Similar evaluates virtual-agent actions across five dimensions, supplying intermediate feedback for training and action selection at inference time.

title: Boosting Virtual Agent Learning and Reasoning: A Step-Wise, Multi-Dimensional, and Generalist Reward Model with Benchmark

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities, yet ensuring their outputs conform to strict structural or grammatical constraints remains challenging, which is critical in function calls and domain-specific language (DSL) generation. Constrained decoding with context-free grammar is a flexible approach to guarantee LLMs’ adherence to a specific format by dynamically building a token logits mask. However, creating this mask requires checking the validity of all tokens in the LLM vocabulary at every decoding step, which often incurs significant overheads in existing constrained decoding engines. To address this challenge, we propose $\textbf{ZapFormat}$, a novel $\textbf{dynamic pruning}$ strategy based on the Earley algorithm that identifies and eliminates invalid or redundant Earley states in real-time, significantly reducing memory occupation of the Earley algorithm’s states. This further enables us to use a state cache to speed up structured generations on a large number of queries. We implemented ZapFormat in a new constrained decoding engine called Formatron which also incorporates existing optimizations. Through comprehensive experiments on structured generation tasks, including JSON generation, JSON Schema validation, and semantic parsing, we demonstrate that Formatron not only $\textbf{consistently maintains}$ high-precision compliant outputs but also achieves $\textbf{significant improvements}$ in inference speed up to 2x compared to state-of-the-art implementations. More importantly, Formatron is generally applicable across various LLM architectures. We release Formatron as open source at https://github.com/Dan-wanna-M/formatron.

This further enables us to use a state cache to speed up structured generations on a large number of queries. We implemented ZapFormat in a new constrained decoding engine called Formatron which also incorporates existing optimizations. Through comprehensive experiments on structured generation tasks, including JSON generation, JSON Schema validation, and semantic parsing, we demonstrate that Formatron not only $\textbf{consistently maintains}$ high-precision compliant outputs but also achieves $\textbf{significant improvements}$ in inference speed up to 2x compared to state-of-the-art implementations. More importantly, Formatron is generally applicable across various LLM architectures. We release Formatron as open source at https://github.com/Dan-wanna-M/formatron.

paragraphs: Language models used for function calls or specialized languages must produce outputs that follow strict structural rules. Grammar-constrained decoding enforces those rules by masking tokens that would make an output invalid. Building this mask can be expensive because existing engines often check the entire vocabulary at each generation step.

The paper introduces ZapFormat, which reduces this overhead through dynamic pruning of Earley parser states. These states track possible ways the generated text fits the grammar. Removing invalid or redundant states as generation proceeds reduces their memory footprint. That reduction also makes it practical to cache states and reuse work across many structured-generation queries.

The authors implement ZapFormat in Formatron, a decoding engine that also includes existing optimizations. Experiments cover JSON generation, JSON Schema validation, and semantic parsing. Formatron maintains high-precision compliant outputs while achieving inference speedups of up to twofold over leading implementations. The engine applies across different language-model architectures, making the contribution relevant to the shared infrastructure used to enforce output formats.
summary.tldr: ZapFormat prunes grammar-parser states to reduce memory use and accelerate structured language-model generation.

title: Earley-Driven Dynamic Pruning for Efficient Structured Decoding

abstract: One-shot subset selection serves as an effective tool to reduce deep learning training costs by identifying an informative data subset based on the information extracted by an information extractor (IE). Traditional IEs, typically pre-trained on the target dataset, are inherently dataset-dependent. Foundation models (FMs) offer a promising alternative, potentially mitigating this limitation. This work investigates two key questions: (1) Can FM-based subset selection outperform traditional IE-based methods across diverse datasets? (2) Do all FMs perform equally well as IEs for subset selection? Extensive experiments uncovered surprising insights: FMs consistently outperform traditional IEs on fine-grained datasets, whereas their advantage diminishes on coarse-grained datasets with noisy labels. Motivated by these finding, we propose RAM-APL (RAnking Mean-Accuracy of Pseudo-class Labels), a method tailored for fine-grained image datasets. RAM-APL leverages multiple FMs to enhance subset selection by exploiting their complementary strengths. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on fine-grained datasets, including Oxford-IIIT Pet, Food-101, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011.

The selection depends on an information extractor, often a model previously trained on the target dataset. This paper investigates whether foundation models can provide a less dataset-dependent alternative and whether their usefulness varies across models.

The experiments reveal that the advantage depends on the dataset. Foundation models consistently outperform traditional information extractors on fine-grained datasets, where categories require detailed distinctions. Their advantage becomes smaller on coarse-grained datasets with noisy labels. These findings motivate a method specifically aimed at fine-grained image selection rather than an assumption that foundation models offer the same benefit everywhere.

The proposed RAM-APL method, short for RAnking Mean-Accuracy of Pseudo-class Labels, combines multiple foundation models to use their complementary strengths. It achieves state-of-the-art results on fine-grained datasets including Oxford-IIIT Pet, Food-101, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011. The contribution links an empirical investigation of information extractors to a selection strategy tailored to the setting where their benefits are strongest.
summary.tldr: RAM-APL combines complementary foundation models to improve one-shot subset selection for fine-grained image datasets.

title: Foundation Model Insights and a Multi-Model Approach for Superior Fine-Grained One-shot Subset Selection

abstract: Anomaly detection in continuous-time event sequences is a crucial task in safety-critical applications. While existing methods primarily focus on developing a superior test statistic, they fail to provide guarantees regarding the false positive rate (FPR), which undermines their reliability in practical deployments. In this paper, we propose CADES (Conformal Anomaly Detection in Event Sequences), a novel test procedure based on conformal inference for the studied task with finite-sample FPR control. Specifically, by using the time-rescaling theorem, we design two powerful non-conformity scores tailored to event sequences, which exhibit complementary sensitivities to different abnormal patterns. CADES combines these scores with Bonferroni correction to leverage their respective strengths and addresses non-identifiability issues of existing methods. Theoretically, we prove the validity of CADES and further provide strong guarantees on calibration-conditional FPR control. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets, covering various types of anomalies, demonstrate that CADES outperforms state-of-the-art methods while maintaining FPR control.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual patterns in events that occur over continuous time requires more than a sensitive anomaly score. A detector also needs control over how often it flags normal sequences. This paper introduces CADES, a conformal testing procedure that combines anomaly detection with finite-sample guarantees on the false positive rate.

CADES uses the time-rescaling theorem to construct two non-conformity scores, which measure departures from expected event behavior. The scores respond to different kinds of abnormalities, making their sensitivities complementary. The method combines them using Bonferroni correction, so using multiple signals is incorporated into the false positive control. It also addresses non-identifiability issues in existing approaches.

The authors prove the procedure’s validity and provide additional guarantees concerning false positive control conditional on calibration data. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets cover several anomaly types and report better performance than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining false positive control. The contribution therefore connects detection quality with statistical reliability, rather than assessing success solely through the strength of an anomaly score.
summary.tldr: CADES combines complementary event-sequence anomaly scores with conformal inference to improve detection while providing finite-sample false positive control.

title: Conformal Anomaly Detection in Event Sequences

abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant *supply-chain* risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.

paragraphs: This position paper examines the risks that accompany downloading and reusing openly available machine learning models. Such access lets people use powerful models without the expertise or computing resources needed to develop them. The authors argue that the same ecosystem also contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have already appeared in real attacks.

The risks span both distribution and development. An attacker could substitute malicious material for a model, while a model’s creation could involve a vulnerable software framework, restricted data, or poisoned data. This framing directs attention to how a model was produced and delivered, alongside the capabilities that make it useful to downstream users.

The paper explores adapting Sigstore, a transparency solution from open-source software, to machine learning models. The proposed use would let publishers sign models and establish properties of the datasets used to create them. The contribution is an argument for stronger transparency around model provenance and inputs. These mechanisms address questions about origin and production history; the abstract does not present them as eliminating every model-related risk.
summary.tldr: Open model ecosystems face supply-chain risks, and the paper explores Sigstore for model signing and dataset transparency.

title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem

abstract: The technique of combining multiple votes to enhance the quality of a decision is the core of boosting algorithms in machine learning. In particular, boosting provably increases decision quality by combining multiple "weak learners"—hypotheses that are only slightly better than random guessing—into a single "strong learner" that classifies data well. There exist various versions of boosting algorithms, which we improve upon through the introduction of QuantumBoost. Inspired by classical work by Barak, Hardt and Kale, our QuantumBoost algorithm achieves the best known runtime over other boosting methods through two innovations. First, it uses a quantum algorithm to compute approximate Bregman projections faster. Second, it combines this with a lazy projection strategy, a technique from convex optimization where projections are performed infrequently rather than every iteration. To our knowledge, QuantumBoost is the first algorithm, classical or quantum, to successfully adopt a lazy projection strategy in the context of boosting.

paragraphs: Boosting combines multiple weak predictors into a stronger classifier. Each individual predictor needs to perform only slightly better than random guessing, but their combined votes can support reliable decisions. QuantumBoost focuses on reducing the computational cost of this process while retaining the goal of learning from weak hypotheses.

The algorithm combines two ideas. First, it uses a quantum procedure to accelerate approximate Bregman projections, an optimization operation used in its boosting process. Second, it applies a lazy projection strategy, performing these operations only intermittently instead of on every iteration. The savings therefore come from both making projections faster and needing them less frequently.

The authors report the best known runtime among boosting methods and identify their approach as the first successful use of lazy projections for boosting, whether classical or quantum. Its conceptual contribution is the combination: a scheduling idea from convex optimization works alongside a quantum computational improvement to accelerate the construction of a strong learner.
summary.tldr: QuantumBoost accelerates boosting by combining faster quantum projections with a strategy that performs projections less often.

title: QuantumBoost: A lazy, yet fast, quantum algorithm for learning with weak hypotheses

abstract: Existing expressivity results for transformers typically rely on hardmax attention, high precision, and other architectural modifications that disconnect them from the models used in practice. We bridge this gap by analyzing standard transformer decoders with softmax attention and rounding of activations and attention weights, while allowing depth and width to grow logarithmically with the context length. As an intermediate step, we construct hardmax transformers with ternary activations and well-separated attention scores that simulate Turing machines using Chain-of-Thought (CoT). This lets us convert the constructions to equivalent softmax transformers without the unrealistic parameter magnitudes or activation precision that prior approaches would require. Using the same technique, we analyze a recently proposed summarized CoT paradigm and show that it simulates Turing machines more efficiently, with model size scaling logarithmically in a space bound rather than a time bound. We empirically test predictions made by our results on a Sudoku reasoning task and find better alignment with learnability than for prior high-precision results. Our code is available at https://github.com/moritzbroe/transformer-expressivity.

This paper studies standard softmax transformer decoders with rounded activations and attention weights. It allows model depth and width to grow logarithmically with context length, bringing the computational analysis closer to practical architectural choices.

The proof first constructs hardmax transformers with three-valued activations and clearly separated attention scores that simulate Turing machines using chain of thought. Those constructions are then converted into equivalent softmax transformers without requiring the unrealistic parameter sizes or activation precision of earlier approaches. The construction establishes expressive capability under the specified resource scaling.

The authors also analyze summarized chain of thought. In that setting, simulation requires model size growing logarithmically with a space bound rather than a time bound, yielding a more efficient resource dependence. Experiments on Sudoku find that the theory's predictions align better with learnability than earlier high-precision results. This empirical connection complements the expressivity result, which concerns what these models can represent rather than guaranteeing that training will discover every construction.
summary.tldr: Low-precision softmax transformers can simulate Turing machines with chain of thought, with more favorable model-size scaling under summarized reasoning.

title: The Expressive Power of Low Precision Softmax Transformers with (Summarized) Chain-of-Thought

abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a widely used technique for controllable generation in diffusion and flow-based models. Despite its empirical success, CFG relies on a heuristic linear extrapolation that is often sensitive to the guidance scale. In this work, we provide a principled interpretation of CFG through the lens of optimization. We demonstrate that the velocity field in flow matching corresponds to the gradient of a sequence of smoothed distance functions, which guides latent variables toward the scaled target image set. This perspective reveals that the standard CFG formulation is an approximation of this gradient, where the prediction gap, the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional outputs, governs guidance sensitivity. Leveraging this insight, we reformulate the CFG sampling as a homotopy optimization with a manifold constraint. This formulation necessitates a manifold projection step, which we implement via an incremental gradient descent scheme during sampling. To improve computational efficiency and stability, we further enhance this iterative process with Anderson Acceleration without requiring additional model evaluations. Our proposed methods are training-free and consistently refine generation fidelity, prompt alignment, and robustness to the guidance scale. We validate their effectiveness across diverse benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements on large-scale models such as DiT-XL-2-256, Flux, and Stable Diffusion 3.5. Code is available at https://github.com/LeonSuZhengYi/CFG-MP.

This paper gives guidance in flow matching an optimization interpretation. It connects the model’s velocity field to gradients of progressively smoothed distance functions that move latent variables toward a scaled target image set.

title: Improving Classifier-Free Guidance of Flow Matching via Manifold Projection

abstract: In clinical practice, patients often present with multiple co-occurring diseases, yet most existing Multi-Label-Diagnosis (MLD) methods treat diagnosis as a rigid discriminative partitioning task, implicitly assuming that overlapping pathologies are separable. This assumption is problematic in medical images, where identical or highly similar visual observations may simultaneously support multiple disease labels, and disease concepts are inherently correlated rather than independent. Enforcing hard decision boundaries under such overlap suppresses shared evidence, biases feature representations, and ultimately undermines model reliability. To address this limitation, we propose Fuzzy Alignment with Comorbidity Topology FACT, a novel paradigm that reformulates MLD as a fuzzy alignment problem between atomic visual evidence and disease semantic anchors. FACT is characterized by three key features: (1) modeling visual polysemy through shared and reusable atomic visual evidence; (2) encoding disease correlation via semantic anchors structured by comorbidity topology; and (3) employing a metric-based fuzzy membership function for non-discriminative visual-semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on three public clinical benchmarks demonstrate that FACT consistently improves diagnostic performance while delivering clinically plausible predictions. The code is available at https://github.com/yyuChen9/FACT.

paragraphs: FACT addresses a mismatch between medical images and rigid classification boundaries. A patient can have several diseases at once, and the same visual finding may support multiple diagnoses. Treating overlapping conditions as cleanly separable can suppress shared evidence and distort the features a model learns.

The framework represents images through small, reusable units of visual evidence and aligns them with semantic representations of diseases. These disease anchors are organized according to comorbidity relationships, allowing the representation to reflect how conditions co-occur. A metric-based fuzzy membership function expresses the degree of alignment between visual evidence and disease concepts, accommodating evidence that is relevant to more than one label.

This formulation gives shared observations an explicit role in multilabel prediction instead of forcing them into exclusive disease categories. Experiments on three public clinical benchmarks show consistent improvements in diagnostic performance and predictions described as clinically plausible. The results support modeling both the multiple meanings of visual findings and relationships among diseases when learning from medical images.
summary.tldr: FACT improves multilabel medical-image diagnosis by sharing visual evidence across correlated diseases through fuzzy semantic alignment.

title: FACT: Fuzzy Alignment with Comorbidity Topology for Reliable Multi-Label Medical Image Diagnosis

abstract: Confidence calibration for classification models is vital in safety-critical decision-making scenarios and has received extensive attention. General confidence calibration methods assume training and test data are independent and identically distributed ($i.i.d.$), limiting their effectiveness under covariate shifts. Previous calibration methods under covariate shift struggle with class-wise or canonical calibrations and often rely on unstable importance weighting when density ratios are large or unbounded. Given the above limitations, this paper rethinks confidence calibration under covariate shifts. First, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for confidence calibration under covariate shifts, named Expectation consistency condition, which reveals covariate shifts do not necessarily lead to uncalibrated confidence and provides a weaker condition for confidence calibration than global covariate distribution alignment. Then, utilizing Expectation consistency condition, this paper proposes an unsupervised domain adaptation loss to calibrate confidence of the target domain, named Expectation consistency loss (ECL), which is compatible with canonical calibration, class-wise calibration, and top-label calibration. Third, we prove that computing ECL loss has the same sample complexity as Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and provide a theoretically grounded mini-batch trainable scheme for ECL loss. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our method on both simulated and real-world covariate shift datasets.

paragraphs: Confidence calibration concerns whether a classifier’s confidence agrees with how often its predictions are correct. A change in the input distribution can challenge calibration methods designed for matching training and test distributions. Existing approaches to this shift can also depend on unstable importance weights, particularly when the ratios used to reweight examples become very large or unbounded.

The paper derives an expectation consistency condition that is necessary and sufficient for calibration under covariate shift. This establishes that a changed input distribution does not automatically imply miscalibrated confidence. The condition is weaker than requiring the entire input distributions to align, identifying a more targeted requirement for preserving calibration.

The authors turn this condition into Expectation Consistency Loss, an unsupervised domain adaptation objective supporting canonical, class-wise, and top-label calibration. They prove that computing it has the same sample complexity as Expected Calibration Error and provide a theoretically supported mini-batch training scheme. Experiments on simulated and real-world shifts support its effectiveness, connecting the characterization to a trainable method.
summary.tldr: Expectation Consistency Loss turns a necessary and sufficient calibration condition under covariate shift into a trainable adaptation objective.

title: Expectation Consistency Loss: Rethink Confidence Calibration under Covariate Shift

abstract: This paper investigates a pivotal yet debated component of reinforcement learning (RL) for training large language models (LLMs): controlling entropy (increasing or decreasing it) during RL fine-tuning. The existing literature presents a dichotomy: some studies posit that increasing entropy facilitates exploration, whereas others argue that decreasing entropy enhances performance. To reconcile these conflicting observations, we provide a theoretical framework showing that the effect of entropy is governed by Entropy Discrepancy, the distributional divergence between positive and negative samples. Guided by this insight, we derive a principled dynamic scheduling method that adaptively modulates the entropy coefficient, effectively switching between entropy maximization and minimization as training evolves. Extensive experiments confirm the correlation between Entropy Discrepancy and the efficacy of entropy control. Furthermore, our adaptive method yields substantial improvements, boosting Pass@K by 6.7% on AIME24 and 17.52% on puzzle tasks compared to vanilla RL, while consistently outperforming recent state-of-the-art reasoning methods.

paragraphs: Entropy control influences how concentrated or varied a language model’s output distribution becomes during reinforcement learning. Existing findings point in opposing directions: increasing entropy can support exploration, while decreasing it can improve performance. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for why either intervention can help.

The proposed explanation centers on Entropy Discrepancy, a distributional divergence between positive and negative samples. The theoretical framework shows that this quantity governs the effect of entropy control. From that analysis, the authors derive a dynamic schedule that adjusts the entropy coefficient as training progresses, switching between encouraging and discouraging entropy.

Experiments confirm a correlation between Entropy Discrepancy and the effectiveness of entropy interventions. The adaptive schedule improves Pass@K by a reported 6.7% on AIME24 and 17.52% on puzzle tasks compared with vanilla reinforcement learning, while outperforming recent reasoning methods in the evaluation. The contribution is a principled basis for adapting entropy control to the evolving training distribution, connecting apparently conflicting empirical recommendations.
summary.tldr: A distribution-based measure guides when to increase or decrease entropy during language-model reinforcement learning, improving reported reasoning performance.

title: Demystifying Entropy Control in LLM RL Training: Theoretical Analysis and Dynamic Scheduling

abstract: When deploying a single predictor across multiple subpopulations, we propose a fundamentally different approach: interpreting group fairness as a bargaining problem among subpopulations. This game-theoretic perspective reveals that existing robust optimization methods such as minimizing worst-group loss or regret correspond to classical bargaining solutions and embody different fairness principles. We propose relative improvement, the ratio of actual risk reduction to potential reduction from a baseline predictor, which recovers the Kalai–Smorodinsky solution. Unlike absolute-scale methods that may not be comparable when groups have different potential predictability, relative improvement provides axiomatic justification including scale invariance and individual monotonicity. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees under mild conditions.

This game-theoretic perspective reveals that existing robust optimization methods such as minimizing worst-group loss or regret correspond to classical bargaining solutions and embody different fairness principles. We propose relative improvement, the ratio of actual risk reduction to potential reduction from a baseline predictor, which recovers the Kalai–Smorodinsky solution. Unlike absolute-scale methods that may not be comparable when groups have different potential predictability, relative improvement provides axiomatic justification including scale invariance and individual monotonicity. paragraphs: When one predictor serves several subpopulations, fairness requires deciding how to balance their competing outcomes. This paper treats that decision as a bargaining problem among groups. From this perspective, familiar methods such as minimizing the worst group's loss or regret correspond to classical bargaining solutions, each expressing a different fairness principle.

The proposed criterion measures relative improvement: the reduction in a group's risk compared with a baseline predictor, divided by the reduction potentially available to that group. This normalization matters when groups differ in how predictable their outcomes can be. Comparing raw losses or absolute reductions can otherwise compare quantities with different amounts of achievable improvement.

The relative-improvement formulation recovers the Kalai–Smorodinsky bargaining solution and has axiomatic support, including scale invariance and individual monotonicity. The authors also establish finite-sample convergence guarantees under mild conditions. The contribution makes the fairness choice explicit through a bargaining principle and a baseline-relative measure, offering a way to reason about group benefit when achievable prediction quality differs.
summary.tldr: The paper frames group fairness as bargaining and compares groups through the fraction of their achievable risk reduction that a predictor delivers.

title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem

abstract: A fundamental challenge in data science is to match disparate point sets with each other. While optimal transport efficiently minimizes point displacements under a bijectivity constraint, it is inherently sensitive to rotations. Conversely, minimizing distortions via the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) framework addresses this limitation but introduces a non-convex, computationally demanding optimization problem. In this work, we identify a broad class of distortion penalties that reduce to a simple alignment problem within a lifted feature space. Leveraging this insight, we introduce an iterative GW solver with a linear memory footprint and quadratic (rather than cubic) time complexity. Our method is differentiable, comes with strong theoretical guarantees, and scales to hundreds of thousands of points in minutes. This efficiency unlocks a wide range of geometric applications and enables the exploration of the GW energy landscape, whose local minima encode the symmetries of the matching problem.

The paper identifies a broad class of distortion penalties that can be expressed as a simpler alignment problem in a lifted feature space. title: Gromov-Wasserstein at Scale, Beyond Squared Norms

abstract: Information design (ID) explores how a sender influence the optimal behavior of receivers to achieve specific objectives. While ID originates from everyday human communication, existing game-theoretic and learning methods often model information structures as numbers, which limits many applications to toy games. This work leverages LLMs and proposes a verbalized framework in Bayesian persuasion (BP), which extends classic BP to real-world games involving human dialogues for the first time. We map the BP to a verbalized mediator-augmented game, where LLMs instantiate the sender and receiver. To efficiently solve the verbalized game, we propose a generalized equilibrium-finding algorithm combining LLM and game solver. The algorithm is reinforced with techniques including verbalized commitment assumptions, verbalized obedience constraints, and information obfuscation. Experiments in dialogue scenarios, such as recommendation letters, law enforcement, diplomacy with press, validate that our framework can reproduce theoretical results in classic BP and discover effective persuasion strategies in more complex natural language and multi-stage scenarios.

Traditional formulations often express information structures numerically, making them difficult to apply to rich dialogue. This paper develops a verbalized framework that brings these information-design questions into natural-language games involving language-model senders and receivers.

The framework maps persuasion into a game augmented by a mediator and combines an LLM with a game solver to find equilibria. Its supporting techniques express commitment assumptions and obedience constraints in language and use information obfuscation. These components connect the game’s strategic requirements to interactions carried out through dialogue.

Experiments include recommendation letters, law enforcement, and diplomacy with the press. The framework reproduces theoretical results from classic Bayesian persuasion and discovers effective strategies in more complex natural-language and multi-stage scenarios. The findings support using verbal interaction as part of a game-theoretic computation, while keeping the sender’s objectives and the receiver’s response incentives central to the analysis.
summary.tldr: A verbalized Bayesian persuasion framework combines LLM dialogue with a game solver to study strategic information sharing in natural-language scenarios.

title: Verbalized Bayesian Persuasion

abstract: Parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) serve as fundamental models across science and engineering, yet constructing fast and accurate surrogate models from sparse, irregularly sampled observations with reliable uncertainty quantification remains challenging. Existing approaches struggle to simultaneously handle variable observation patterns, preserve physics consistency, and provide well-calibrated predictive uncertainty. We introduce Bias-Spectrum Neural Processes (BSNP), a unified meta-learning framework that systematically integrates weak structural priors (translation equivariance, locality) with strong physical priors (governing equations and boundary conditions). BSNP addresses two critical obstacles: discretization overfitting through stochastic collocation that resamples residual evaluation points, and uncertainty collapse through mean-field enforcement that applies PDE constraints only to predictive means while preserving learned uncertainty. Comprehensive experiments on nonlinear Poisson equations, Burgers dynamics, and Navier-Stokes flows demonstrate that BSNP achieves superior accuracy and well-calibrated uncertainty quantification in sparse-data regimes.

paragraphs: Predicting solutions to physical equations from a few scattered measurements requires a model to handle changing observation locations and express uncertainty about what it cannot observe. Bias-Spectrum Neural Processes (BSNP) addresses these demands through a unified meta-learning framework. It combines architectural preferences, such as local interactions and consistent behavior under spatial translations, with explicit constraints from governing equations and boundary conditions.

The framework targets two specific failure modes. First, a model can become overly adapted to the particular points where its physical consistency is checked. BSNP resamples these evaluation points through stochastic collocation. Second, enforcing physical constraints can collapse predictive uncertainty. BSNP therefore applies those constraints to the predicted mean while preserving its learned uncertainty.

Experiments cover nonlinear Poisson equations, Burgers dynamics, and Navier-Stokes flows. The authors report superior accuracy and well-calibrated uncertainty when observations are sparse. The contribution is a way to combine different strengths of prior knowledge while addressing how physics enforcement affects both prediction quality and uncertainty.
summary.tldr: BSNP combines architectural and physical constraints to predict PDE solutions accurately while preserving calibrated uncertainty from sparse observations.

title: Bias-Spectrum Neural Processes for Parametric PDEs: Architecture Priors Meet PDE Constraints

abstract: Iterative self-improvement fine-tunes an autoregressive large language model (LLM) on reward-verified outputs generated by the LLM itself. In contrast to the empirical success of self-improvement, the theoretical foundation of this generative, iterative procedure in a practical, finite-sample setting remains limited. We make progress toward this goal by modeling each round of self-improvement as maximum-likelihood fine-tuning on a reward-filtered distribution and deriving finite-sample guarantees for the expected reward. Our analysis reveals an explicit feedback loop where better models accept more data per iteration, supporting sustained self-improvement while explaining eventual saturation of such improvement. Adopting a task-centric view by considering reasoning tasks with multiple difficulty levels, we further prove quantifiable conditions on model initialization, task difficulty, and sample budget where easy-to-hard curricula provably achieve better guarantees than training on fixed mixtures of tasks. Our analyses are validated through Monte-Carlo simulations and experiments spanning a synthetic graph-based reasoning task and multiple standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Iterative self-improvement trains a language model on its own outputs after a reward signal filters out unsuitable examples. This paper develops a theory for that process when each training round has only a finite number of samples. It represents each round as maximum-likelihood training on the filtered output distribution and derives guarantees for the model’s expected reward.

The analysis identifies a feedback loop: a better model produces more outputs that pass verification, providing more accepted training data for the next round. This helps explain how improvement can sustain itself across iterations. The same analysis also explains why improvement eventually saturates, rather than continuing indefinitely.

The authors then consider tasks at different difficulty levels. They prove conditions involving the starting model, task difficulty, and sample budget under which an easy-to-hard curriculum has better guarantees than a fixed task mixture. Simulations, synthetic graph reasoning, and mathematical reasoning experiments support the analysis. The curriculum advantage is conditional on those factors, rather than a claim that every model benefits from the same ordering.
summary.tldr: A finite-sample theory explains self-improvement feedback and identifies conditions under which easy-to-hard curricula offer better reward guarantees.

title: A Task-centric Theory for Iterative Self-Improvement with Easy-to-Hard Curricula

abstract: Continual learning (CL) with large pre-trained models aims to incrementally acquire knowledge without catastrophic forgetting. Existing LoRA-based Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) methods expand capacity by adding isolated new experts while freezing old ones, but still suffer from redundancy, interference, routing ambiguity, and consequent forgetting. We investigate the issues stemming from coarse-grained expert granularity. Coarse-grained experts (e.g., high-rank LoRA) encode low-specialty information, leading to expert duplication/interference and routing degradation/confusion as experts accumulate. In this work, we propose MoRAM (Mixture of Rank-1 Associative Memory). Grounded in the view that weight matrices act as linear associative memories, MoRAM achieves CL as incremental expansion of reusable atomic rank-1 experts as memory. Each rank-1 adapter acts as a fine-grained MoE expert or an associative memory unit. By viewing rank-1 experts as key-value memory pairs, we eliminate explicit MoE-LoRA routers with self-activation, where each memory atom evaluates its relevance via its intrinsic key. The inference process thus becomes a content-addressable retrieval and recall over the incrementally accumulated memory of learning snapshots. Extensive experiments on CLIP and LLMs show that MoRAM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a better plasticity–stability trade-off, stronger generalization, and reduced forgetting. Project page: https://artificer-ai-lab.github.io/MoRAM.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a pretrained model to acquire new knowledge while retaining what it already knows. Adding separate low-rank experts and freezing earlier ones can still cause forgetting. The paper attributes part of this problem to experts that are too coarse: they store overlapping information, interfere with one another, and become increasingly difficult to route inputs among.

MoRAM replaces these larger experts with reusable rank-one adapters viewed as atomic associative memories. Each atom has a key–value interpretation, and its own key determines how relevant it is to the current input. This self-activation removes the need for an explicit mixture-of-experts router. Inference becomes retrieval and recall from an expanding collection of memory atoms.

Experiments on CLIP and language models show significant improvements over state-of-the-art continual-learning methods, including less forgetting, stronger generalization, and a better balance between acquiring knowledge and preserving it. The findings support using finer memory units to organize incremental learning. They also show why freezing old parameters alone may leave important interference and routing problems unresolved.
summary.tldr: MoRAM incrementally adds self-activating rank-one memory experts to improve continual learning while reducing forgetting.

title: Little By Little: Continual Learning via Incremental Mixture of Rank-1 Associative Memory Experts

abstract: Accurate survival prediction in kidney transplantation is critical yet challenging due to the complex interplay between functional biomarkers and patient characteristics under censoring. To address this, we propose a functional censored quantile neural network (FunCQNet), a novel framework that integrates deep neural networks with a censoring-adjusted sequential quantile loss to approximate interaction-dependent coefficient functions. We further introduce a conformal inference approach to rigorously assess the significance of functional-scalar interactions, ensuring interpretability alongside predictive power. Extensive simulations demonstrate that FunCQNet robustly recovers functional effects under varying noise and censoring levels. When applied to kidney transplant data, the model yields precise multi-quantile predictions and reveals clinically significant, age-dependent interaction patterns between donor type and recipient survival.
