paragraphs: Predicting kidney transplant survival requires combining functional biomarkers with patient characteristics while accounting for censoring. Censoring means that the survival outcome is not fully observed for every patient. FunCQNet addresses these issues through a neural network designed to predict multiple quantiles of survival, rather than compressing the prediction into a single value.

The method combines deep networks with a sequential quantile loss adjusted for censoring. It approximates coefficient functions that depend on interactions, allowing functional biomarker effects to vary with patient characteristics. The authors also introduce conformal inference to assess the significance of interactions between functional and scalar variables, connecting predictive modeling with interpretable statistical assessment.

Simulations show that the method robustly recovers functional effects across different noise and censoring levels. Applied to kidney transplant data, it produces precise predictions across multiple quantiles and identifies clinically significant, age-dependent interaction patterns involving donor type and recipient survival. These results demonstrate how the framework can describe variation in predicted survival while exposing interaction patterns relevant to interpreting its predictions.
summary.tldr: FunCQNet models censored kidney transplant survival across multiple quantiles while assessing interactions between functional biomarkers and patient characteristics.

title: FunCQNet: A Functional Censored Quantile Neural Network for Predicting Long-Term Post-Transplant Kidney Survival

abstract: Computational protein design holds immense promise across diverse domains, but existing approaches face significant challenges: traditional physics-based methods require substantial domain expertise, while emerging deep learning methods often rely on restricted functional ontologies, struggle to bridge the semantic gap between text and protein sequences, or lack closed-loop optimization mechanisms. In this paper, we present PDAgent, an LLM-driven autonomous agent framework that enables in silico protein design through template-based directed mutation. Our framework accepts natural language specifications of desired protein properties and employs a ReAct-style reasoning loop comprising five phases: THINK, PLAN, ACT, OBSERVE, and REFLECT. PDAgent integrates template retrieval, conservation-aware mutation strategies, and domain-specific computational tools for property optimization across seven biophysical dimensions. Experiments on 100 diverse protein design tasks demonstrate that PDAgent achieves a 91.86% average constraint satisfaction rate with high structural quality (mean pLDDT 87.69), substantially outperforming both direct LLM generation and specialized deep learning methods. We provide the source code at https://github.com/Gift-OYS/PDAgent.

paragraphs: Computational protein design must connect desired properties to changes in protein sequences. Existing approaches can require substantial expertise, restrict the properties users can express, or lack a feedback loop for improving candidates. PDAgent addresses these issues through an autonomous language-model agent that accepts natural-language specifications and designs proteins through template-based directed mutation.

The framework cycles through thinking, planning, acting, observing, and reflecting. It combines template retrieval, mutation strategies that account for conservation, and specialized computational tools. These components support iterative property optimization across seven biophysical dimensions, allowing the agent to use observations from its actions when deciding what to try next.

The findings support combining language-based goals, existing protein templates, and tool feedback into a closed-loop in silico design process.
summary.tldr: PDAgent turns natural-language protein goals into iterative, tool-assisted template mutations, achieving strong constraint satisfaction in computational design experiments.

title: PDAgent: An LLM-Driven Autonomous Agent Framework Towards *In Silico* Protein Design via Directed Mutation

abstract: Tokenizing music to fit the general framework of language models is a compelling challenge, especially considering the diverse symbolic structures in which music can be represented (e.g., sequences, grids, and graphs). To date, most approaches tokenize symbolic music as sequences of musical events, such as onsets, pitches, time shifts, or compound note events. This strategy is intuitive and has proven effective in Transformer-based models, but it treats the regularity of musical time implicitly: individual tokens may span different durations, resulting in non-uniform time progression. In this paper, we instead consider whether an alternative tokenization is possible, where a uniform-length musical step (e.g., a beat) serves as the basic unit. Specifically, we encode all events within a single time step at the same pitch as one token, and group tokens explicitly by time step, which resembles a sparse encoding of a piano-roll representation. We evaluate the proposed tokenization on music continuation and accompaniment generation tasks, comparing it with mainstream event-based methods. Results show improved musical quality and structural coherence, while additional analyses confirm higher efficiency and more effective capture of long-range patterns with the proposed tokenization.

paragraphs: Music models need a representation that turns notes and timing into tokens. Common approaches encode events such as pitches, note starts, and time shifts. These representations work well with Transformers, but advancing by one token does not correspond to advancing by a fixed amount of musical time. Regular timing is therefore represented only indirectly.

BEAT organizes symbolic music around equal-length time steps, such as beats. Within each step, it combines all events at the same pitch into a token, then explicitly groups tokens by that step. The resulting representation resembles a sparse piano roll: pitch and time remain central, while tokens describe the events occurring at particular positions.

The authors compare this tokenization with mainstream event-based alternatives on music continuation and accompaniment generation. They report better musical quality and structural coherence, alongside analyses showing greater efficiency and stronger capture of long-range patterns. These findings suggest that making regular musical time explicit can help models organize generated music beyond individual note events, connecting the choice of input representation to both computational behavior and musical structure.
summary.tldr: BEAT groups symbolic music into uniform time steps, improving generation quality, structural coherence, and efficiency in the reported evaluations.

title: BEAT: Tokenizing and Generating Symbolic Music by Uniform Temporal Steps

abstract: Reliable reward models (RMs) are critical for ensuring the safe alignment of large language models (LLMs). However, current RM evaluation methods focus solely on preference perception accuracies in given specific scenarios, obscuring the critical vulnerabilities of RMs in real-world scenarios. We identify the true challenge lies in assessing a novel dimension: Suitability, defined as conditional reliability under specific real-world perturbations. To this end, we introduce Reward Auditor, a hypothesis-testing framework specifically designed for RM suitability inference. Rather than answering “How accurate is the RM’s preference perception for given samples?”, it employs scientific auditing to answer: “Can we infer RMs exhibit systematic vulnerabilities in specific real-world scenarios?". Under real-world perturbed scenarios, Reward Auditor quantifies statistical significance and effect size by auditing distribution degradation of RM preference perception confidence. This enables inference of both the certainty and severity of RM vulnerabilities across diverse real-world scenarios, thereby laying a solid foundation for building next-generation LLM alignment systems that are verifiably safe, more robust, and trustworthy.

paragraphs: Reward models help guide language-model alignment by judging preferences, but accuracy on a given sample set can conceal vulnerabilities under changing conditions. Reward Auditor studies suitability: whether a reward model remains conditionally reliable under particular real-world perturbations. The focus is on drawing statistical conclusions about systematic weaknesses in specified scenarios.

The framework uses hypothesis testing to audit degradation in the distribution of preference-confidence scores. It quantifies both statistical significance and effect size. These serve different purposes: significance addresses the strength of evidence for a vulnerability, while effect size describes the magnitude of the observed degradation.

This makes an audit more informative than a single preference-accuracy score. It can distinguish the evidence for a problem from how severe that problem is, while tying the conclusion to the perturbation being examined. The paper presents this framework as groundwork for safer and more robust alignment systems. Its concrete contribution is a way to assess scenario-dependent reward-model reliability, supplying evidence that can inform whether a model is suitable for a particular setting.
summary.tldr: Reward Auditor tests reward-model reliability under specific perturbations, quantifying both evidence for vulnerabilities and their severity.

title: Reward Auditor: Inference on Reward Modeling Suitability in Real-World Perturbed Scenarios

abstract: Navigation in complex environments relies on internal spatial representations that guide action. While the brain employs a diverse repertoire of spatial tuning cells—including grid, place, and head-direction cells—a normative theory linking these static neural codes to the dynamic process of navigation remains elusive. In this work, we propose a Unified Laplacian Framework derived from first principles of representational smoothness and efficiency. We first demonstrate that diverse spatial codes emerge naturally as spectral decompositions of the Laplace operator. Crucially, bridging the gap from representation to action, we derive a computational-level navigation policy based on the Green’s function potential. We show that this potential encodes the environment’s intrinsic geometry to enable geometry-aware gradient ascent, achieving improved sample efficiency and generalization in goal-reaching tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these spectral representations can be learned directly from high-dimensional visual inputs, supporting their learnability from sensory experience. Our results suggest that the “cognitive map" can be viewed as a spectral embedding of the Laplacian, providing a normative computational account that is biologically consistent with observed spatial-code phenomenology and useful for artificial agents.

paragraphs: Spatial representations are useful for navigation only if they can guide movement. This paper develops a mathematical framework connecting patterns resembling the brain’s spatial codes with a policy for reaching goals. It starts from principles of representational smoothness and efficiency, seeking a shared explanation for both representing an environment and acting within it.

The authors show how diverse spatial codes arise from spectral decompositions of the Laplace operator. They then derive a navigation policy using a Green’s function potential. This potential reflects the environment’s intrinsic geometry, allowing an agent to follow its gradient in a way that takes the shape of the environment into account.

title: From Representation to Action: A Unified Laplacian Framework for Spatial Representation and Path Planning

abstract: In the past decade, considerable research effort has been devoted to securing machine learning (ML) models that operate in adversarial settings. Yet, progress has been slow even for simple "toy" problems (e.g., robustness to small adversarial perturbations) and is often hindered by non-rigorous evaluations. Today, adversarial ML research has shifted towards studying larger, general-purpose language models. In this position paper, we argue that the situation is now even worse: in the era of LLMs, the field of adversarial ML studies problems that are (1) less clearly defined, (2) harder to solve, and (3) even more challenging to evaluate. As a result, we caution that yet another decade of work on adversarial ML may be failing to produce meaningful progress.

Today, adversarial ML research has shifted towards studying larger, general-purpose language models. In this position paper, we argue that the situation is now even worse: in the era of LLMs, the field of adversarial ML studies problems that are (1) less clearly defined, (2) harder to solve, and (3) even more challenging to evaluate. paragraphs: This position paper questions whether adversarial machine learning is producing meaningful progress as attention shifts toward large language models. The authors begin with an assessment of earlier work: even relatively simple robustness problems, such as handling small adversarial changes to inputs, have advanced slowly. They identify insufficiently rigorous evaluation as a recurring obstacle to judging whether systems have actually become more secure.

The move to general-purpose language models, they argue, makes the research problem more difficult along three dimensions. The problems being studied are less precisely defined, solutions are harder to obtain, and evaluations are harder to conduct convincingly. These concerns connect problem formulation to evidence: progress is difficult to establish when the target itself is unclear and assessments cannot reliably demonstrate improvement.

The paper’s contribution is a critique of the field’s direction and its ability to substantiate progress. Its warning is qualified: another decade of effort may fail to deliver meaningful advances. The abstract does not establish that every individual result is worthless; it challenges whether the overall research trajectory supports confidence in improved adversarial security.
summary.tldr: The authors warn that poorly defined problems and weak evaluations may prevent LLM adversarial research from delivering meaningful security progress.

abstract: In real-world machine learning problems, it is very common that part of the input feature vector is incomplete: either not available, missing, or corrupted. In this paper, we present a boosting approach that integrates features with incomplete information and those with complete information to form a strong classifier. By introducing hidden variables to model missing information, we form loss functions that combine fully labeled data with partially labeled data to effectively learn normalized and unnormalized models. The primal problems of the proposed optimization problems with these loss functions are provided to show their close relationships and the motivations behind them. We use auxiliary functions to bound the change of the loss functions and derive explicit parameter update rules for the learning algorithms. We demonstrate encouraging results on two real-world problems - visual object recognition in computer vision and named entity recognition in natural language processing - to show the effectiveness of the proposed boosting approach.

paragraphs: A learning system often receives examples whose features are unavailable, missing, or corrupted. This paper develops a boosting approach that combines those incomplete features with fully observed features to construct a strong classifier. The central idea is to represent missing information explicitly within learning, so incomplete observations can participate in the model's training objective.

The authors introduce hidden variables for the unobserved information and construct loss functions that bring together fully labeled and partially labeled data. Their treatment covers both normalized and unnormalized models. They also give the primal optimization problems associated with these losses, explaining the relationships among the formulations and the reasons for choosing them.

To obtain learning procedures, the paper uses auxiliary functions that bound changes in the losses and yield explicit parameter updates. Experiments apply the approach to visual object recognition and named entity recognition. The authors describe the results as encouraging, supporting the usefulness of the framework in those two application areas without establishing a universal advantage for every pattern of incomplete information.
summary.tldr: A boosting framework models missing information with hidden variables and combines complete and incomplete observations in its learning objectives.

title: Boosting with incomplete information

abstract: Similarity measures in many real applications generate indefinite similarity matrices. In this paper, we consider the problem of classification based on such indefinite similarities. These indefinite kernels cannot be used in standard kernel-based algorithms as the optimization problems become non-convex. In order to adapt kernel methods for similarity-based learning, we introduce a method that aims to simultaneously find a reproducing kernel Hilbert space based on the given similarities and train a classifier with good generalization in that space. The method is formulated as a convex optimization problem. We propose a simplified version, that can reduce overfitting and whose associated convex conic program can be solved in a very efficient way due to its special structure. We compare the proposed methods with five other methods on a collection of real data sets.

paragraphs: Practical similarity measures do not always produce matrices suitable for standard kernel methods. In particular, an indefinite similarity matrix can make the associated optimization nonconvex. This paper studies how to classify data using such similarities while recovering a formulation that supports convex optimization.

The proposed method jointly seeks a reproducing kernel Hilbert space based on the supplied similarities and a classifier intended to generalize well within that space. The representation and prediction problem are therefore addressed together. The authors formulate this joint task as a convex optimization problem, providing a route from indefinite similarities to kernel-based classification.

They also develop a simplified version that can reduce overfitting. Its optimization is a convex conic program whose special structure allows very efficient solution. The paper compares the proposed methods with five alternatives on real datasets. The abstract specifies that comparison without claiming a particular ranking of results. The main contribution is the joint convex formulation and its simpler variant, which make otherwise problematic similarity information usable for learning.
summary.tldr: A convex formulation jointly learns a valid kernel space and classifier from indefinite similarities, with an efficient simplified variant.

title: Learning kernels from indefinite similarities

abstract: Transfer learning can be described as the distillation of abstract knowledge from one learning domain or task and the reuse of that knowledge in a related domain or task. In categorization settings, transfer learning is the modification by past experience of prior expectations about what types of categories are likely to exist in the world. While transfer learning is an important and active research topic in machine learning, there have been few studies of transfer learning in human categorization. We propose an explanation for transfer learning effects in human categorization, implementing a model from the statistical machine learning literature -- the hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) -- to make empirical evaluations of its ability to explain these effects. We present two laboratory experiments which measure the degree to which people engage in transfer learning in a controlled setting, and we compare our model to their performance. We find that the HDP provides a good explanation for transfer learning exhibited by human learners.

paragraphs: Past learning can shape how people approach a new categorization task. In this paper, transfer means that experience changes prior expectations about which kinds of categories are likely to exist. The research question is whether a statistical learning model can explain this reuse of abstract knowledge across related human learning tasks.

The authors propose the hierarchical Dirichlet process, or HDP, as a model of these transfer effects. They bring a model from machine learning into an empirical study of human categorization. The goal is to compare the model's account of experience-dependent expectations with the transfer behavior that people actually exhibit in controlled settings.

Two laboratory experiments measure the degree of transfer in human learners, and the authors compare the HDP model with participants' performance. They find that it provides a good explanation of the observed transfer. The result supports the HDP as an account of these experimental effects, connecting a statistical model of shared learning with changes in human category expectations.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Dirichlet process model explains transfer effects observed in two laboratory experiments on human categorization.

title: Modeling Transfer Learning in Human Categorization with the Hierarchical Dirichlet Process

abstract: This paper introduces a novel multiagent learning algorithm, Convergence with Model Learning and Safety (or CMLeS in short), which achieves convergence, targeted optimality against memory-bounded adversaries, and safety, in arbitrary repeated games. The most novel aspect of CMLeS is the manner in which it guarantees(in a PAC sense) targeted optimality against memory-bounded adversaries, via efficient exploration and exploitation. CMLeS is fully implemented and we present empirical results demonstrating its effectiveness.

The most novel aspect of CMLeS is the manner in which it guarantees(in a PAC sense) targeted optimality against memory-bounded adversaries, via efficient exploration and exploitation. paragraphs: Learning in a repeated game requires an agent to adapt while other participants also influence its results. This paper introduces Convergence with Model Learning and Safety, abbreviated CMLeS, to address several goals together. The algorithm achieves convergence, safety, and targeted optimality against opponents whose behavior depends on a bounded amount of memory.

The main technical contribution concerns that targeted optimality guarantee. CMLeS combines efficient exploration with exploitation, connecting the process of learning about opponents to the process of using that knowledge. The guarantee is expressed in a probably approximately correct, or PAC, sense. It therefore has a probabilistic and approximate form, with memory-bounded adversaries defining the stated target class.

The paper places these results in arbitrary repeated games and also presents a full implementation with empirical evidence of effectiveness. The contribution is the combination of the three learning objectives within one algorithm. Its targeted optimality result specifically retains the memory restriction on adversaries, while the experiments provide evidence about the implemented method's behavior.
summary.tldr: CMLeS combines convergence and safety with PAC-style targeted optimality against memory-bounded adversaries in repeated games.

title: Convergence, Targeted Optimality, and Safety in Multiagent Learning

abstract: A standard assumption in machine learning is the exchangeability of data; in other words, the examples are assumed to be generated from the same probability distribution independently. This paper is devoted to testing the assumption of exchangeability on-line: the examples arrive one by one, and after receiving each example we would like to have a valid measure of the degree to which the assumption of exchangeability has been falsified. Such measure are provided by exchangeability martingales. We extend known techniques for constructing exchangeability martingales and show that our new method is competitive to martingales introduced before. Finally we investigate the performance of our testing method on two benchmark datasets, USPS and Statlog Satellite data; for the former, the known techniques give satisfactory results, but for the latter our new more flexible method becomes necessary.

paragraphs: Learning methods often rely on assumptions about how examples are generated. This paper studies online testing of exchangeability, seeking a valid measure of evidence against that assumption after each new example arrives. The objective is to monitor the accumulating data rather than wait until a complete dataset has been collected.

Exchangeability martingales provide the measures used for this sequential assessment. The authors extend existing techniques for constructing them and introduce a more flexible method. The contribution concerns how to build an evolving measure of incompatibility with the assumption, keeping the testing process aligned with the arrival of individual observations.

Experiments compare the approach with earlier martingale constructions on USPS and Statlog Satellite data. Existing techniques give satisfactory results on USPS, while the authors report that the new flexibility becomes necessary for the Satellite dataset. The findings therefore distinguish between settings where established constructions suffice and one where the proposed extension is needed. Overall, the method is reported to be competitive with previous martingales.
summary.tldr: A more flexible martingale construction tests exchangeability as observations arrive and addresses a benchmark where earlier techniques were insufficient.

title: Plug-in martingales for testing exchangeability on-line
